note: Written by scripts/generate-hy.mjs: two questions a high-yield topic (data/mcq/high-yield-topics.json), each kept only when an independent examiner answered it blind to the same key. Kind ai.

items.topic: Occupational lung disease: silicosis from engineered stone (banned in Australia from July 2024), asbestosis and mesothelioma
items.stem: A stonemason cutting engineered stone inhales fine dust. Which inhaled agent, found in very high concentration in engineered stone, drives the pulmonary fibrosis of silicosis?
items.why: Engineered stone contains over 90% crystalline silica. Ingested by alveolar macrophages, it causes inflammasome activation and nodular fibrosis.
notes: Asbestos causes asbestosis, pleural plaques and mesothelioma, not silicosis.
Coal dust causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis, not typical engineered stone disease.
Beryllium causes chronic beryllium disease, a granulomatous condition.

items.topic: Parkinson's disease: clinical diagnosis, levodopa, drug-induced parkinsonism
items.stem: A 72-year-old woman on regular prochlorperazine for nausea develops symmetrical bradykinesia, rigidity and a tremor over 3 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Dopamine antagonists (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, antipsychotics) cause subacute, usually symmetrical parkinsonism. Stop the drug where possible; it generally resolves over weeks to months.
notes: Idiopathic PD typically starts asymmetrically and develops insidiously.
PSP features vertical gaze palsy and early falls, not a subacute drug-linked onset.
Essential tremor lacks bradykinesia and rigidity.

items.topic: Breast lump: triple assessment, breast cancer referral, BreastScreen Australia
items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a new 2 cm firm, irregular breast lump. Which combination makes up the standard triple assessment?
options: Mammogram, ultrasound and fine-needle cytology only
items.why: Triple assessment is clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound ± mammography) and core needle biopsy for histology. Concordance of all three gives high diagnostic accuracy.
notes: MRI and tumour markers are not part of standard triple assessment.
Two imaging tests are not three modalities, and core biopsy is preferred over cytology.
History and genetics do not replace examination and tissue sampling.

items.topic: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: weight-based IM adrenaline, ASCIA action plans, early allergen introduction
items.stem: A child with peanut allergy develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension minutes after exposure. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?
options: Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, causing mediator release
Immune complex deposition activating complement in vessels
Allergen-specific T-cell mediated delayed cytokine release
Cytotoxic IgG binding to cell-surface antigens
items.why: Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity: allergen cross-links IgE bound to mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine, tryptase and other mediators within minutes.
notes: Describes type III hypersensitivity (e.g. serum sickness), which occurs days later.
Describes type IV hypersensitivity, which is delayed by 48-72 hours.
Describes type II hypersensitivity, such as haemolytic transfusion reactions.

items.topic: Strongyloides, scabies and skin sores in remote communities: ivermectin, impetigo and APSGN/ARF links
items.stem: A 6-year-old in a remote community has weeping crusted sores on the legs and itchy burrows between the fingers. Several household members are itchy. Which treatment best addresses the underlying cause and household spread?
options: Permethrin 5% cream or oral ivermectin for the child and contacts
Oral flucloxacillin for the child only
Oral albendazole single dose to the household
items.why: Scabies drives secondary impetigo in remote communities, so treat scabies for the whole household (permethrin or ivermectin) and treat sores as needed. Treating infection without controlling scabies leads to recurrence.
notes: Treating only the child ignores household transmission and the scabies source.
Steroids may worsen infected sores and do not treat scabies.
Albendazole treats intestinal helminths, not scabies mites.

items.topic: Rhabdomyolysis: CK, myoglobinuria, fluids, hyperkalaemia
items.stem: A 28-year-old man is found down after a 12-hour collapse. CK is 48,000 U/L, urine is dark with blood on dipstick but no red cells, K+ is 6.9 mmol/L with peaked T waves. After IV calcium gluconate, what is the next best step?
options: Insulin with glucose, and aggressive IV 0.9% sodium chloride
items.why: Calcium stabilises the myocardium, then insulin/glucose shifts potassium into cells while aggressive isotonic crystalloid protects the kidneys. Dialysis is needed if refractory.
notes: Fluid restriction would worsen kidney injury; diuretics are not first-line without volume repletion.
Bicarbonate alone is not proven and does not rapidly treat hyperkalaemia as insulin does.
Resonium is slow and inadequate for life-threatening hyperkalaemia.

items.topic: Inherited bleeding disorders: haemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, preoperative assessment
items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has menorrhagia and easy bruising. Her father has similar problems. Platelets normal, APTT mildly prolonged, PT normal. Which test pattern best supports von Willebrand disease type 1?
options: Low vWF antigen and low vWF activity with proportionate reduction
Normal vWF levels and low factor IX
Low platelet count with large platelets
Prolonged thrombin time with low fibrinogen
items.why: Type 1 vWD is a partial quantitative deficiency: vWF antigen and activity (ristocetin cofactor) are reduced proportionately, often with low factor VIII. Inheritance is autosomal dominant.
notes: Low factor IX is haemophilia B, X-linked, rare in women.
Large platelets with thrombocytopenia suggest Bernard-Soulier or MYH9 disorders.
Prolonged thrombin time with low fibrinogen suggests dysfibrinogenaemia or DIC.

items.topic: Phaeochromocytoma: paroxysmal symptoms, plasma metanephrines, alpha-blockade before surgery
items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has episodes of headache, sweating, palpitations and severe hypertension. Which is the best initial biochemical test for phaeochromocytoma?
items.why: Plasma free metanephrines (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines) are the most sensitive initial tests; imaging follows biochemical confirmation.
notes: That screens for primary aldosteronism.
That screens for Cushing syndrome.
That tests for carcinoid syndrome.

items.topic: Snakebite: pressure immobilisation bandage, coagulopathy testing (20-minute whole blood clotting test), antivenom indications
items.stem: A 30-year-old bushwalker was bitten on the calf by an unidentified snake 1 hour ago, and a pressure immobilisation bandage is on. He has vomiting and headache. The 20-minute whole blood clotting test shows no clot. What is the best next step?
options: Remove the bandage and observe for 6 hours
items.why: Systemic symptoms plus venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (no clot at 20 minutes) indicate significant envenomation and need antivenom. Factor replacement is not first-line.
notes: Observation alone is inappropriate with confirmed coagulopathy and symptoms; the bandage stays until antivenom is ready.
FFP does not neutralise venom and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding after antivenom.
Tranexamic acid does not treat venom-induced consumption coagulopathy; antivenom does.

items.topic: Interstitial lung disease: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, drug-induced (amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin)
items.stem: A 70-year-old man has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnoea and dry cough. He has finger clubbing and bibasal fine inspiratory crackles. HRCT shows subpleural basal honeycombing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Older patient with clubbing, crackles and basal subpleural honeycombing (UIP pattern) on HRCT is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Antifibrotics such as nintedanib or pirfenidone slow decline.
notes: Typically upper or mid-zone, centrilobular nodules and ground glass with exposure history.
Sarcoid favours hilar nodes and upper-zone perilymphatic disease.
Heart failure gives effusions and septal lines, not honeycombing.

items.topic: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: weight-based IM adrenaline, ASCIA action plans, early allergen introduction
items.stem: A 4-year-old girl (16 kg) develops urticaria, stridor and pallor after eating a cashew nut. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Adrenaline 0.16 mg (1 mg/mL) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh
items.why: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh is first line for anaphylaxis; a 16 kg child gets 0.16 mg (or a 0.15 mg autoinjector). Repeat every 5 minutes if needed.
notes: Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise and must not delay adrenaline.
Salbutamol does not treat upper airway obstruction or shock; adrenaline comes first.
IV bolus adrenaline risks arrhythmia; reserved for specialist-monitored settings, with IM first line.

items.topic: Dysphagia: oesophageal cancer, Barrett's oesophagus, achalasia, endoscopy first
items.stem: What is the underlying pathology of primary achalasia?
options: Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons, causing failed LOS relaxation and absent peristalsis
Hypertrophy of the upper oesophageal sphincter
Metaplasia of squamous to columnar epithelium
items.why: Degeneration of inhibitory (NO/VIP) neurons in the myenteric plexus leaves the LOS hypertensive with incomplete relaxation and aperistalsis, causing dysphagia to solids and liquids.
notes: This does not describe achalasia, which affects the lower sphincter and body.
This describes Barrett's oesophagus.
This describes Zenker's diverticulum.

items.topic: Prescribing in older adults: polypharmacy, deprescribing, anticholinergic burden, drugs that cause falls
items.stem: An 82-year-old is prescribed a drug that is mainly renally cleared and has a narrow therapeutic index. Which age-related change most explains the increased risk of toxicity at usual doses?
items.why: GFR falls with age, often with a normal serum creatinine because muscle mass is also reduced. Renally cleared drugs such as digoxin and lithium accumulate.
notes: First-pass metabolism and hepatic blood flow decrease with age, not increase.
Gastric acid secretion tends to fall with age and has little effect on this problem.
Albumin tends to fall with age, raising free levels of highly bound drugs; it does not increase.

items.topic: Pulmonary embolism: Wells and PERC, CTPA vs V/Q (pregnancy, renal impairment), anticoagulation, thrombolysis for massive PE
items.stem: A patient with a large pulmonary embolism is hypoxaemic. Which mechanism is the main cause of the hypoxaemia?
options: Diffusion impairment across a thickened membrane
Anatomical right-to-left shunt through alveolar collapse
items.why: Obstructed pulmonary arteries leave ventilated alveoli unperfused (dead space), and blood diverted to other regions is relatively under-ventilated, producing V/Q mismatch. PaCO2 is often low from hyperventilation.
notes: Diffusion across the membrane is normal in PE; the problem is blood flow, not membrane thickness.
Alveolar collapse shunt is typical of ARDS or atelectasis, not the primary mechanism in PE.
Patients with PE usually hyperventilate, with low or normal PaCO2, not hypoventilate.

items.topic: Prostate: BPH, PSA testing with shared decision-making, prostate cancer
items.stem: A 68-year-old man has hesitancy, weak stream and nocturia. Benign prostatic hyperplasia causes these symptoms mainly by enlargement of which zone of the prostate?
items.why: BPH arises in the transition zone surrounding the urethra, so it compresses the prostatic urethra. Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone.
notes: The peripheral zone is where most cancers arise and is palpable on DRE; it is not the main site of BPH.
The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is rarely the site of hyperplasia or cancer.
The anterior fibromuscular stroma has no glandular tissue so is not the site of BPH.

items.topic: Australian zoonoses: Q fever, leptospirosis, brucellosis, psittacosis, occupational exposure
items.stem: A 45-year-old abattoir worker has had 3 weeks of fever, sweats and headache. ALT is raised, CRP is high and chest X-ray is clear. Q fever serology is positive for acute infection. Echocardiography is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.why: Acute Q fever without valvular disease is treated with doxycycline for 14 days. Doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for 18 months is for Q fever endocarditis or chronic disease.
notes: Coxiella is an intracellular organism and beta-lactams are ineffective.
A single dose is inadequate for systemic infection.
This long regimen is for chronic Q fever or endocarditis, which is not present here.

items.topic: Burns: TBSA estimation, fluid resuscitation, ANZBA referral criteria, airway burns
items.stem: Which of these adults with a burn meets ANZBA criteria for referral to a burn centre?
options: 5% TBSA superficial sunburn to the back
8% TBSA partial-thickness scald to the thigh
3% TBSA partial-thickness burn to the hand
items.why: ANZBA referral criteria include burns involving the hands, face, feet, genitalia, perineum or major joints, regardless of size (partial thickness or deeper), and >10% TBSA in adults.
notes: Superficial burns are not counted, and 5% is below threshold.
8% partial-thickness to the thigh is below the 10% adult threshold.
Superficial 1% burn does not meet criteria.

items.topic: Common GP presentations: fatigue, low back pain red flags, skin checks and sun protection, PSA shared decision-making
items.stem: A 55-year-old asymptomatic man asks about PSA testing. He has no family history. After discussing benefits and harms, he chooses testing and the PSA is 2.0 ng/mL. What is the most appropriate recommendation under current Australian guidelines?
items.why: Australian guidelines (2025) advise men 50–69 who choose testing to have PSA every 2 years; a PSA under 3.0 ng/mL is repeated in 2 years. Higher results prompt further assessment, usually MRI.
notes: Referral is for PSA 3.0 ng/mL or above, or an abnormal exam.
Biopsy isn't done on a low PSA, and MRI usually precedes it.
Three-monthly testing isn't needed and increases overdiagnosis.

items.topic: Ovarian masses: torsion, cyst rupture, ovarian cancer (CA-125, risk of malignancy)
items.stem: Ovarian torsion twists the vascular pedicle and cuts off blood flow to the ovary. Which peritoneal fold carries the ovarian artery and vein to the ovary?
items.why: The suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament carries the ovarian vessels, nerves and lymphatics from the pelvic brim. Twisting of this pedicle causes venous then arterial occlusion.
notes: The round ligament runs from the uterine fundus to the labium majus and carries no ovarian vessels.
The ovarian ligament joins ovary to uterus and holds only small anastomotic branches, not the main ovarian supply.
The cardinal ligament supports the cervix and carries uterine vessels, not ovarian vessels.

items.topic: Opioids and analgesia: dose conversion, constipation, naloxone, Schedule 8 rules and real-time prescription monitoring
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with cancer pain takes modified-release oral morphine 60 mg twice daily. Her GP wishes to switch to oral oxycodone. Using standard equianalgesic ratios (oral morphine:oxycodone 3:2), what total daily oxycodone dose is approximately equivalent?
items.why: Total morphine is 120 mg/day; dividing by 1.5 gives about 80 mg oxycodone per day. Dose reduction for incomplete cross-tolerance is often applied, so titrate to response.
notes: 40 mg would be a 3:1 conversion, which underestimates the equivalent dose.
60 mg treats the single morphine dose as the daily total, or uses a 2:1 ratio.
120 mg ignores the conversion and gives the morphine dose, risking overdose.

items.topic: Hyperthyroidism: Graves vs toxic nodule vs thyroiditis, thyroid storm, carbimazole agranulocytosis
items.stem: What is the underlying mechanism of Graves disease?
options: Destruction of follicles releasing stored hormone
items.why: Graves disease is caused by TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies, producing diffuse goitre, hyperthyroidism, orbitopathy and diffuse increased uptake on scintigraphy.
notes: Describes toxic adenoma, which gives focal uptake.
Describes thyroiditis, with low uptake and transient thyrotoxicosis.
Rare TSHoma gives high TSH, unlike Graves where TSH is suppressed.

items.topic: Cardiovascular drugs: ACEi/ARB hyperkalaemia and the triple whammy, beta-blockers, digoxin and amiodarone toxicity
items.stem: Which action of digoxin on the cardiac myocyte underlies both its positive inotropy and its toxicity?
options: Inhibition of the Na-K-ATPase pump, raising intracellular calcium
items.why: Digoxin inhibits Na-K-ATPase, raising intracellular sodium, reducing calcium extrusion via the Na-Ca exchanger and increasing contractility. Hypokalaemia increases toxicity.
notes: That is the action of verapamil and diltiazem.
That is the action of beta-blockers.
Potassium channel opening is not digoxin's mechanism.

items.topic: Community-acquired pneumonia: severity scoring (SMART-COP/CORB), eTG empirical antibiotics, atypical cover
items.stem: Why are beta-lactam antibiotics alone inadequate for Legionella or Mycoplasma pneumonia?
options: They are intracellular or lack a cell wall
They are too rapidly renally cleared
items.why: Legionella is intracellular and Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so atypical cover needs macrolides, doxycycline or fluoroquinolones.
notes: Renal clearance is not the reason for ineffectiveness.
Beta-lactams penetrate lung adequately for typical pathogens.
Exotoxin production is not what makes these organisms resistant.

items.topic: Haemochromatosis: HFE C282Y, ferritin and transferrin saturation, venesection
items.stem: A 45-year-old man has fatigue and arthralgia of the second and third MCP joints. Ferritin is 1200 µg/L and transferrin saturation 80%. What is the next test?
items.why: Raised ferritin with transferrin saturation above 45% suggests haemochromatosis; HFE genotyping (C282Y homozygosity) confirms it.
notes: Bone marrow biopsy is not needed for diagnosis.
Caeruloplasmin is for Wilson disease.
Hepatitis A is unrelated to iron overload.

items.topic: Pneumothorax: primary vs secondary, tension physiology, observe vs aspirate vs drain
items.stem: A 22-year-old tall, thin man has 1 day of right pleuritic chest pain. Obs: RR 16, SpO2 98% on air, HR 76, BP 120/75. CXR shows a 1.5 cm apical rim, no effusion. No prior lung disease. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observation with outpatient review and analgesia
items.why: A small, minimally symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a stable patient can be observed with analgesia and early review. Aspirate or drain if breathless or large.
notes: Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise.
Drainage is not needed for a small, stable primary pneumothorax.
Pleurodesis is for recurrence prevention, not a first episode.

items.topic: Tuberculosis screening: latent TB before biologics, active TB in migrants
items.stem: A 40-year-old woman born in India is to start adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis. Her chest X-ray is normal and she has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate screening test for latent TB?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay (or tuberculin skin test)
items.why: Before biologics, screen for latent TB with an IGRA or TST plus chest X-ray. Treat latent TB first if positive, after excluding active disease.
notes: Gram stain is not used; active TB would need acid-fast stain and culture.
Serological TB antibody tests are not recommended and are unreliable.
Delaying and relying on imaging alone will miss latent infection.

items.topic: Antibiotics: eTG empirical choices, gentamicin dosing and monitoring, penicillin allergy
items.stem: Which feature of gentamicin pharmacology underlies once-daily dosing with level monitoring?
options: Concentration-dependent killing with a post-antibiotic effect
Bacteriostatic action by binding the 50S subunit
items.why: Aminoglycosides kill in a concentration-dependent manner with a post-antibiotic effect, so high peaks with a low trough limit toxicity. Trough levels guide nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity risk.
notes: Time-dependent killing describes beta-lactams, not aminoglycosides.
Gentamicin is renally excreted unchanged, not hepatically metabolised.
Gentamicin binds the 30S subunit and is bactericidal.

items.topic: Hypothyroidism: TFT interpretation, levothyroxine dosing, subclinical disease, pregnancy
items.stem: A woman with treated hypothyroidism on levothyroxine confirms a pregnancy at 5 weeks. TSH is 3.5 mIU/L. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Increase levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 4 weeks
Continue the same dose and recheck after delivery
items.why: Levothyroxine requirements rise in early pregnancy (often 25–30%). Increase the dose promptly and monitor TSH every 4 weeks, aiming for the lower pregnancy-specific range (about under 2.5–4 mIU/L).
notes: Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks miscarriage and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
Stopping risks fetal harm; the fetus depends on maternal T4 in the first trimester.
Combination T3 therapy is not recommended.

items.topic: Acute appendicitis: clinical scores, imaging in children and in pregnancy
items.stem: A 19-year-old has appendicitis. Early in the illness she feels dull central abdominal pain, which later moves to the right iliac fossa. What best explains the later localised pain?
options: Referred pain from the lumbar spine
Inflamed appendix irritating the parietal peritoneum
Distension of the caecum causing midgut pain
Mesenteric ischaemia of the terminal ileum
items.why: Early visceral pain from the midgut-derived appendix is poorly localised (periumbilical, T10). Once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, somatic pain localises to the right iliac fossa.
notes: Not a spinal referred pain; the shift reflects peritoneal involvement.
Caecal distension is not the mechanism of localisation in appendicitis.
Ischaemia of the terminal ileum is not the cause of the shift.

items.topic: Iron deficiency anaemia: ferritin interpretation, oral vs IV iron, finding the cause
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has heavy periods and fatigue. Hb is 98 g/L, MCV 71 fL, ferritin 6 microgram/L. She has taken oral iron before without GI intolerance. What is the best initial management?
options: Oral iron on alternate days or daily, and treat the menorrhagia
Intravenous iron as first-line for all
items.why: Oral iron is first-line for uncomplicated iron deficiency when tolerated; alternate-day dosing improves absorption. Also address the cause (menorrhagia) and recheck Hb in 2–4 weeks.
notes: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic instability or severe symptomatic anaemia; she is stable with Hb 98.
IV iron is for intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing losses exceeding oral replacement or need for rapid repletion, not routine first-line.
B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis; her picture is microcytic with very low ferritin.

items.topic: Obstructive sleep apnoea: screening tools, CPAP, commercial and private driver fitness
items.stem: What is the main mechanism of airway obstruction in obstructive sleep apnoea?
options: Loss of pharyngeal dilator muscle tone during sleep causing upper airway collapse
Absent central respiratory drive to the diaphragm
Bronchospasm of the small airways during REM sleep
items.why: In sleep, pharyngeal dilator tone falls and a narrowed, fatty or crowded airway collapses despite ongoing respiratory effort.
notes: Absent effort with no drive describes central sleep apnoea, not OSA.
Bronchospasm is lower airway disease, not the mechanism of OSA.
Reflux can aggravate symptoms but is not the mechanism of OSA.

items.topic: Pituitary disease: prolactinoma, acromegaly, hypopituitarism, bitemporal hemianopia
items.stem: A 46-year-old man has enlarging hands and jaw, new sweating and carpal tunnel symptoms. Fasting IGF-1 is markedly raised. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
options: Failure of GH suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
items.why: Acromegaly is confirmed by GH failing to suppress (nadir above about 1 mcg/L) after 75 g oral glucose, with raised IGF-1. Random GH is pulsatile and unreliable.
notes: Random GH is pulsatile and cannot confirm or exclude acromegaly.
This tests for Cushing syndrome.
This tests for GH or ACTH deficiency, the opposite problem.

items.topic: Acute stroke: FAST, CT and CT perfusion, thrombolysis and endovascular clot retrieval eligibility
items.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents 9 hours after waking with left hemiparesis and gaze deviation. CT shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography shows right proximal middle cerebral artery occlusion; CT perfusion shows a small core with a large penumbra. What is the best management?
options: Intravenous thrombolysis only, as within 24 hours
Endovascular clot retrieval, as perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue
Antiplatelet therapy alone as the window has passed
Conservative care, as thrombectomy is limited to 6 hours
items.why: Extended-window ECR (up to 24 hours) is indicated for large vessel occlusion with a favourable core-penumbra mismatch on perfusion imaging.
notes: Thrombolysis is not a standard option at 9 hours, and does not replace retrieval for proximal LVO.
Antiplatelet alone would miss a treatable large vessel occlusion with salvageable brain.
The 6-hour limit has been extended to 24 hours with perfusion imaging selection.

items.topic: Medication safety and the law: Poisons Standard schedules (S2, S3, S4, S8), PBS authority, medication errors
items.stem: A GP discovers they prescribed 10 times the intended dose of a drug to a patient, who has taken one dose and is well. After ensuring patient safety, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Open disclosure to the patient and report via the incident system
Alter the medical record to show the intended dose
Wait to see whether harm occurs before telling the patient
Report only to the pharmacist who dispensed it
items.why: After a medication error, ensure safety, then use open disclosure (explain, apologise) and report the incident for learning. Records must never be altered.
notes: Altering records is dishonest and unprofessional; add a clear, dated entry instead.
Open disclosure is required even without harm and should be prompt.
The pharmacist may help but does not replace disclosure to the patient and incident reporting.

items.topic: Cardiovascular drugs: ACEi/ARB hyperkalaemia and the triple whammy, beta-blockers, digoxin and amiodarone toxicity
items.stem: Why does an ACE inhibitor cause hyperkalaemia, particularly in a patient with reduced renal function?
options: Lower angiotensin II reduces aldosterone, decreasing distal potassium secretion
It directly blocks the Na-K-ATPase pump in muscle
It inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop of Henle
It increases proximal potassium reabsorption through bradykinin
items.why: Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, so less potassium secretion in the collecting duct. Reduced GFR further limits potassium excretion.
notes: ACE inhibitors do not block the Na-K-ATPase; digoxin does.
That is loop diuretic action, which causes hypokalaemia.
Bradykinin accumulation causes cough and angioedema, not hyperkalaemia.

items.topic: Orthopaedic emergencies: hip fracture and orthogeriatric care, compartment syndrome, open fractures, septic arthritis
items.stem: A 35-year-old man arrives with an open tibial fracture with a 3 cm contaminated wound. Tetanus status is unknown. Alongside wound cover and splinting, what is the most important early drug management?
options: Intravenous flucloxacillin only after culture results
Intravenous cefazolin within 1 hour plus tetanus prophylaxis
Topical antibiotics and review in 48 hours
items.why: Open fractures need IV antibiotics (such as cefazolin) as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour, plus tetanus toxoid and immunoglobulin if status unknown and wound contaminated.
notes: Oral therapy is inadequate for initial open fracture cover.
Waiting for cultures delays the time-critical dose.
Topical agents do not replace systemic antibiotics and delay is harmful.

items.topic: Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending weakness, FVC monitoring, IVIG
items.stem: In classic acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barré), which structure is the main target of the immune attack?
items.why: AIDP is an immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves and roots, often after Campylobacter or viral infection, causing slowed conduction and areflexia.
notes: Receptor antibodies at the NMJ cause myasthenia gravis.
Anterior horn cell loss occurs in poliomyelitis and motor neurone disease.
Central myelin is targeted in multiple sclerosis.

items.topic: Perinatal mental health: postnatal depression (EPDS), puerperal psychosis, drugs in breastfeeding
items.stem: A primiparous woman, 5 days postpartum, is confused, euphoric, and sleepless, with delusions that her baby is special and hears voices. She has no insight. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent psychiatric admission, ideally mother-baby unit, with antipsychotic
Sertraline and review in two weeks
items.why: Rapid onset psychosis in the first weeks postpartum suggests puerperal psychosis, a psychiatric emergency with risks of suicide and infanticide. It needs admission, ideally to a mother-baby unit, and antipsychotic or mood stabiliser treatment.
notes: An antidepressant alone is inadequate for psychosis and may worsen possible bipolar illness.
Blues is mild, transient, and does not involve psychosis.
Psychotherapy alone is inappropriate for acute psychosis without insight and with risk to mother and baby.

items.topic: Sarcoidosis: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, hypercalcaemia, steroid indications
items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has tender red shins, ankle arthralgia and fever. Chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lungs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and arthralgia define Löfgren syndrome, an acute sarcoidosis with good prognosis, often self-resolving and managed with NSAIDs.
notes: Lymphoma is possible but is less likely with this triad and a young woman with erythema nodosum.
Primary TB usually causes unilateral adenopathy.
GPA causes cavitating nodules and renal or sinus disease, not hilar nodes.

items.topic: Type 1 diabetes: new presentation, sick-day rules, insulin regimens
items.stem: What is the underlying pathology of type 1 diabetes mellitus?
options: Peripheral insulin resistance with relative deficiency
Excess glucagon secretion from an alpha-cell tumour
Impaired incretin response from the gut
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
items.why: Type 1 diabetes results from T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency and ketosis-proneness.
notes: This describes type 2 diabetes.
Glucagonoma is rare and not the cause of type 1 diabetes.
Reduced incretin effect is a feature of type 2 diabetes.

items.topic: Common GP presentations: fatigue, low back pain red flags, skin checks and sun protection, PSA shared decision-making
items.stem: Which type of ultraviolet radiation is the main cause of sunburn and direct DNA damage producing cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers?
items.why: UVB is absorbed in the epidermis and causes sunburn and pyrimidine dimers. UVA penetrates deeper, contributing to photoageing and indirect damage.
notes: UVA penetrates deeper and causes ageing and indirect oxidative damage, but less sunburn.
Infrared causes heat, not DNA dimers.
UVC is absorbed by the ozone layer and doesn't reach the ground.

items.topic: Stable angina and chest pain work-up: risk stratification, stress testing vs CT coronary angiography
items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has exertional chest tightness, relieved by rest. Resting ECG and troponin are normal. She has low-intermediate pretest probability of coronary disease. Which test is most appropriate?
items.why: CT coronary angiography has a high negative predictive value and suits low-to-intermediate pretest probability of obstructive CAD, allowing exclusion of disease.
notes: Invasive angiography is reserved for high-risk features or positive non-invasive testing.
A resting echo does not assess for inducible ischaemia or coronary anatomy.
Waiting leaves symptomatic angina uninvestigated.

items.topic: Electrolyte emergencies: hyperkalaemia, severe hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia
items.stem: Why does intravenous calcium gluconate protect against arrhythmia in hyperkalaemia?
options: It stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane potential
It binds potassium in the gut
items.why: Calcium raises the threshold potential, restoring the gap to resting membrane potential; it does not lower serum potassium, so a shift agent is still needed.
notes: Insulin with glucose and salbutamol shift potassium, not calcium.
Diuretics increase renal excretion; calcium acts on the membrane.
Resonium-type binders act in the gut; calcium does not.

items.topic: Tuberculosis: latent vs active, migrants from high-incidence countries, notification and contact tracing
items.stem: A 35-year-old man has sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis confirmed in Australia. He lives with his wife and two children. What is the most appropriate public health action?
options: Notify the state health authority and begin contact tracing
Notify only if drug resistance is confirmed
Advise household contacts to take isoniazid empirically
Contact trace only after culture results are final
items.why: TB is notifiable in Australia on diagnosis; state TB services lead contact tracing and screen household contacts promptly, without waiting for culture.
notes: Notification is required for all cases, not just resistant ones.
Contacts are screened first; treatment is based on results and TB service advice.
Tracing starts on smear-positive diagnosis; waiting delays identifying secondary cases.

items.topic: Pericarditis and cardiac tamponade: ECG changes, echo, Beck's triad, colchicine
items.stem: A 28-year-old man has sharp central chest pain, worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward, after a viral illness. ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
items.why: Acute viral pericarditis is treated with an NSAID (aspirin or ibuprofen) plus colchicine, which reduces recurrence. Steroids are second-line, and rest from exercise is advised.
notes: Corticosteroids alone increase recurrence risk and are reserved for refractory cases or contraindications to NSAIDs.
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression is not an occlusive coronary lesion; PCI is not indicated.
Anticoagulation is not indicated and risks haemopericardium.

items.topic: Hypothyroidism: TFT interpretation, levothyroxine dosing, subclinical disease, pregnancy
items.stem: Which thyroid function pattern indicates primary hypothyroidism?
items.why: In primary hypothyroidism, loss of negative feedback from low thyroxine raises TSH. Low TSH with low free T4 suggests central hypothyroidism.
notes: Suggests central (pituitary or hypothalamic) hypothyroidism.
Suggests primary hyperthyroidism.
Suggests TSH-secreting adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance.

items.topic: Bradyarrhythmias and heart block: ECG recognition, drug causes, pacing indications
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman collapses. She is pale and confused, BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 30/min. ECG shows complete heart block with a wide-complex escape rhythm. IV atropine 600 microgram has no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: Unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine needs pacing (transcutaneous, then transvenous), with adrenaline infusion as a bridge. Complete heart block with a wide escape is usually atropine-resistant.
notes: Cardioversion treats tachyarrhythmias, not bradycardia.
Amiodarone slows conduction further and is unsafe in heart block.
Digoxin slows AV conduction and would worsen the block; it is also too slow to act.

items.topic: Alcohol: NHMRC guideline (no more than 10 standard drinks a week and 4 on any day), brief intervention
items.stem: In a healthy adult, blood alcohol falls at a roughly constant rate of about one standard drink an hour, regardless of concentration. What explains this?
options: Rapid renal clearance proportional to concentration
items.why: Alcohol dehydrogenase saturates at low concentrations, so elimination is zero-order: a constant amount per hour, not a constant fraction.
notes: Under 10% of alcohol is excreted unchanged, and clearance is not first-order.
CYP2E1 contributes only minor metabolism, and the pattern is saturable not first-pass.
Ethanol is water-soluble and distributes into total body water, not fat.

items.topic: Venous thromboembolism: DVT diagnosis, DOAC vs warfarin, duration, cancer-associated thrombosis
items.stem: A 62-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is diagnosed with proximal DVT. eGFR is normal and he has no GI luminal tumour concerns. What is the best anticoagulant choice?
items.why: For cancer-associated VTE, DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or LMWH are preferred over warfarin. Continue while the cancer is active or under treatment, at least 3–6 months.
notes: Warfarin is inferior to LMWH/DOAC in cancer-associated VTE.
Aspirin is not adequate treatment for acute proximal DVT.
Proximal DVT needs anticoagulation to prevent extension and pulmonary embolism.

items.topic: Child and adolescent mental health: ADHD, autism, adolescent depression, HEADSS assessment
items.stem: A 15-year-old presents with low mood. In a HEADSS assessment, which approach is most appropriate when asking about sensitive topics?
options: Interview the adolescent alone after explaining the limits of confidentiality
Interview with a parent present throughout
Ask about suicide only if the adolescent raises it
Ask the sensitive questions first to build urgency
items.why: HEADSS is best done with the adolescent alone, after explaining confidentiality and its limits (risk of serious harm). Start with less sensitive topics (home, education) and ask directly about self-harm and suicide.
notes: A parent present often inhibits honest disclosure about drugs, sex and mood.
Asking about suicide does not increase risk and should be asked directly in low mood.
Begin with non-threatening domains such as home and education to build rapport before sensitive topics.

items.topic: Drug dosing in renal impairment: metformin, DOACs, gentamicin, lithium
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73m² (stable CKD). She takes metformin 1 g bd. What is the most appropriate action?
items.why: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 because of the risk of lactic acidosis. Dose reduction is advised at eGFR 30 to 45.
notes: The full dose is unsafe at this eGFR.
Dose reduction applies at eGFR 30 to 45, not below 30.
Glibenclamide risks prolonged hypoglycaemia in renal impairment and is avoided in older adults.

items.topic: Mosquito-borne viruses: Ross River, Barmah Forest, Murray Valley encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, dengue in north Queensland
items.stem: A 6-year-old child in the Kimberley has fever, then drowsiness and seizures after wet-season flooding. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. Murray Valley encephalitis is suspected. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.why: No specific antiviral exists for Murray Valley encephalitis or Japanese encephalitis; management is supportive, including seizure control and ICU care. Prevention is by mosquito avoidance.
notes: Ribavirin has no proven benefit for flaviviruses.
Doxycycline is antibacterial.
Oseltamivir acts on influenza only.

items.topic: Cancer screening programs: bowel (iFOBT 45-74), breast (mammography 50-74), cervical (HPV 25-74), lung (LDCT 50-70)
items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has her first cervical screening test. Oncogenic HPV type 16 is detected and liquid-based cytology is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months
Repeat the cervical screening test in 5 years
items.why: HPV 16 or 18 detected is higher risk regardless of cytology and needs direct referral for colposcopy. A 12-month repeat applies to other oncogenic types with negative or low-grade cytology.
notes: A 12-month repeat applies to oncogenic HPV types other than 16/18 with negative or low-grade cytology.
Five-yearly screening applies only when oncogenic HPV is not detected.
Early repeat HPV testing is not used for HPV 16/18; these patients go straight to colposcopy.

items.topic: Syncope: cardiac red flags, ECG clues (long QT, Brugada, HCM), driving advice
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains exertional syncope in a patient with severe aortic stenosis?
options: Fixed cardiac output with exercise-induced peripheral vasodilation
Excess vagal tone causing sinus arrest
items.why: Fixed outflow obstruction prevents cardiac output rising as exercise vasodilates peripheral vessels, so cerebral perfusion falls. Exertional syncope is a cardiac red flag.
notes: Not the mechanism in aortic stenosis; there is no thromboembolic source in this setting.
Vagal sinus arrest underlies reflex syncope, not fixed outflow obstruction.
Haemorrhage is not part of the mechanism in aortic stenosis.

items.topic: Labour and fetal surveillance: progress of labour, CTG interpretation (RANZCOG), instrumental birth
items.stem: A nulliparous woman at 39 weeks is fully dilated with an epidural, pushing for 2 hours with a persistent occipito-anterior head at +2 station. The CTG is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Assisted vaginal birth by an experienced operator after assessment
Start oxytocin to augment second stage only
items.why: Prolonged second stage in a nullip (about 3 hours with epidural, with no progress) warrants senior review; with an engaged OA head and normal CTG, instrumental birth is appropriate.
notes: Prolonged pushing without descent increases maternal and fetal morbidity.
Caesarean is not first line when the head is low and instrumental birth is feasible.
Oxytocin may help but this woman has already had a long second stage; assessment for assisted birth is needed.

items.topic: Liver function test patterns: hepatocellular vs cholestatic, isolated unconjugated bilirubin (Gilbert)
items.stem: Which mechanism underlies Gilbert syndrome?
options: Reduced hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity impairs bilirubin conjugation
Defective canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin
Impaired hepatic uptake due to biliary obstruction
Increased red cell haemolysis overwhelming conjugation
items.why: Gilbert syndrome is a UGT1A1 promoter variant giving about 30% enzyme activity. Unconjugated bilirubin rises with fasting or illness, and other liver tests are normal.
notes: That describes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
Obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and cholestatic enzymes.
Haemolysis is not the cause in Gilbert syndrome; haemoglobin and reticulocytes are normal.

items.topic: Preterm labour and PPROM: antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium for neuroprotection, tocolysis, antibiotics
items.stem: Antenatal corticosteroids are given to a woman at 30 weeks in threatened preterm birth. What is the main mechanism by which they reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
options: Induce fetal type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant production
items.why: Corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation by stimulating type II pneumocytes to produce surfactant (and thin alveolar septa), reducing RDS, IVH and NEC.
notes: Not the mechanism; steroids act on structural and surfactant maturation, not bronchial tone.
Steroids promote lung liquid absorption at birth, not increased secretion.
Steroids have no tocolytic effect; that is a separate intervention.

items.topic: Obesity: metabolic complications, GLP-1 RA pharmacotherapy, bariatric surgery
items.stem: Which mechanism most directly links visceral obesity to type 2 diabetes?
options: Free fatty acid excess causing insulin resistance in liver and muscle
items.why: Visceral fat releases free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines, causing hepatic and muscle insulin resistance. Adiponectin falls in obesity.
notes: That causes type 1 diabetes.
GLP-1 is not increased in a way that explains this; it would be protective.
Adiponectin is reduced, not raised, in obesity.

items.topic: Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, myasthenic crisis, drugs that worsen it
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia worsening by evening, improved by rest. Pupils are normal. What is the most specific initial blood test?
items.why: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils suggest myasthenia gravis; AChR antibodies are positive in about 85% of generalised disease. Also image the thymus with CT.
notes: Anti-dsDNA relates to lupus.
CK is raised in myopathies and is typically normal in myasthenia.
Anti-GAD relates to stiff-person syndrome and type 1 diabetes.

items.topic: Lithium and therapeutic drug monitoring: toxicity triggers (dehydration, NSAIDs, thiazides)
items.stem: A patient has been on a stable lithium dose for years. When should a blood sample be taken to measure the lithium level correctly?
options: 12 hours after the last dose, before the next dose
Any time, as lithium has no peak
items.why: Lithium levels are taken as a trough about 12 hours after the last dose, at steady state (about 5 days after a change). The usual target is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.
notes: One hour after the dose captures the peak, giving falsely high values.
A 4-hour sample is not standardised and is near peak.
Timing matters because levels vary with absorption and clearance.

items.topic: Thyroid nodules and thyroid cancer: ultrasound features, FNA, papillary carcinoma
items.stem: Histology of a papillary thyroid carcinoma is reported. Which nuclear feature is most characteristic of this tumour?
options: Vascular and capsular invasion with follicles
Hürthle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm
items.why: Papillary carcinoma shows optically clear 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei, grooves and pseudo-inclusions, often with psammoma bodies. It spreads via lymphatics to cervical nodes.
notes: Amyloid stroma with C-cell nests describes medullary carcinoma, derived from parafollicular C cells.
Vascular and capsular invasion defines follicular carcinoma, which spreads haematogenously.
Hürthle cells characterise oncocytic (Hürthle cell) neoplasms, not papillary carcinoma.

items.topic: Gestational diabetes: OGTT at 24-28 weeks (ADIPS criteria), management, postnatal follow-up
items.stem: What is the basic pathophysiology of gestational diabetes mellitus?
options: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells in pregnancy
Placental hormone-induced insulin resistance with inadequate beta-cell compensation
Lowered renal threshold for glucose reabsorption in pregnancy
items.why: Placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol) increase insulin resistance; GDM occurs when maternal beta cells cannot compensate.
notes: Autoimmune destruction describes type 1 diabetes, not typical GDM.
Lowered renal threshold causes glycosuria, which is common in pregnancy but does not cause hyperglycaemia.
Fetal hyperinsulinism is a result of maternal hyperglycaemia, not its cause.

items.topic: HIV: testing, PrEP, PEP timing, opportunistic infections
items.stem: Tenofovir disoproxil with emtricitabine is used as HIV PrEP. What is their shared mechanism of action?
items.why: Both are nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitors that terminate proviral DNA chain elongation, preventing establishment of infection.
notes: Integrase inhibitors include dolutegravir.
Protease inhibitors include darunavir.
CCR5 antagonists include maraviroc.

items.topic: Sexually transmitted infections: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, the syphilis outbreak and congenital syphilis, contact tracing
items.stem: A 22-year-old woman is 20 weeks pregnant and has a positive syphilis serology after an outbreak-area screen. She has no symptoms or prior treatment and the stage is unknown (likely latent, over 2 years). Which is the best management?
options: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IM weekly for 3 doses
Single dose of azithromycin 2 g orally
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 28 days
Defer treatment until after delivery and treat the neonate
items.why: Pregnant women with late or unknown-duration latent syphilis need benzathine benzylpenicillin weekly for 3 doses, which prevents congenital syphilis. Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy.
notes: Azithromycin is unreliable due to resistance and not recommended.
Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Delaying treatment risks congenital syphilis and stillbirth.

items.topic: Hernias: inguinal vs femoral, incarceration and strangulation
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman has a tender irreversible groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with vomiting and abdominal distension. What is the best management?
items.why: Femoral hernias have a high strangulation risk. An irreducible tender one with obstruction needs urgent resuscitation and emergency surgery.
notes: Reduction risks reducing necrotic bowel.
Delay risks bowel ischaemia.
A truss is inappropriate with obstruction or a femoral hernia.

items.topic: Gestational diabetes: OGTT at 24-28 weeks (ADIPS criteria), management, postnatal follow-up
items.stem: A 34-year-old had diet-controlled gestational diabetes and gave birth 2 days ago. Her glucose readings are now normal. Which test is recommended 6 to 12 weeks postpartum?
options: No testing if inpatient glucose levels normalised
items.why: Women with GDM need a 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum to detect persisting diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance. Then screen regularly (every 1 to 3 years) for type 2 diabetes.
notes: HbA1c can be unreliable early postpartum and is less sensitive; OGTT is preferred at this stage.
A random glucose is insensitive for detecting diabetes.
Normal early postpartum glucose does not exclude persistent diabetes; testing is still needed.

items.topic: Epidemiology and evidence: study designs, bias and confounding, screening principles, lead-time bias
items.stem: Screening detects a cancer 2 years earlier than symptoms would, but death occurs at the same age as without screening. Five-year survival from diagnosis appears improved. Which bias explains this?
items.why: Earlier diagnosis lengthens measured survival without delaying death. Mortality, not survival from diagnosis, should be used to evaluate screening.
notes: Length-time bias is over-detection of slow-growing, indolent cancers by screening; death timing is not the issue here.
Selection bias concerns how participants are chosen, such as healthy volunteers.
Recall bias concerns differential memory of exposures in case-control studies.

items.topic: Hepatitis B in pregnancy and the newborn: HBsAg screening, birth-dose vaccine and HBIG
items.stem: A baby is born at term to a mother who is HBsAg positive. What is the most appropriate management in the first 12 hours?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine at 2 months only
Hepatitis B vaccine only, within 7 days
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine, at separate sites
Oral antivirals for the infant for 6 months
items.why: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers should receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the birth-dose vaccine within 12 hours of birth, at separate sites, then complete the schedule.
notes: Far too late; the birth dose is needed within 12 hours.
Vaccine alone within 7 days is too late and omits immunoglobulin.
Infant antivirals are not standard prophylaxis.

items.topic: Diabetes drugs: metformin and eGFR, SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA, sick-day rules), insulin errors
items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin and empagliflozin. She has 2 days of vomiting and poor intake. Glucose 8 mmol/L, pH 7.20, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, ketones 5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop empagliflozin; give IV fluids and insulin with glucose infusion
Continue empagliflozin and give oral fluids
Give IV fluids alone as glucose is normal
Give sodium bicarbonate and restart metformin
items.why: This is euglycaemic DKA: stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and treat with IV fluids and fixed-rate insulin with dextrose to clear ketones. Normal glucose does not exclude DKA.
notes: SGLT2 inhibitor must stop; oral fluids are inadequate for DKA.
Insulin is needed to suppress ketogenesis, with dextrose.
Bicarbonate is not routine and metformin should be withheld in acidosis.

items.topic: Influenza and COVID-19: antivirals for high-risk patients, vaccination, infection control
items.stem: Oseltamivir reduces influenza severity by inhibiting which viral target?
options: Neuraminidase, preventing release of new virions
items.why: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor that blocks release of progeny virions from infected cells. It works best started within 48 hours of symptom onset.
notes: That is the target of baloxavir (cap-dependent endonuclease) or nirmatrelvir-type drugs differ; oseltamivir does not act here.
Haemagglutinin mediates attachment, but oseltamivir does not target it.
M2 blockers (amantadine) are no longer effective against circulating influenza.

items.topic: Childhood asthma: preventer criteria, spacers, acute management
items.stem: A 6-year-old with asthma presents with moderate exacerbation: talking in sentences, mild subcostal recession, SpO2 94% in air. Which is the best initial treatment?
options: Salbutamol 6 puffs (100 microgram) via spacer, reassess after 20 minutes
Oral prednisolone alone, then reassess in 4 hours
Ipratropium alone via nebuliser every 20 minutes
items.why: For moderate asthma in children, give salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer (12 if over 6 years in some protocols), repeat as needed, plus oral corticosteroid. Magnesium is for severe or life-threatening cases.
notes: Steroids are added but a bronchodilator is the first-line immediate treatment.
IV magnesium is reserved for severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to initial therapy.
Ipratropium is an add-on in moderate to severe asthma, not alone.

items.topic: Mosquito-borne viruses: Ross River, Barmah Forest, Murray Valley encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, dengue in north Queensland
items.stem: A 35-year-old woman from coastal Queensland has fever, rash and symmetrical small-joint pain and swelling of hands and ankles for 1 week after camping near wetlands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Acute polyarthritis with rash and fever after mosquito exposure in coastal Australia suggests Ross River virus. Confirm with IgM serology or PCR; treat with NSAIDs.
notes: RA would not cause acute fever and rash after mosquito exposure.
Q fever causes hepatitis or pneumonia, not typical polyarthritis.
Melioidosis does not cause this picture.

items.topic: Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis: eTG antibiotics, pregnancy, catheters, asymptomatic bacteriuria
items.stem: Which organism causes most community-acquired urinary tract infections, using fimbriae to adhere to uroepithelium?
items.why: Uropathogenic E. coli, using P fimbriae to ascend from the perineum, causes about 75-80% of community UTIs.
notes: Proteus is less common and is associated with struvite stones and alkaline urine.
S. saprophyticus is a notable cause in young sexually active women but is much less common.
Enterococcus is more typical of healthcare-associated or catheter-related infection.

items.topic: Glomerulonephritis: IgA nephropathy, post-streptococcal GN in First Nations children, ANCA vasculitis
items.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community has cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and BP 130/85 three weeks after impetigo. What is the expected complement finding?
items.why: Post-streptococcal GN activates the alternative pathway, causing low C3 with normal C4, usually normalising within 6-8 weeks. Persistent low C3 suggests another diagnosis.
notes: Normal complement would favour IgA nephropathy or ANCA vasculitis.
Low C4 suggests classical pathway activation, as in lupus nephritis.
Complement is consumed, not raised, in PSGN.

items.topic: Tachyarrhythmias: SVT (vagal manoeuvres, adenosine), VT, torsades de pointes, synchronised cardioversion
items.stem: A 45-year-old man has palpitations. HR 190/min regular, narrow-complex, BP 118/76 mmHg, alert, no chest pain. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre fails to terminate it. What is the next step?
items.why: For stable regular narrow-complex SVT, vagal manoeuvres come first, then adenosine 6 mg rapid IV bolus with saline flush, then 12 mg. Cardioversion is reserved for instability.
notes: He is haemodynamically stable, so cardioversion is not first-line.
Amiodarone is not first-line for SVT and is slower to act.
Verapamil is second-line if adenosine fails or is contraindicated.

items.topic: Peripheral arterial disease: claudication, ankle-brachial index, risk-factor control, when to refer
items.stem: A 68-year-old smoker has calf claudication at 200 metres and an ankle-brachial index of 0.7. Pulses are absent at the foot, with no rest pain or tissue loss. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Smoking cessation, supervised exercise, antiplatelet and statin
items.why: Stable claudication is managed with risk-factor control: stop smoking, supervised walking, antiplatelet and statin, and BP and diabetes control. Refer for revascularisation if there is critical limb ischaemia or lifestyle-limiting symptoms despite treatment.
notes: Bypass is for critical limb ischaemia or disabling claudication that fails conservative care.
Anticoagulation does not treat chronic PAD and adds bleeding risk.
Amputation is reserved for unsalvageable limbs.

items.topic: Tuberculosis screening: latent TB before biologics, active TB in migrants
items.stem: A 28-year-old refugee from Sudan has 6 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows right upper lobe cavitation. What is the most appropriate initial investigation and precaution?
options: Three sputum samples for TB microscopy, culture and PCR, with airborne isolation
Bronchoscopy only after a trial of amoxicillin
items.why: Suspected pulmonary TB needs sputum for smear, culture and nucleic acid testing (including rifampicin resistance), with airborne precautions. IGRA cannot distinguish latent from active disease.
notes: IGRA cannot diagnose active TB and does not replace microbiological testing.
Delaying with antibiotics is inappropriate when cavitation and symptoms suggest TB.
Mantoux does not diagnose active disease, and TB needs airborne, not droplet, precautions.

items.topic: Meningitis and encephalitis: LP, empirical ceftriaxone with or without benzylpenicillin and aciclovir, dexamethasone, contacts
items.stem: Which cerebrospinal fluid pattern best fits acute bacterial meningitis?
options: Lymphocytes, mildly raised protein, normal glucose
Lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose
Normal cells, high protein, normal glucose
items.why: Bacteria cause a neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein and low CSF glucose (consumed by bacteria and neutrophils). Viral meningitis gives lymphocytes with normal glucose.
notes: This is the typical viral meningitis or encephalitis pattern.
Lymphocytes with very high protein and low glucose suggest tuberculous or fungal meningitis.
This albuminocytological dissociation suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome.

items.topic: Developmental milestones and red flags: speech delay, autism, motor delay referral
items.stem: A 2-year-old boy has about 5 words, no pointing, poor eye contact and does not respond to his name. His mother reports he lined up cars for hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Audiology assessment and referral for developmental assessment
Review again at 3 years if speech has not improved
Reassure that boys commonly talk late
Refer for speech therapy only after a trial of waiting
items.why: Language delay with social communication concerns and repetitive play suggests autism. Hearing must be tested and he should be referred early for developmental assessment without waiting.
notes: Waiting delays diagnosis and intervention; early referral is recommended.
Late-talking reassurance is wrong when there are social communication red flags.
Delaying therapy is inappropriate; intervention should start without waiting for a diagnosis.

items.topic: Atrial fibrillation: CHA2DS2-VA stroke risk (Australian 2018 guideline), DOAC choice, rate vs rhythm control
items.stem: Why does atrial fibrillation increase the risk of ischaemic stroke?
options: Atrial stasis promotes thrombus formation, usually in the left atrial appendage
Rapid ventricular rates cause paradoxical embolism through the foramen ovale
Loss of atrial kick causes cerebral hypoperfusion only
Atrial fibrillation directly damages cerebral arteries
items.why: Fibrillating atria do not contract effectively, so blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage and thrombus can embolise to the brain.
notes: Paradoxical embolism is a venous-sided mechanism and not the main one in AF.
Reduced cardiac output may cause hypotension but not the thromboembolic stroke risk.
AF does not directly damage cerebral vessels; the mechanism is embolic.

items.topic: Preterm labour and PPROM: antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium for neuroprotection, tocolysis, antibiotics
items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 29+0 weeks has confirmed PPROM. She is afebrile, with no contractions, and the CTG is normal. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: IV azithromycin stat or erythromycin with IV/oral amoxicillin per local protocol
items.why: Antibiotics after PPROM prolong latency and reduce chorioamnionitis and neonatal morbidity. Use a macrolide plus amoxicillin per guideline; avoid amoxicillin-clavulanate (NEC risk).
notes: Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended to prolong latency and reduce infection.
Erythromycin alone is inferior to combination regimens in standard protocols.
Co-amoxiclav is avoided in PPROM because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis.

items.topic: Upper GI bleeding: Glasgow-Blatchford score, PPI, endoscopy timing, variceal bleed (terlipressin, antibiotics)
items.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents with haematemesis, HR 120, BP 90/60. He has been resuscitated cautiously. Besides urgent endoscopy, which pair of drugs should be started now?
items.why: Suspected variceal bleeding needs a splanchnic vasoconstrictor (terlipressin) plus antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone) before endoscopy with band ligation. Antibiotics reduce infection and mortality.
notes: Tranexamic acid is not recommended and raises thrombosis risk; octreotide is an alternative but this pairing lacks antibiotics.
Beta-blockers are contraindicated in acute hypotensive bleeding; PPI alone is not variceal therapy.
Oral amoxicillin is not appropriate; IV ceftriaxone is used, and terlipressin is the preferred vasoactive agent.

items.topic: Hyperkalaemia: ECG changes, calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, finding the cause
items.stem: Why does insulin with glucose lower serum potassium in hyperkalaemia?
options: It stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, shifting potassium into cells
It binds potassium in the gut lumen
It stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane potential
items.why: Insulin stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in skeletal muscle, moving potassium intracellularly. The effect is temporary, so total body potassium must still be removed.
notes: Excretion is promoted by diuretics or dialysis, not insulin.
Gut binding is the action of resins such as sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.
Membrane stabilisation is the action of calcium.

items.topic: Pulmonary embolism: Wells and PERC, CTPA vs V/Q (pregnancy, renal impairment), anticoagulation, thrombolysis for massive PE
items.stem: A 68-year-old man is 5 days post hip replacement. He collapses with BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 130/min, SpO2 86% and a raised JVP. Bedside echo shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle. No contraindications. What is the best next treatment?
items.why: Haemodynamically unstable (massive) PE with RV strain warrants systemic thrombolysis, e.g. alteplase, plus unfractionated heparin, without delaying for imaging when bedside echo supports the diagnosis.
notes: Oral DOACs are suitable for stable patients, not for shock needing rapid clot lysis.
An IVC filter is reserved for those with contraindications to anticoagulation; it does not treat shock.
Delaying reperfusion for CTPA in a peri-arrest patient is unsafe; LMWH alone is inadequate in shock.

items.topic: Perioperative medicine: fasting, managing anticoagulants and diabetes drugs, VTE prophylaxis
items.stem: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin is booked for elective colectomy tomorrow. Which advice about empagliflozin is best?
options: Continue it through the perioperative period
Withhold it for 3 days before surgery
Withhold it only on the morning of surgery
Switch it to glibenclamide on the day of surgery
items.why: SGLT2 inhibitors are withheld for 3 days (ie the 3 days before surgery) to reduce risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis. Restart when eating and drinking normally.
notes: Continuing raises the risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis when fasting.
Omitting only on the morning is too short given the prolonged effect.
Sulfonylureas add hypoglycaemia risk while fasting and are not a recommended substitute.

items.topic: Eating disorders: anorexia nervosa medical admission criteria, refeeding syndrome
items.stem: A 16-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa has BMI 14 kg/m². Her HR is 38 bpm, lying and standing BP 80/50 mmHg with postural dizziness, and K+ 2.9 mmol/L. She and her parents want outpatient care. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Medical admission for stabilisation and cautious refeeding
Oral potassium and review in two weeks
Admission to a psychiatric unit only for therapy
items.why: Marked bradycardia, postural hypotension and hypokalaemia are medical instability criteria mandating admission. Start refeeding cautiously with thiamine and monitor phosphate, K+, Mg2+ and glucose.
notes: Family-based treatment is first line for adolescents but only when medically stable.
Outpatient management is unsafe with this degree of instability and electrolyte disturbance.
She needs medical stabilisation first, with psychiatric input in parallel, not a psychiatric-only admission.

items.topic: Obesity: metabolic complications, GLP-1 RA pharmacotherapy, bariatric surgery
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains how GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide cause weight loss?
options: Reduced appetite via central action and delayed gastric emptying
Inhibited intestinal lipase causing fat malabsorption
Increased thermogenesis through beta-3 receptor activation
items.why: GLP-1 RAs act on hypothalamic and brainstem centres to increase satiety and slow gastric emptying, also enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
notes: That is orlistat's mechanism.
That describes SGLT2 inhibitors, which cause modest weight loss.
Not a GLP-1 RA mechanism.

items.topic: Biostatistics: sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, NNT, relative vs absolute risk
items.stem: In a trial, the event rate is 10% with placebo and 6% with a new drug. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one event?
items.why: NNT = 1/absolute risk reduction = 1/0.04 = 25. Relative risk reduction is 40%, which is not the NNT.
notes: 4 is the ARR in percentage points, not its reciprocal.
10 is the control event rate, not related to NNT.
40 is the relative risk reduction (%), a common confusion with NNT.

items.topic: Bites and rabies-type exposures: Australian bat lyssavirus post-exposure prophylaxis, tetanus, animal bite antibiotics
items.stem: How does Australian bat lyssavirus reach the central nervous system after a bite or scratch?
options: Haematogenous spread across the blood–brain barrier
Retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves
Spread via the cerebrospinal fluid from the gut
Aerosol spread via the olfactory epithelium only
items.why: Lyssaviruses replicate locally in muscle, then travel by retrograde axonal transport to the CNS. This is why prompt wound cleaning and post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms can prevent disease.
notes: Viraemia is not the usual route; the virus travels along nerves.
The gut is not a route of entry for lyssavirus.
Aerosol transmission is rare and not the mechanism after a bite.

items.topic: Absolute cardiovascular risk and the Heart Health Check: 2023 Australian CVD risk calculator
items.stem: A 32-year-old Aboriginal man who smokes attends for a health check. He has no known diabetes, kidney disease or cardiovascular disease. What is the most appropriate approach to his cardiovascular risk?
options: Defer risk assessment until he turns 45 years
Defer risk assessment until he turns 35 years
Start a statin empirically because of his smoking
Calculate absolute CVD risk now using the 2023 Australian calculator
items.why: Absolute CVD risk assessment is recommended from age 30 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, versus 45 for others. Treatment is then guided by the calculated risk.
notes: Age 45 is the starting age for non-Indigenous Australians; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people start at 30.
The threshold for this group is 30 years, not 35.
Treatment is guided by calculated absolute risk, not by a single risk factor such as smoking.

items.topic: Atrial fibrillation: CHA2DS2-VA stroke risk (Australian 2018 guideline), DOAC choice, rate vs rhythm control
items.stem: A 72-year-old man with non-valvular AF has hypertension and diabetes (CHA2DS2-VA 3). eGFR is 70 mL/min/1.73 m2 and he has no bleeding risk factors. What is the most appropriate stroke prevention?
items.why: Anticoagulation is recommended for CHA2DS2-VA of 2 or more; DOACs such as apixaban are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF.
notes: Aspirin alone is not recommended for AF stroke prevention.
Warfarin is second line to DOACs and adding aspirin raises bleeding without benefit.
His score of 3 clearly warrants anticoagulation.

items.topic: Gallstone disease: biliary colic, cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis (Charcot's triad), ERCP
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. She is hypotensive (BP 85/50 mmHg) and confused. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone. After fluid resuscitation, blood cultures and IV antibiotics, what is the next best step?
items.why: Severe (Tokyo grade III) cholangitis with shock and confusion needs urgent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction or stenting, alongside antibiotics.
notes: Cholecystectomy is for later, once the ducts are cleared; it does not treat the obstruction.
Delay for imaging is unsafe in septic obstruction; the stone is already shown.
Ursodeoxycholic acid does not relieve acute obstruction.

items.topic: Transfusion: indications, reactions (TRALI, TACO, haemolytic), Patient Blood Management
items.stem: Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)?
options: Volume load exceeding cardiac capacity causing hydrostatic pulmonary oedema
Donor anti-HLA antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in lungs
Recipient anti-A antibodies destroying donor red cells
Bacterial endotoxin in the blood product causing vasodilatation
items.why: TACO is hydrostatic pulmonary oedema from too much volume or too rapid a rate, especially in elderly, cardiac or renal patients. It typically has hypertension and raised JVP, and responds to diuretics.
notes: This describes TRALI, a non-hydrostatic capillary leak with normal or low BP.
This describes acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility.
This describes septic transfusion reaction from contaminated product.

items.topic: Spinal and limb trauma: C-spine clearance (NEXUS, Canadian C-spine), Ottawa ankle and knee rules
items.stem: In the NEXUS low-risk criteria for cervical spine imaging, which feature must be absent for the spine to be clinically cleared?
items.why: NEXUS criteria: no midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no painful distracting injury. Age and mechanism belong to the Canadian C-spine rule.
notes: Active rotation is part of the Canadian C-spine rule, not NEXUS.
Age 65 or over is a Canadian rule item, not part of NEXUS.
Mechanism is part of the Canadian rule, not NEXUS.

items.topic: HIV: testing, PrEP, PEP timing, opportunistic infections
items.stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV has a CD4 count of 60 cells/µL, 2 weeks of dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, hypoxaemia and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. LDH is raised. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Subacute dry cough, hypoxia, bilateral interstitial infiltrates and raised LDH with CD4 below 200 suggest PJP. Confirm with PCR or stain of bronchoalveolar lavage; treat with high-dose co-trimoxazole.
notes: Pneumococcus typically gives lobar consolidation and acute onset.
TB commonly gives cavitation or upper lobe disease and is less typical here.
Cryptococcus presents with headache and meningism.

items.topic: Postoperative complications: fever by postoperative day, anastomotic leak, wound infection, AKI
items.stem: A 70-year-old woman on postoperative day 1 after hip surgery has urine output of 0.2 mL/kg/h for 8 hours and a creatinine rise from 80 to 130 micromol/L. She is hypovolaemic with a palpable bladder? A bladder scan shows 80 mL. What is the best next step?
options: Fluid resuscitation with crystalloid and review nephrotoxins
items.why: This is likely prerenal AKI from hypovolaemia. Give crystalloid, stop nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors, and monitor. Diuretics worsen hypovolaemia.
notes: Frusemide does not improve outcomes and worsens hypovolaemia.
Obstruction is unlikely with a low bladder volume and no hydronephrosis evidence.
RRT is reserved for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, overload or uraemia.

items.topic: Delirium: causes, non-drug management, telling it from dementia
items.stem: Which feature best distinguishes delirium from dementia?
items.why: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that fluctuates over hours to days. Dementia is gradual with preserved alertness until late.
notes: Memory impairment occurs in both conditions.
Gradual onset over years favours dementia.
Language difficulty occurs in both and does not discriminate.

items.topic: Antepartum haemorrhage: placenta praevia vs abruption, no vaginal examination until praevia is excluded
items.stem: What is the underlying mechanism of bleeding in placental abruption?
options: Rupture of fetal vessels running over the cervical os
Rupture of maternal decidual vessels with retroplacental haematoma
Cervical ectropion trauma from the presenting part
Tearing of the uterine scar at the lower segment
items.why: Abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta because decidual spiral vessels bleed, forming a retroplacental clot. Blood may be concealed and the uterus tender.
notes: That describes vasa praevia, which causes fetal bleeding.
Cervical lesions cause minor bleeding and are not the mechanism of abruption.
That describes uterine rupture, a different cause of bleeding and pain.

items.topic: Pelvic inflammatory disease and STIs in women: empirical treatment, ectopic and infertility risk
items.stem: A woman has previously had pelvic inflammatory disease. Which mechanism best explains her increased risk of both ectopic pregnancy and infertility?
options: Persistent cervical mucus plugging blocking sperm entry
Scarring of the fallopian tube with loss of ciliary function and lumen patency
Reduced ovarian follicle numbers from ovarian abscess
Adhesion of the endometrium causing Asherman syndrome
items.why: Salpingitis damages tubal mucosa and cilia and causes adhesions. Total blockage causes infertility; partial damage lets sperm through but delays the embryo, so it implants in the tube.
notes: PID does not cause cervical mucus plugging as its main fertility effect.
Ovarian reserve is not the main effect of PID; tubal damage is.
Intrauterine adhesions are not the usual result of PID and do not explain ectopic pregnancy.

items.topic: Dysphagia: oesophageal cancer, Barrett's oesophagus, achalasia, endoscopy first
items.stem: A 66-year-old man has 3 months of progressive dysphagia, first for solids then liquids, with 8 kg weight loss. He has long-standing reflux. What is the most appropriate first investigation?
items.why: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss suggests oesophageal cancer; urgent endoscopy with biopsy is the first test, allowing diagnosis and tissue.
notes: Barium does not give tissue and is not first line for alarm features.
Manometry is for suspected motility disorders after endoscopy excludes obstruction.
Delaying with empiric PPI is inappropriate with alarm features.

items.topic: The surgical abdomen in children: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting)
items.stem: A 5-week-old boy has projectile vomiting from pyloric stenosis. Which acid-base and electrolyte disturbance is expected?
items.why: Loss of gastric HCl causes hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; volume depletion drives aldosterone, so renal K+ and H+ are lost, giving hypokalaemia and paradoxical aciduria.
notes: Acidosis would be expected with diarrhoea or bicarbonate loss, not gastric acid loss.
Gastric loss causes hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia, and alkalosis rather than acidosis.
Respiratory alkalosis is not the primary disturbance; hypoventilation compensates for the alkalosis.

items.topic: Postpartum haemorrhage: the 4 Ts, uterotonics, escalation
items.stem: Which mechanism chiefly stops bleeding from the placental bed after delivery?
options: Contraction and retraction of myometrial fibres compressing spiral arteries
items.why: Myometrial fibres contract and retract (living ligatures), compressing the spiral arteries. Uterine atony is therefore the commonest cause of PPH.
notes: Catecholamines have only a minor role in placental bed haemostasis.
Fibrinolysis would increase, not stop, bleeding.
The ductus venosus is a fetal structure and unrelated.

items.topic: Acute pancreatitis: gallstones and alcohol, lipase, fluid resuscitation, severity and complications
items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has acute pancreatitis with lipase 4 times normal, and ultrasound shows gallstones with a normal CBD. She is haemodynamically stable with mild disease. What is the best fluid management?
options: Moderate-rate Hartmann's solution titrated to clinical response
Nil fluids, as oral intake only
Aggressive normal saline 1 L/hour for 24 hours
items.why: Early goal-directed moderate crystalloid resuscitation (lactated Ringer's/Hartmann's, ~1.5 mL/kg/h after bolus if hypovolaemic) is preferred; aggressive fluids increase fluid overload without benefit.
notes: Hypovolaemia needs IV fluids in the first 24 hours.
Aggressive fluids increase complications and have not improved outcomes.
Colloids offer no advantage over crystalloid.
