items.topic: Opioids and analgesia: dose conversion, constipation, naloxone, Schedule 8 rules and real-time prescription monitoring
items.stem: A 45-year-old man is found unresponsive after injecting heroin. RR is 4/min, SpO2 is 78%, and pupils are pinpoint. Bag-valve-mask ventilation has begun with oxygen. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Naloxone 100 to 400 microgram IV, titrated to respiratory rate
Naloxone 2 mg IV bolus, repeated every minute until alert
items.why: After ventilation support, titrate small naloxone doses to restore adequate breathing without precipitating withdrawal, agitation or pulmonary oedema. Repeat or infuse because naloxone is shorter acting than many opioids.
notes: Large boluses risk acute withdrawal and aspiration; titrate small doses unless there is peri-arrest.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
Intubation is rarely needed first; a rapidly reversible cause should be treated with ventilation and naloxone.

items.topic: Peripheral neuropathy and nerve palsies: diabetes, B12, carpal tunnel, common peroneal nerve
items.stem: A footballer is struck on the lateral aspect of the knee, at the fibular neck. Which finding best reflects injury to the common peroneal nerve at this site?
options: Foot drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot
Loss of sensation over the sole of the foot
Weak knee extension with loss of knee jerk
items.why: The common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck and supplies ankle dorsiflexors and evertors plus dorsal foot skin. Injury causes foot drop and dorsal foot sensory loss.
notes: Plantarflexion is supplied by the tibial nerve, which is not injured at the fibular neck.
The sole is supplied by the tibial nerve (medial and lateral plantar branches).
Knee extension and knee jerk depend on the femoral nerve (L3-4).

items.topic: HIV: testing, PrEP, PEP timing, opportunistic infections
items.stem: A 30-year-old man presents 24 hours after condomless anal sex with a partner of unknown HIV status. He is not on PrEP. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start 28 days of PEP now, with baseline HIV testing
Wait for a 4-week HIV test before deciding
Advise PEP is no longer effective after 24 hours
Start PrEP and review in 3 months
items.why: PEP should start as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, after a substantial exposure. Give a 28-day course of three-drug therapy and test at baseline and follow-up.
notes: Waiting delays PEP, which is time-critical.
PEP is recommended up to 72 hours.
PrEP is not a substitute for PEP after exposure.

items.topic: Smoking and vaping cessation: Ask-Advise-Help, NRT and varenicline, the 2024 vaping reforms
items.stem: A 38-year-old woman smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Varenicline and combination NRT have each failed despite good adherence and counselling. She asks about vaping. What is the best advice under the 2024 Australian reforms?
options: Buy a nicotine vape from a tobacconist
Import vapes online for lower cost
Vapes are first-line, so stop other therapy
Consider a pharmacy-supplied nicotine vape with support
items.why: Vapes are a second-line option if evidence-based treatments have failed. They are supplied through pharmacies, not retail shops, with behavioural support and a plan to stop.
notes: Retail sale of vapes, including tobacconists, is banned.
Unregulated or imported products are unlawful and not quality-assured.
Vapes are not first-line; NRT and varenicline with behavioural support come first.

items.topic: Alcohol use disorder and withdrawal: AUDIT, withdrawal scales, thiamine before glucose, acamprosate and naltrexone
items.stem: A 45-year-old woman is abstinent from alcohol for one week after inpatient withdrawal. She has normal liver function and wants medication to reduce cravings. She takes no opioids. Which is the most appropriate option?
items.why: Acamprosate (glutamate modulator) or naltrexone supports relapse prevention after withdrawal. With no opioid use, naltrexone is also suitable; acamprosate fits as the listed option.
notes: Disulfiram is second-line due to toxicity and adherence issues.
Benzodiazepines are for withdrawal only, with misuse risk and no relapse-prevention role.
Baclofen is off-label second-line and that dose is excessive.

items.topic: Venous thromboembolism: DVT diagnosis, DOAC vs warfarin, duration, cancer-associated thrombosis
items.stem: Which coagulation factor is directly inhibited by the DOAC rivaroxaban?
items.why: Rivaroxaban and apixaban directly inhibit factor Xa. Dabigatran is the direct thrombin inhibitor.
notes: Thrombin is inhibited by dabigatran, not rivaroxaban.
Factor VIII is not a target of DOACs.
Warfarin reduces vitamin K-dependent factors including VII; rivaroxaban acts directly on Xa.

items.topic: Bowel obstruction: small vs large bowel, adhesions, hernias, volvulus, conservative vs operative care
items.stem: An 82-year-old nursing home resident has massive abdominal distension and constipation. Abdominal X-ray shows a large, dilated 'coffee bean' loop arising from the pelvis toward the right upper quadrant. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: A coffee bean loop pointing from the pelvis to the right upper quadrant is classic for sigmoid volvulus in elderly, institutionalised patients. Caecal volvulus typically displaces the loop to the left upper quadrant.
notes: Caecal volvulus is a dilated loop in the left upper quadrant, often with small bowel dilatation.
Toxic megacolon shows colitis with loss of haustra, not a coffee bean loop.
Carcinoma gives proximal colonic dilatation without a single twisted loop.

items.topic: Orthopaedic emergencies: hip fracture and orthogeriatric care, compartment syndrome, open fractures, septic arthritis
items.stem: A 22-year-old man has a tibial shaft fracture after a motorcycle crash. Pain is severe and out of proportion, worse with passive toe extension, and the calf is tense. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment after tibial fracture indicate compartment syndrome, a clinical diagnosis needing urgent fasciotomy.
notes: DVT is unlikely acutely and does not cause tense compartments with pain on passive stretch.
Fat embolism causes respiratory, neurological and petechial features, usually after 24 to 72 hours.
Nerve palsy causes foot drop and sensory loss, not escalating tense pain.

items.topic: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: sepsis and obstetric causes, coagulation profile
items.stem: Which laboratory finding best distinguishes DIC from isolated liver failure in a bleeding patient with prolonged PT?
options: Markedly raised D-dimer with low fibrinogen and platelets, and low factor VIII
Low factor V and normal factor VIII
items.why: In DIC all factors are consumed, including factor VIII, with raised D-dimer. In liver disease factor VIII is normal or raised (endothelial synthesis) while other factors fall.
notes: Low factor V with normal factor VIII is the pattern of liver disease.
Normal platelets and D-dimer argue against DIC.
Low factor VII only is an early vitamin K deficiency or liver pattern, not DIC.

items.topic: Respiratory failure and ABG interpretation: type 1 vs type 2, when to start NIV
items.stem: Which mechanism underlies type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure?
items.why: Type 2 failure has PaCO2 above 45–50 mmHg (6 kPa) because of inadequate alveolar ventilation, as in COPD or neuromuscular weakness.
notes: V/Q mismatch typically causes hypoxaemia with normal or low CO2 (type 1).
Diffusion impairment causes hypoxaemia, usually with normal CO2.
Shunt causes hypoxaemia unresponsive to oxygen, usually with normal CO2.

items.topic: Australian zoonoses: Q fever, leptospirosis, brucellosis, psittacosis, occupational exposure
items.stem: A 30-year-old banana farm worker in north Queensland has 5 days of fever, severe myalgia, headache and bilateral conjunctival suffusion after flooding. Bilirubin and creatinine are raised. Which is the best diagnostic test early in illness?
options: Blood culture on standard media at 48 hours
items.why: In the first week (leptospiraemic phase) PCR on blood detects Leptospira; serology (MAT) is often negative until after about day 7-10 and needs paired samples.
notes: Leptospira is fastidious and routine culture is insensitive.
Rose Bengal is used for brucellosis.
Weil-Felix is an obsolete rickettsial test.

items.topic: Paracetamol overdose: Australian nomogram, acetylcysteine regimen, staggered and modified-release ingestions
items.stem: In paracetamol overdose, hepatic glutathione stores are depleted. Which toxic metabolite accumulates to cause hepatocyte injury?
items.why: At high doses, glucuronidation and sulfation saturate and more drug is oxidised by CYP2E1 to NAPQI. When glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins.
notes: Glucuronide is a non-toxic conjugate that is excreted.
Sulfate is a non-toxic conjugate that is excreted.
Acetaldehyde is an ethanol metabolite, not related to paracetamol.

items.topic: Environmental emergencies: heat stroke, hypothermia, drowning
items.stem: A marathon runner collapses on a hot humid day with a core temperature of 41.5°C and confusion. Which mechanism best explains why heat loss fails in this setting?
options: High ambient humidity impairs evaporation of sweat
Hypothalamic set point rises as in fever
Reduced basal metabolic rate limits radiation
items.why: In hot humid conditions evaporation, the main heat loss route when ambient temperature approaches skin temperature, fails. Heat stroke is thermoregulatory failure, not a raised set point as in fever.
notes: Heat stress causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction; conduction is also minor.
Fever involves a raised set point; in heat stroke the set point is unchanged and regulation is overwhelmed.
Exertion raises metabolic heat production; radiation also fails when ambient temperature is high.

items.topic: Valve disease: aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation murmurs, severity markers, TAVI vs surgical referral
items.stem: Chronic severe aortic stenosis causes which adaptive change in the left ventricle?
options: Thinning of the wall from volume overload
items.why: Fixed outflow obstruction raises systolic wall stress, so sarcomeres replicate in parallel and produce concentric hypertrophy, which impairs diastolic filling and raises myocardial oxygen demand.
notes: Wrong: eccentric hypertrophy with dilatation is the response to volume overload, as in chronic mitral or aortic regurgitation.
Wrong: wall thickening, not thinning, occurs initially; thinning and dilatation occur only late in decompensation.
Wrong: aortic stenosis loads the left ventricle; the right ventricle is affected only late via pulmonary hypertension.

items.topic: Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants: adrenal suppression, TB and hepatitis B screening before biologics
items.stem: A patient has taken prednisolone 20 mg daily for three months. Which mechanism explains why abrupt cessation may cause adrenal crisis?
options: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses CRH and ACTH, causing adrenal atrophy
Prednisolone permanently destroys adrenal medullary cells
Prednisolone blocks aldosterone receptors in the distal tubule
items.why: Negative feedback from chronic exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses the HPA axis, so the adrenal cortex atrophies and cannot respond when the drug stops. Taper after prolonged courses.
notes: The cortex (not medulla) atrophies, and it is reversible rather than destructive.
Prednisolone has mineralocorticoid activity; aldosterone is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and is largely preserved.
Anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies cause autoimmune Addison disease, not steroid-induced suppression.

items.topic: Cushing's syndrome: exogenous steroids as the commonest cause, screening tests
items.stem: A patient on long-term prednisolone develops central obesity and striae. What is the state of the patient's ACTH and endogenous cortisol?
items.why: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses the HPA axis by negative feedback, so ACTH and endogenous cortisol are low, and the adrenals atrophy. Prednisolone does not cross-react in most cortisol assays.
notes: This pattern fits ACTH-dependent Cushing disease, not exogenous steroid.
Low cortisol with high ACTH is primary adrenal insufficiency.
Low ACTH with high cortisol suggests an autonomous adrenal source, not exogenous steroid.

items.topic: Burns: TBSA estimation, fluid resuscitation, ANZBA referral criteria, airway burns
items.stem: A man is rescued from an enclosed house fire with singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth, hoarse voice and mild stridor. What is the best next step?
options: Humidified oxygen and observe for 24 hours
Urgent early intubation by an experienced operator
Bronchoscopy on the ward in the morning
items.why: Stridor, hoarseness and soot suggest inhalational airway burns with progressive oedema. Secure the airway early by intubation before swelling makes it impossible.
notes: Observation risks airway loss as oedema progresses.
Adrenaline is temporising and discharge is unsafe.
Delay is dangerous with stridor; secure the airway first.

items.topic: The Australian health system: Medicare, PBS, safety nets, authority scripts, mental health treatment plans
items.stem: In the Australian health system, what does the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) do?
options: Subsidises the cost of listed prescription medicines
Pays for all private hospital admissions
items.why: The PBS is a federal scheme that subsidises listed medicines; Medicare Benefits Schedule rebates cover medical services.
notes: Private hospital costs are covered by private health insurance, not the PBS.
Public hospitals are funded by state and federal agreements.
GP rebates are provided through the MBS, not the PBS.

items.topic: Consent, capacity and confidentiality: mature minors (Gillick), substitute decision-makers, exceptions
items.stem: A 14-year-old girl attends a GP alone requesting contraception and asks that her parents not be told. She understands the risks, benefits and alternatives. What is the best approach?
options: Provide contraception if she is Gillick competent, maintaining confidentiality
Refer to child protection in all cases
items.why: A mature minor who has sufficient understanding and intelligence to fully appreciate the decision (Gillick competence) can consent, and confidentiality applies. Consider safety concerns such as coercion or abuse.
notes: Parental consent is not required for a competent minor.
Disclosing to parents breaches confidentiality without a safety justification.
Mandatory reporting depends on risk of harm, not on contraception request alone.

items.topic: Primary aldosteronism: aldosterone-renin ratio, hypertension with hypokalaemia
items.stem: A 45-year-old man has resistant hypertension on three drugs. K+ is 3.1 mmol/L with metabolic alkalosis. Plasma renin is suppressed and aldosterone is elevated. After confirmatory testing, what is the next step to determine laterality before surgery?
items.why: In confirmed primary aldosteronism, CT cannot reliably distinguish unilateral from bilateral disease, so adrenal vein sampling guides adrenalectomy decisions.
notes: Metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma, which does not cause suppressed renin with high aldosterone.
Dexamethasone suppression tests for Cushing syndrome, not aldosterone excess.
Renal artery stenosis causes high renin, not suppressed renin.

items.topic: Bites and rabies-type exposures: Australian bat lyssavirus post-exposure prophylaxis, tetanus, animal bite antibiotics
items.stem: A 28-year-old bat carer, never vaccinated against rabies, was scratched by a flying fox. The wound was washed. Which post-exposure regimen is appropriate?
items.why: For unvaccinated people with a bat exposure in Australia, give rabies immunoglobulin (infiltrated around the wound) plus a 4-dose vaccine course. Bats cannot be reliably observed.
notes: Observation is used for some dogs/cats overseas, not for bats.
Tetanus cover may be needed but does not address lyssavirus.
Vaccine alone omits immunoglobulin, which is required in unvaccinated people.

items.topic: Gastroenteritis and dehydration: clinical dehydration assessment, oral rehydration, ondansetron
items.stem: Oral rehydration solution works in secretory diarrhoea such as that from rotavirus because which intestinal transport mechanism remains intact?
options: Passive paracellular sodium diffusion in the colon
Sodium-hydrogen exchange in the crypt cells
items.why: SGLT1 couples sodium and glucose uptake, and water follows osmotically. This pathway stays intact in gastroenteritis, which is why low-osmolarity ORS works.
notes: Paracellular diffusion is not the glucose-linked route that ORS relies on; it does not explain the effect.
Sodium-hydrogen exchange is reduced in diarrhoea and is not the target of ORS.
CFTR chloride secretion drives fluid loss in secretory diarrhoea; it is not what ORS uses.

items.topic: End of life: advance care directives, voluntary assisted dying (state and territory law), palliative care
items.stem: An 82-year-old with advanced dementia lacks capacity. Her valid advance care directive refuses CPR and intubation. She has a cardiac arrest in hospital and her son demands full resuscitation. What is the correct approach?
options: Follow the valid directive and withhold CPR
Resuscitate as the son is next of kin
Resuscitate and then review the directive
Seek a court order before any decision
items.why: A valid, applicable advance care directive refusing treatment must be followed; it expresses the person's own decision and overrides substitute views.
notes: A substitute decision-maker cannot override a valid applicable refusal made by the patient.
Resuscitating contravenes the patient's refusal and risks battery.
Court involvement is only needed if validity is genuinely uncertain.

items.topic: Transient ischaemic attack: urgent assessment, secondary prevention, carotid endarterectomy
items.stem: Transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) from carotid atheroembolism results from embolus to a branch of which artery?
options: Ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid
Facial artery, a branch of the external carotid
items.why: The ophthalmic artery arises from the internal carotid and gives the central retinal artery, so emboli from carotid plaque cause ipsilateral transient monocular blindness.
notes: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital cortex; occlusion causes homonymous hemianopia, not monocular loss.
The external carotid branches do not supply the retina.
Basilar disease causes brainstem and bilateral or posterior symptoms, not monocular loss.

items.topic: Stable angina and chest pain work-up: risk stratification, stress testing vs CT coronary angiography
items.stem: What is the main mechanism of exertional angina in a patient with fixed coronary stenosis?
options: Myocardial oxygen demand exceeding supply through the narrowed artery
Acute plaque rupture with occlusive thrombus
items.why: A fixed stenosis limits the rise in coronary flow during exertion, so increased demand outstrips supply and causes reversible ischaemia, relieved by rest.
notes: Rest vasospasm describes Prinzmetal angina, not exertional angina.
Plaque rupture with thrombus causes acute coronary syndrome.
Pericarditis causes pleuritic, positional pain, not exertional.

items.topic: Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome: distinguishing features, management
items.stem: A 30-year-old man on sertraline took tramadol yesterday. He now has agitation, diaphoresis, temperature 38.8°C, inducible clonus and hyperreflexia. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Cease serotonergic drugs and give benzodiazepines
items.why: Serotonin syndrome is managed by stopping serotonergic agents, supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation. Cyproheptadine can be added if this fails; antipyretics are ineffective.
notes: Dantrolene and bromocriptine are used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome and are not first-line for serotonin syndrome.
Continuing the offending agent is unsafe, and paracetamol does not lower temperature as the heat is from muscle activity.
Antipsychotics such as haloperidol can worsen the condition and risk confusing the picture with NMS.

items.topic: Pleural effusion: Light's criteria, transudate vs exudate causes, empyema drainage
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains a pleural effusion in congestive cardiac failure?
options: Raised hydrostatic pressure in pleural capillaries
Bacterial infection of the pleural space
items.why: In heart failure, raised hydrostatic pressure drives protein-poor fluid into the pleural space, producing a transudate. Exudates arise from increased permeability or impaired lymphatics.
notes: Increased permeability produces exudates, as in pneumonia or malignancy.
Lymphatic obstruction by tumour causes an exudate, not the cardiac failure mechanism.
Infection causes parapneumonic effusion or empyema, which are exudates.

items.topic: Kidney disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people: earlier screening, remote dialysis access
items.stem: A 28-year-old Aboriginal man in a remote community has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate kidney screening for him?
options: Annual eGFR, urine ACR and blood pressure from age 30
No screening until age 50 unless he has symptoms
Screening only if he develops diabetes
items.why: The CKD guideline recommends annual kidney health checks (eGFR, urine ACR, blood pressure) for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from age 30, and earlier if other risk factors are present. At 28 he is just under this age, so the answer applies from 30 or sooner with any risk factor.
notes: Waiting until 50 misses the high early burden of CKD.
Imaging is not a screening test for CKD.
Screening is not restricted to people with diabetes.

items.topic: Paracetamol and NSAIDs: maximum doses, NSAID renal, GI and cardiovascular risks
items.stem: A 72-year-old man with heart failure on ramipril and furosemide takes regular ibuprofen for knee pain. He presents with weight gain, oedema and creatinine rising from 90 to 160 µmol/L. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowering filtration pressure
items.why: NSAIDs inhibit vasodilatory prostaglandins, constricting the afferent arteriole; with ACE inhibitor and diuretic ('triple whammy') GFR falls. Stop the NSAID and use paracetamol.
notes: Crystal nephropathy is not the NSAID mechanism here.
NSAIDs can cause minimal change or interstitial nephritis, but this haemodynamic picture is the common cause.
ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole; NSAIDs constrict the afferent.

items.topic: Perioperative medicine: fasting, managing anticoagulants and diabetes drugs, VTE prophylaxis
items.stem: A healthy adult is having elective surgery under general anaesthetic at 1 pm. According to ANZCA fasting guidance, until when may they have clear fluids?
items.why: ANZCA allows clear fluids until 2 hours before anaesthesia, with solids stopped 6 hours before. Clear fluids may reduce thirst, hypovolaemia and PONV.
notes: Fasting from midnight is outdated and unnecessarily prolonged.
Six hours applies to solid food, not clear fluids.
Four hours is not the recommended cut-off for clear fluids in adults.

items.topic: Bowel cancer: red flags, National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (iFOBT every 2 years: mailed at 50-74, by request from 45), colonoscopy surveillance
items.stem: Most colorectal cancers arise through the adenoma–carcinoma sequence. Which early molecular event typically initiates it?
items.why: Biallelic APC loss (Wnt pathway activation) is the earliest event, followed by KRAS activation and later TP53 loss. Germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis.
notes: TP53 loss is a late event enabling progression to carcinoma.
SMAD4 loss occurs late in the sequence.
KRAS mutation follows APC loss and promotes adenoma growth.

items.topic: Aortic dissection: presentation, CT angiography, Stanford A vs B management
items.stem: In the Stanford classification of aortic dissection, which description defines a type A dissection?
options: Any dissection involving the ascending aorta
Dissection confined to the abdominal aorta
Dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery only
Dissection limited to the aortic arch branches
items.why: Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta regardless of the origin of the tear; type B involves only the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery.
notes: Abdominal-only dissection does not involve the ascending aorta, so it is not type A.
This describes type B.
Involvement of the ascending aorta, not arch branches alone, defines type A.

items.topic: Antipsychotics: extrapyramidal effects, metabolic syndrome, QT prolongation, clozapine monitoring
items.stem: Which pharmacological property of antipsychotics best explains acute dystonia and parkinsonism?
options: Dopamine D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway
Histamine H1 blockade in the cortex
Muscarinic M1 agonism in the striatum
items.why: Blocking D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway disrupts the dopamine and acetylcholine balance, causing extrapyramidal effects. Anticholinergics such as benztropine treat acute dystonia.
notes: 5-HT2C antagonism is linked to weight gain, not extrapyramidal effects.
H1 blockade causes sedation and weight gain.
Antipsychotics do not agonise muscarinic receptors; anticholinergic activity would reduce, not cause, EPS.

items.topic: Menopause: menopausal hormone therapy benefits and risks, premature ovarian insufficiency
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 6 months of amenorrhoea, hot flushes and vaginal dryness. Pregnancy test is negative and FSH is 68 IU/L on two samples 4 weeks apart. She has no contraindications. What is the best management?
options: Short-course hormone therapy for 12 months, then cease
Bisphosphonate for bone protection and reassurance
Menopausal hormone therapy until about the age of natural menopause
No hormonal treatment because of breast cancer risk
items.why: This is premature ovarian insufficiency. Replacing oestrogen until about age 50–51 protects bone and cardiovascular health; the breast risk applies to older women, not replacement here.
notes: Stopping early leaves years of oestrogen deficiency, with bone and cardiovascular risk.
Bisphosphonates do not treat symptoms and are not appropriate in young women; oestrogen is the bone therapy.
Breast cancer risk concerns do not apply to replacement in POI, where benefits clearly outweigh risks.

items.topic: Antibiotics: eTG empirical choices, gentamicin dosing and monitoring, penicillin allergy
items.stem: A 30-year-old woman reports a childhood rash after amoxicillin, with no airway symptoms and no recent reaction. She needs treatment for cellulitis. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Penicillin allergy assessment; flucloxacillin is likely safe if low risk
Give cefalexin only, as cephalosporins are always safe
Give vancomycin as the first-line option
items.why: A remote benign rash is low risk; most such labels are not true allergy. Risk-stratify (eg PEN-FAST) and consider direct challenge or delabelling per eTG/ASCIA.
notes: Lifelong avoidance is unnecessary for low-risk histories and drives worse outcomes.
Cross-reactivity depends on side chain; cephalosporins are not always safe, and this is not required here.
Vancomycin is inferior for MSSA and unnecessary in low-risk history.

items.topic: End of life: advance care directives, voluntary assisted dying (state and territory law), palliative care
items.stem: Which mechanism explains why opioids such as morphine relieve dyspnoea and pain in palliative care?
options: Agonism at mu-opioid receptors reducing perceived pain and air hunger
Blockade of NMDA receptors in the spinal cord only
Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase reducing prostaglandin synthesis
Antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
items.why: Morphine is a mu-opioid receptor agonist; central action reduces the perception of pain and breathlessness.
notes: NMDA antagonism is ketamine's action, not morphine's.
COX inhibition is the NSAID mechanism.
D2 antagonism is how haloperidol and metoclopramide work as antiemetics.

items.topic: Mental health law and capacity: state and territory Mental Health Acts, involuntary treatment criteria, consent
items.stem: A 24-year-old with first-episode psychosis in an emergency department in Victoria refuses admission, believing he is well. He has persecutory delusions and has threatened to harm his mother. Which is the most appropriate step?
options: Assess against involuntary treatment criteria under the Mental Health Act
Discharge him as he has refused treatment
Seek a court order for guardianship
Ask his mother to consent on his behalf
items.why: Involuntary treatment criteria require mental illness, need for immediate treatment, risk of serious harm and no less restrictive option. A psychiatrist assesses and makes an order under the state Mental Health Act.
notes: Refusal does not prevent involuntary assessment when criteria are met and there is risk to others.
Guardianship applies to long-term incapacity decisions, not acute psychiatric treatment orders.
A relative cannot consent to involuntary treatment for a competent adult; the Act provides the pathway.

items.topic: Common GP presentations: fatigue, low back pain red flags, skin checks and sun protection, PSA shared decision-making
items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue. Examination is normal. Which initial investigation set is most appropriate?
options: FBC, ferritin, TSH, glucose, UEC, LFT and coeliac serology
items.why: Initial fatigue workup is guided by history and includes FBC, ferritin, TSH, glucose, renal and liver function, and consider coeliac serology. Screen for depression, sleep and medication causes too.
notes: Imaging isn't indicated without localising features.
Adrenal testing is for suggestive features, not first line.
No serology panel diagnoses chronic fatigue; it is a clinical diagnosis after exclusions.

items.topic: Kawasaki disease: diagnostic criteria, IVIG and aspirin, coronary aneurysms
items.stem: A 3-year-old has had 5 days of fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, rash and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.why: Complete Kawasaki disease is treated with single-dose IVIG 2 g/kg, ideally within 10 days of onset, plus aspirin, to reduce coronary aneurysm risk. Echocardiography is also required.
notes: Antibiotics are not effective; the cause is not bacterial infection.
Steroids alone are not standard first line; they may be adjuncts in high-risk cases.
Aspirin alone does not prevent coronary aneurysms; IVIG is essential.

items.topic: Adverse drug reactions and interactions: CYP450 inducers and inhibitors, reporting to the TGA
items.stem: A patient stable on warfarin starts rifampicin for tuberculosis. Which effect on warfarin is expected, through what mechanism?
options: Lowered INR from CYP induction increasing warfarin metabolism
Raised INR from displacement from albumin only
Unchanged INR because warfarin is renally cleared
items.why: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of CYP enzymes (including CYP2C9 and 3A4), speeding warfarin clearance and lowering the INR. Dose requirements rise and the effect persists after stopping.
notes: Rifampicin induces rather than inhibits CYP2C9.
Protein displacement is minor and rifampicin does not act this way.
Warfarin is hepatically metabolised, not renally cleared.

items.topic: Tachyarrhythmias: SVT (vagal manoeuvres, adenosine), VT, torsades de pointes, synchronised cardioversion
items.stem: Adenosine terminates AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Blocks L-type calcium channels in the AV node
Opens potassium channels, causing transient AV nodal block
Blocks fast sodium channels in the His-Purkinje system
Blocks beta-1 receptors in the AV node
items.why: Adenosine acts on A1 receptors to open K+ channels, hyperpolarising the AV node and briefly blocking conduction, which breaks the re-entry circuit. Its half-life is under 10 seconds.
notes: That is the mechanism of verapamil, not adenosine.
Sodium channel blockers (class I) act mainly on atrial and ventricular tissue, not the AV node.
That is the mechanism of beta-blockers such as metoprolol, which act longer than adenosine.

items.topic: Paracetamol overdose: Australian nomogram, acetylcysteine regimen, staggered and modified-release ingestions
items.stem: A 22-year-old presents 6 hours after ingesting 20 g of immediate-release paracetamol in a single acute ingestion. She is asymptomatic. The 4-hour level was 1.4 times above the treatment line... Actually the 4-hour level is not available; the level taken now is above the nomogram treatment line. What is the next step?
options: Repeat level at 8 hours before deciding
Await liver function tests before treating
items.why: A level above the Australian treatment line (150 mg/L at 4 h) after a single acute ingestion warrants acetylcysteine without waiting for LFTs. Start promptly.
notes: Delay is unnecessary when the level is already above the line.
Charcoal alone is inadequate when treatment criteria are met.
LFTs are normal early and must not delay treatment.

items.topic: COPD: spirometry diagnosis, COPD-X stepwise inhalers, exacerbations, oxygen target 88-92%
items.stem: Which spirometry finding after bronchodilator confirms airflow limitation in COPD?
options: FEV1 increase of more than 12% and 200 mL
items.why: Persistent airflow limitation is a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 (COPD-X uses this). A restrictive pattern has a normal or high ratio.
notes: A normal or high ratio with low FVC suggests restriction, not obstruction.
Raised DLCO is not diagnostic of COPD; emphysema typically lowers it.
Marked reversibility suggests asthma, and COPD is defined by incomplete reversibility.

items.topic: Prostate: BPH, PSA testing with shared decision-making, prostate cancer
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains why finasteride reduces prostate volume?
options: Blocks alpha-1A receptors on smooth muscle
Inhibits conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
items.why: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors block conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, shrinking the gland over months and lowering PSA by about half.
notes: That is tamsulosin, which relaxes smooth muscle without shrinking the gland.
Androgen receptor antagonists such as bicalutamide are used in prostate cancer.
LH suppression is by GnRH agonists used in prostate cancer.

items.topic: Acute stroke: FAST, CT and CT perfusion, thrombolysis and endovascular clot retrieval eligibility
items.stem: In acute ischaemic stroke, a region of brain with reduced blood flow but still viable and potentially salvageable by reperfusion is called which of the following?
items.why: The penumbra is hypoperfused, functionally impaired but viable tissue surrounding the core. Reperfusion therapies (thrombolysis, clot retrieval) aim to save it; CT perfusion mismatch identifies it.
notes: The core is irreversibly infarcted tissue with severely reduced flow; reperfusion cannot save it.
Watershed zones lie between arterial territories and are vulnerable to hypotension; this is a location, not salvageable tissue.
Luxury perfusion is hyperaemia of infarcted tissue after reperfusion; it is not salvageable penumbra.

items.topic: Urinary tract infection: cystitis vs pyelonephritis, resistance, pregnancy
items.stem: Which mechanism most commonly confers resistance to cefalexin and ceftriaxone in E. coli causing community UTI?
options: Efflux of drug via tetracycline pumps
Modification of the ribosomal binding site
items.why: ESBLs hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins and penicillins in Enterobacterales; carbapenems (e.g. meropenem) are usually needed for serious infection. PBP2a (mecA) is a staphylococcal mechanism.
notes: PBP2a alteration underlies MRSA, not Gram-negative cephalosporin resistance.
Tetracycline efflux does not explain cephalosporin resistance.
Ribosomal modification affects macrolides and aminoglycosides, not cephalosporins.

items.topic: Anticoagulant reversal and major bleeding: vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran
items.stem: Warfarin impairs synthesis of which group of clotting factors by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase?
items.why: Vitamin K is needed for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S). Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, so these become inactive.
notes: Factors I, V, VIII and XIII are not vitamin K dependent.
Factors VIII, XI and XII are not vitamin K dependent; this mixes intrinsic pathway factors.
Factors V and XI are not vitamin K dependent.

items.topic: Anxiety disorders: GAD and panic disorder, CBT first, SSRIs, avoiding benzodiazepine dependence
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 8 months of excessive worry, restlessness and poor sleep, diagnosed as generalised anxiety disorder. She has no other conditions. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
items.why: Psychological therapy, particularly CBT, is first-line for GAD in Australian guidelines. An SSRI or SNRI is added if therapy is unavailable or insufficient; benzodiazepines are avoided or limited to short use.
notes: Benzodiazepines risk tolerance and dependence and are not recommended long term.
Antipsychotics are not first-line for GAD.
Beta-blockers may ease somatic symptoms but do not treat GAD.

items.topic: Community-acquired pneumonia: severity scoring (SMART-COP/CORB), eTG empirical antibiotics, atypical cover
items.stem: A 60-year-old man has pneumonia with a CORB score of 2 (confusion, respiratory rate 32), so it is moderate to severe. What empirical antibiotic regimen does eTG recommend?
options: Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline or azithromycin
items.why: Moderate CAP in eTG is treated with IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or azithromycin for atypical cover. Severe cases need broader cover.
notes: Oral amoxicillin alone suits mild CAP and gives no atypical cover.
Doxycycline alone is for mild CAP, not for a moderate case needing IV therapy.
Gentamicin alone has poor pneumococcal activity.

items.topic: Strongyloides, scabies and skin sores in remote communities: ivermectin, impetigo and APSGN/ARF links
items.stem: Strongyloides stercoralis can persist for decades after leaving an endemic area and cause hyperinfection with immunosuppression. What life-cycle feature explains this?
options: Autoinfection by larvae penetrating gut mucosa or perianal skin
Encystment of adult worms within skeletal muscle
Egg shedding that reinfects through faecal-oral spread
items.why: Rhabditiform larvae mature into filariform larvae in the gut and reinvade, perpetuating infection. Corticosteroids can drive hyperinfection, so screen and treat before immunosuppression.
notes: Muscle encystment describes Trichinella, not Strongyloides.
Strongyloides eggs hatch in the gut; larvae, not eggs, are passed and infect via skin.
Hydatid cysts are due to Echinococcus.

items.topic: Anticoagulants: warfarin INR and interactions, DOAC dosing in renal impairment, peri-procedural plans
items.stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. He needs elective cataract-unrelated hernia repair (low bleeding risk) with eGFR 70 mL/min. What is the most appropriate peri-procedural plan?
options: Withhold apixaban for 24 hours before; no bridging
Withhold apixaban for 5 days before; bridge with enoxaparin
Continue apixaban and give vitamin K the night before
Change to warfarin 5 days before the procedure
items.why: For low-bleeding-risk procedures with preserved renal function, omit the DOAC for about 24 hours (one dose-free day). DOACs need no bridging because of their rapid offset.
notes: Five days is for warfarin, and bridging is not needed with DOACs.
Vitamin K does not reverse DOACs and continuing them raises bleeding risk.
Switching to warfarin adds delay and risk without benefit.

items.topic: Hypertension in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia: aspirin for high-risk women, magnesium sulfate, timing of birth
items.stem: A 31-year-old at 32 weeks has BP 170/112 mmHg, severe headache, visual disturbance and brisk reflexes with clonus. Urine protein is 3+. Which drug is given to prevent eclampsia?
items.why: Magnesium sulfate (4 g IV load then 1 g/h) is first-line to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures in severe pre-eclampsia. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.
notes: Diazepam is inferior to magnesium for eclampsia and sedates mother and baby.
Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium sulfate for eclampsia.
Levetiracetam is not first-line for eclampsia prevention.

items.topic: Lung cancer: presentations, paraneoplastic syndromes, National Lung Cancer Screening Program (LDCT for 50-70 with 30+ pack-years, from July 2025)
items.stem: Under the National Lung Cancer Screening Program, which asymptomatic person is eligible for low-dose CT screening?
options: A 62-year-old current smoker with a 35 pack-year history
A 45-year-old current smoker with a 30 pack-year history
A 66-year-old who quit 25 years ago with 40 pack-years
A 72-year-old current smoker with a 50 pack-year history
items.why: Eligibility is age 50–70, asymptomatic, at least 30 pack-years, and currently smoking or quit within the past 10 years. LDCT is offered every 2 years.
notes: Age 45 is below the 50–70 eligible range.
Quitting more than 10 years ago makes this person ineligible.
Age 72 is above the upper limit of 70.

items.topic: Strongyloides, scabies and skin sores in remote communities: ivermectin, impetigo and APSGN/ARF links
items.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal child from a remote community has haematuria, periorbital oedema and hypertension 2 weeks after skin sores. Complement C3 is low. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Post-streptococcal GN follows Group A Streptococcus skin infection after 2–3 weeks, with nephritic features and low C3. Skin sore control is the key preventive measure.
notes: IgA nephropathy causes haematuria concurrent with infection (1–2 days), with normal C3.
Minimal change gives nephrotic syndrome without haematuria and with normal C3.
ARF follows streptococcal infection with carditis or arthritis, not nephritic syndrome.

items.topic: Mosquito-borne viruses: Ross River, Barmah Forest, Murray Valley encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, dengue in north Queensland
items.stem: Ross River virus causes a polyarthritis in adults. Which mechanism best explains the joint symptoms?
options: Viral replication in synovial macrophages with an inflammatory immune response
Immune complex deposition after streptococcal infection
Urate crystal deposition in the joint
Direct bacterial invasion of the synovial space
items.why: Ross River virus, an alphavirus, infects macrophages in synovium and muscle, causing inflammatory arthritis and myalgia that can last months.
notes: This describes acute rheumatic fever.
This describes gout.
Ross River is a virus, not a bacterium.

items.topic: Type 2 diabetes: HbA1c diagnosis, stepwise therapy, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs for cardiorenal benefit, annual cycle of care
items.stem: Which mechanism explains how an SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin lowers blood glucose and reduces the risk of heart failure hospitalisation?
options: Reduced proximal tubular glucose reabsorption causing glycosuria and natriuresis
Reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis through AMPK activation
Delayed gastric emptying and suppressed glucagon release
items.why: SGLT2 in the proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered glucose; blocking it causes glycosuria with osmotic diuresis and natriuresis, lowering preload and intraglomerular pressure.
notes: This describes sulfonylureas (and partly GLP-1 RAs); SGLT2 inhibitors act independently of insulin.
This describes metformin's main action, not SGLT2 inhibition.
This describes GLP-1 receptor agonists, not SGLT2 inhibitors.

items.topic: Child protection: non-accidental injury patterns, mandatory reporting
items.stem: Which bruising site in a 6-month-old non-mobile infant is most concerning for non-accidental injury?
items.why: Bruising on the ears, neck, torso, buttocks or in a non-mobile infant is concerning. Shins, forehead and bony prominences are typical sites of accidental bruising in mobile children.
notes: Shins are common accidental sites in walking children.
Forehead bruises are common with falls.
Bony prominences are typical accidental sites.

items.topic: Bipolar disorder: mania, lithium levels, toxicity and renal/thyroid monitoring, valproate in women of childbearing potential
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, not using contraception, is stable on sodium valproate. She wants to conceive. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Continue valproate and add folic acid 5 mg only
Stop it abruptly now and use no mood stabiliser
Plan a switch to a safer alternative before conception
Valproate is safe if kept below 1000 mg daily
items.why: Valproate is highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental disorders) and should be avoided in women of childbearing potential. Plan a gradual switch before conception, with contraception meanwhile.
notes: Folate does not remove the risk.
Abrupt cessation risks relapse; switch should be planned and supervised.
Risk is dose-related but there is no safe dose.

items.topic: Microcytosis: thalassaemia trait vs iron deficiency, antenatal carrier screening
items.stem: A woman at 8 weeks' gestation has MCV 66 fL, normal ferritin and HbA2 5.2%. Her partner's carrier status is unknown. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Offer partner testing with FBE and haemoglobin studies
Start oral iron and repeat in 3 months
items.why: Raised HbA2 indicates beta-thalassaemia trait. Test the partner promptly; if also a carrier, offer genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis.
notes: Iron is not indicated with normal ferritin.
Her baby may be severely affected if the partner is a carrier.
Prenatal diagnosis is premature before partner status is known.

items.topic: Lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, staging
items.stem: Which feature best explains why chronic lymphocytic leukaemia often causes hypogammaglobulinaemia and recurrent infections?
options: Accumulation of dysfunctional clonal mature B cells that fail to make effective antibody
Excess T-cell suppression of neutrophil production
Loss of complement components from chronic haemolysis
items.why: CLL is a clonal expansion of mature, functionally incompetent B cells, so normal plasma cell antibody production falls. Recurrent bacterial infections follow.
notes: Neutropenia may occur from marrow infiltration, but T-cell suppression is not the main mechanism of the infection risk.
Autoimmune haemolysis can occur in CLL, but it does not explain hypogammaglobulinaemia.
The thymus is not destroyed in CLL.

items.topic: Airway emergencies: upper airway obstruction, rapid sequence intubation principles, tension pneumothorax
items.stem: In tension pneumothorax, which mechanism is the main cause of cardiovascular collapse?
options: Direct compression of the coronary arteries
Reduced venous return from raised intrathoracic pressure
Primary left ventricular failure from hypoxia
items.why: A one-way valve traps air, raising intrathoracic pressure and mediastinal shift, kinking the great veins and cutting venous return and cardiac output. Hypoxia contributes but is not the primary cause.
notes: Coronary compression is not the mechanism.
Hypoxia contributes, but obstructive shock from reduced preload dominates.
No pericardial fluid is present; this is obstructive shock but not tamponade.

items.topic: Fatty liver (MASLD) and alcohol-related liver disease: fibrosis assessment, abstinence, alcoholic hepatitis
items.stem: A 45-year-old man with heavy alcohol use presents with jaundice, fever and tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin is 250 µmol/L, INR 2.0, AST 180 U/L, ALT 70 U/L. Infection is excluded and Maddrey score is 45. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.why: Severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey ≥32) without infection or GI bleed is treated with prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days, plus nutrition and abstinence support. Lille score assesses response.
notes: NAC alone is not standard treatment for alcoholic hepatitis.
TIPS is for portal hypertension complications, not this.
UDCA has no proven benefit and is not used.

items.topic: Trauma primary survey: EMST/ATLS ABCDE, haemorrhagic shock, massive transfusion
items.stem: A 30-year-old man arrives after a motorcycle crash, talking in short sentences. He has absent breath sounds on the right, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation and BP 70/40. What is the immediate management?
options: Needle or finger decompression of the right chest
items.why: This is tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis. Immediate decompression (finger thoracostomy or needle) then intercostal catheter; do not wait for imaging.
notes: Delaying for imaging risks cardiac arrest.
Positive pressure ventilation without decompression worsens tension physiology.
Pericardiocentesis is for tamponade; here breath sounds are absent with tracheal deviation.

items.topic: Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, myasthenic crisis, drugs that worsen it
items.stem: A 55-year-old with myasthenia gravis, a day after starting ciprofloxacin, has dysphagia, a weak cough and a falling forced vital capacity. What is the best management?
options: Admit to ICU, stop ciprofloxacin, and give IVIG or plasma exchange
Increase pyridostigmine at home and review in a week
Start high-dose prednisolone alone as an outpatient
items.why: This is myasthenic crisis precipitated by a fluoroquinolone. Secure the airway with close FVC monitoring in ICU, remove the trigger and give IVIG or plasma exchange.
notes: Outpatient care is unsafe with bulbar and respiratory involvement.
Steroids alone can transiently worsen weakness and act too slowly.
Aminoglycosides also worsen myasthenia gravis.

items.topic: Myeloproliferative neoplasms: polycythaemia vera (JAK2), essential thrombocythaemia
items.stem: A 58-year-old man has headaches, itching after hot showers and a ruddy face. Haemoglobin is 205 g/L, haematocrit 0.62, platelets 520 x10^9/L, neutrophils raised. Serum erythropoietin is low. What is the most appropriate next test?
options: JAK2 V617F mutation analysis on peripheral blood
Bone marrow biopsy for ringed sideroblasts
items.why: Raised haemoglobin/haematocrit with low erythropoietin suggests polycythaemia vera; JAK2 V617F is present in over 95%. Test JAK2 first (exon 12 if negative).
notes: BCR-ABL1 is for CML; it is not the first test for erythrocytosis with low erythropoietin.
Carbon monoxide causes secondary polycythaemia with normal or high erythropoietin, and would not explain pruritus and thrombocytosis.
Ringed sideroblasts suggest myelodysplasia, not PV.

items.topic: Environmental emergencies: heat stroke, hypothermia, drowning
items.stem: A 22-year-old footballer collapses in a hot summer match. He is confused, core temperature 42°C, HR 140, BP 100/60. After airway and IV access, what is the most effective immediate treatment?
options: Rapid cooling by cold water immersion
items.why: Exertional heat stroke needs immediate rapid cooling, ideally cold or ice-water immersion, aiming to cool below 39°C quickly. Antipyretics and dantrolene do not work.
notes: Antipyretics act on the hypothalamic set point and are ineffective in heat stroke.
Dantrolene has no proven benefit in heat stroke.
Tepid sponging is too slow for exertional heat stroke; rapid cooling lowers mortality.

items.topic: Acute pancreatitis: gallstones and alcohol, lipase, fluid resuscitation, severity and complications
items.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Which finding best confirms the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
options: Serum lipase greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal
Serum amylase above the upper limit of normal
items.why: Diagnosis requires two of three: typical pain, lipase (or amylase) >3 times the upper limit, and imaging findings. Lipase is more specific than amylase.
notes: Amylase is less specific and any mild elevation is not diagnostic.
ALP is a cholestatic marker, not diagnostic.
CRP is a nonspecific severity marker.

items.topic: Sepsis: recognition, blood cultures, empirical antibiotics within the hour, source control
items.stem: In septic shock, which mechanism best explains the profound hypotension despite a normal or high cardiac output early on?
options: Cytokine-mediated vasodilation and increased capillary permeability
Primary failure of the sinoatrial node
Adrenal overproduction of catecholamines causing vasodilation
Direct bacterial toxin blockade of cardiac calcium channels
items.why: Endotoxin and cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) induce nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation and endothelial leak, lowering systemic vascular resistance and effective volume (distributive shock).
notes: The SA node is not the primary problem; tachycardia is typical in early sepsis.
Catecholamines cause vasoconstriction; relative adrenal insufficiency, not excess, may occur.
Myocardial depression may occur later but is not the main cause of early hypotension.

items.topic: Sepsis and septic shock: fluids, vasopressors, lactate
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has pneumonia. BP is 78/40 mmHg, lactate 5.2 mmol/L. She has received 30 mL/kg crystalloid and remains hypotensive with a MAP of 55 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give a further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus
Give IV hydrocortisone as the sole therapy
items.why: Fluid-refractory septic shock needs a vasopressor, with noradrenaline first-line, targeting MAP of at least 65 mmHg. Continue antibiotics and source control.
notes: Repeated large boluses risk overload; vasopressors are indicated after initial resuscitation.
Dopamine is not first-line and is more arrhythmogenic than noradrenaline.
Steroids are adjunctive for ongoing vasopressor need, not sole therapy.

items.topic: Fever in the returned traveller: malaria (thick and thin films), dengue, typhoid
items.stem: A man returns from Papua New Guinea with fever. The thick film is positive, but parasitaemia must be quantified and species identified. Which film is best for identifying species and calculating percentage parasitaemia?
items.why: The thick film is more sensitive for detecting parasites, while the thin film shows red cell morphology for species identification and percent parasitaemia. A rapid antigen test or PCR supports this.
notes: The thick film is for sensitivity, not species or percentage.
Gram stain does not identify malaria.
Bone marrow is unnecessary.

items.topic: Hepatitis B and C: serology interpretation, DAA cure for hepatitis C, HCC surveillance, migrant and First Nations prevalence
items.stem: A 52-year-old man born in Vietnam has chronic hepatitis B with compensated cirrhosis. What surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma is recommended?
options: Liver ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months
items.why: Australian guidelines recommend 6-monthly ultrasound (with or without AFP) for people with cirrhosis and for many with hepatitis B from higher-risk groups.
notes: Annual CT is too infrequent and involves radiation.
AFP alone is insensitive and 12 months is too long.
Biopsy is not a surveillance tool.

items.topic: Burns: TBSA estimation, fluid resuscitation, ANZBA referral criteria, airway burns
items.stem: Which process mainly explains the large fluid shift in the first 24 hours after a major burn?
options: Increased capillary permeability with loss of plasma into interstitium
items.why: Inflammatory mediators increase capillary permeability, causing plasma and protein loss into tissue, hypovolaemia and oedema. Fluid resuscitation replaces this.
notes: Renal losses are not the main cause of early burn shock.
GI bleeding is a late complication, not the main early shift.
ADH is typically raised, not reduced, after burns.

items.topic: Aortic dissection: presentation, CT angiography, Stanford A vs B management
items.stem: A 62-year-old hypertensive man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 200/110 mmHg. CT angiography shows a dissection of the ascending aorta. After analgesia and heart rate and BP control, what is the definitive management?
items.why: Acute type A dissection is a surgical emergency with high mortality. Meanwhile give IV beta-blockade (e.g. esmolol or labetalol) targeting HR below 60 and systolic BP 100–120 mmHg.
notes: Medical therapy alone is for uncomplicated type B dissection.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated and would be fatal.
Delay is unacceptable; type A needs immediate surgery.

items.topic: Febrile neutropenia: piperacillin-tazobactam within an hour, risk assessment
items.stem: A patient on chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 0.2 x10^9/L. Which defence mechanism is mainly lost, making rapid bacterial sepsis the main risk?
items.why: Neutrophils are the main phagocytes that ingest and kill bacteria and fungi. Their loss allows rapid bacteraemia, often with few localising signs.
notes: Antibody production is a B-cell function and is not primarily affected by neutropenia.
Complement is a plasma protein system and is unaffected by a low neutrophil count.
Cytotoxic T and NK cells handle virus-infected cells; they are not neutrophils.

items.topic: Acute behavioural disturbance: de-escalation, safe sedation, medical causes
items.stem: A 35-year-old agitated man in the ED is threatening staff. Verbal de-escalation has failed and oral medication is refused. Before sedating, which action is most important?
options: Exclude hypoglycaemia with a bedside glucose
items.why: Rapidly reversible medical causes such as hypoglycaemia must be excluded early in acute behavioural disturbance, with bedside glucose and observations, without delaying needed safe sedation.
notes: CT may be needed later but not before sedating and would delay care.
Drug screens are slow and rarely change immediate management.
Psychiatric review follows medical assessment and should not precede it.

items.topic: Breast lump: triple assessment, breast cancer referral, BreastScreen Australia
items.stem: A woman has a breast cancer in the upper outer quadrant. To which lymph node group does most of the breast's lymph drain, making it the first site of spread?
items.why: About 75% of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes, so the sentinel node is usually axillary. Internal mammary drainage is more relevant to medial tumours.
notes: Receives a smaller share, mainly from medial and central tumours; not the main first station.
Supraclavicular nodes are a higher, later echelon; involvement indicates advanced disease.
Contralateral drainage is an uncommon route of late spread.

items.topic: Early pregnancy bleeding: ectopic pregnancy (beta-hCG, ultrasound, methotrexate), miscarriage
items.stem: A woman at 8 weeks has bleeding and cramping. Ultrasound shows an intrauterine embryo with a crown–rump length of 8 mm and no fetal heartbeat. The cervical os is closed. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: A CRL of 7 mm or more with no heartbeat confirms embryonic demise. With the embryo retained and the os closed, this is a missed (delayed) miscarriage.
notes: Threatened miscarriage has a viable pregnancy with a heartbeat.
Incomplete miscarriage means some products have been passed; here the embryo is still in situ with a closed os.
An intrauterine embryo is seen, so ectopic is not the diagnosis.

items.topic: The surgical abdomen in children: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting)
items.stem: A 9-month-old boy has episodic inconsolable crying with drawing up of legs, pallor between episodes and a redcurrant jelly stool. Which test is the investigation of choice?
items.why: This is intussusception; ultrasound shows the target or doughnut sign and is the preferred diagnostic test. Treatment is by air enema reduction if stable.
notes: X-ray is insensitive and may be normal; it is not the best test.
Used for malrotation, not intussusception.
Gastroenteritis does not explain colicky pain with redcurrant jelly stool and delays diagnosis.

items.topic: Influenza and COVID-19: antivirals for high-risk patients, vaccination, infection control
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with COPD has had 24 hours of fever, myalgia and cough. She tests positive for influenza A on PCR and is hypoxic on arrival to hospital. What is the most appropriate antiviral management?
options: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, started now
No antiviral as she presented after 24 hours
Oral oseltamivir only if chest x-ray shows pneumonia
Oral nirmatrelvir with ritonavir for 5 days
items.why: Hospitalised patients with influenza should receive oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days (adjusted for renal function) as soon as possible, without waiting for confirmation.
notes: She is within 48 hours and is also hospitalised, so treatment is indicated.
Treatment does not depend on radiological pneumonia.
Nirmatrelvir with ritonavir is for COVID-19, not influenza.

items.topic: Epidemiology and evidence: study designs, bias and confounding, screening principles, lead-time bias
items.stem: Which study design is best suited to investigating the cause of a rare disease, by comparing past exposures in affected and unaffected people?
items.why: Case-control studies start with outcome and look back at exposure, so they are efficient for rare diseases. They give odds ratios.
notes: Cohorts follow exposed people forward and need huge numbers for rare outcomes.
Cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence at one time and cannot establish past exposure well.
RCTs test interventions and are impractical for investigating harmful exposures.

items.topic: Other poisonings: tricyclics (sodium bicarbonate), opioids, benzodiazepines, toxic alcohols, Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26
items.stem: A 40-year-old man presents after a suspected methanol ingestion with visual blurring, HCO3 10 mmol/L and a high anion gap. Which treatment is most appropriate, after calling the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26)?
items.why: Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid. Fomepizole blocks this enzyme; haemodialysis is used for severe acidosis, visual symptoms or high levels.
notes: Charcoal does not bind alcohols effectively.
Naloxone reverses opioids, not toxic alcohols.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and is not relevant here.

items.topic: Bradyarrhythmias and heart block: ECG recognition, drug causes, pacing indications
items.stem: Which structure normally acts as the dominant pacemaker of the heart because it has the fastest rate of spontaneous phase 4 depolarisation?
items.why: The SA node has the steepest phase 4 slope (about 60-100 beats/min) and overdrives slower subsidiary pacemakers. If it fails, lower pacemakers take over at slower rates.
notes: The AV node's intrinsic rate is slower (about 40-60/min); it is an escape pacemaker only if the SA node fails.
The His bundle has a slower intrinsic rate and is only a subsidiary pacemaker.
Purkinje fibres fire at about 20-40/min and are the last-resort escape focus.

items.topic: Fitness to drive and work: Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive', the doctor's duties, workers' compensation
items.stem: A 66-year-old private car driver is diagnosed with moderate obstructive sleep apnoea and excessive daytime sleepiness. According to Austroads principles, what is the most appropriate advice?
options: Do not drive until treated and sleepiness is controlled, with review
items.why: Untreated OSA with excessive sleepiness is a conditional licence matter: stop driving until treated effectively and sleepiness is controlled, then review. It is not permanent.
notes: Sleepiness significantly raises crash risk; driving should stop until controlled.
Permanent restriction isn't needed if treatment works.
Night driving is no safer; sleepiness is the issue.

items.topic: Atrial fibrillation: CHA2DS2-VA stroke risk (Australian 2018 guideline), DOAC choice, rate vs rhythm control
items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has permanent AF with a mechanical mitral valve. Her GP considers a DOAC for stroke prevention. Which anticoagulant is appropriate?
items.why: Mechanical valves require warfarin. DOACs are contraindicated (dabigatran was inferior and harmful in the RE-ALIGN trial).
notes: DOACs are not recommended with mechanical valves.
DOACs are not recommended with mechanical valves.
Dabigatran increased thromboembolism and bleeding in mechanical valves.

items.topic: The febrile child: serious bacterial infection red flags, febrile infant under 3 months, urine testing
items.stem: Why are febrile infants under 3 months at higher risk of serious bacterial infection and meningitis than older children?
options: Immature cell-mediated and humoral immunity with poor localising signs
Maternal IgG levels peak at this age
Fever is a poor marker of infection at this age
Higher gastric pH kills fewer bacteria
items.why: Neonatal and young infant immunity is immature (reduced opsonisation, neutrophil function), and signs are non-specific, so infection can disseminate silently.
notes: Maternal IgG falls after birth, reaching a nadir around 3-4 months.
Fever is a significant marker; any fever of 38.0°C or more needs assessment.
Gastric pH is a minor factor; it is not the main reason.

items.topic: Cervical screening: HPV test every 5 years from 25 to 74 including self-collection, managing results
items.stem: Which HPV type pair accounts for the majority of cervical squamous cell carcinomas and is reported individually by the Australian cervical screening test?
items.why: HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers and are genotyped separately; other high-risk types are reported as a pooled group.
notes: These cause genital warts and are low-risk.
These are high-risk but less common and are reported in the pooled 'other oncogenic' group.
These cause cutaneous warts.

items.topic: Cirrhosis complications: ascites and SBP, hepatic encephalopathy, varices, Child-Pugh
items.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has tense ascites, fever and abdominal tenderness. Ascitic fluid neutrophils are 0.45 × 10^9/L (450/mm3). Creatinine is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.why: Ascitic neutrophils ≥0.25 × 10^9/L indicate SBP. Treat with IV third-generation cephalosporin plus albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3) to reduce renal failure and mortality.
notes: Oral prophylaxis is not treatment of established SBP.
Paracentesis does not treat the infection.
SBP is primary peritonitis and is not managed surgically; anaerobic cover is not required.

items.topic: Multiple sclerosis: optic neuritis, MRI, relapse treatment
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis has 4 days of new visual loss and pain on movement in her right eye, consistent with optic neuritis. She is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days
Oral prednisolone 5 mg daily long term
items.why: Acute disabling MS relapses are treated with high-dose corticosteroids, usually IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days. This speeds recovery but doesn't change long-term outcome.
notes: Low-dose long-term steroids are not a relapse treatment and cause harm.
IVIg is not standard for MS relapse.
Plasma exchange is reserved for severe relapses unresponsive to steroids.

items.topic: Pneumothorax: primary vs secondary, tension physiology, observe vs aspirate vs drain
items.stem: Normally the intrapleural pressure is subatmospheric at end-expiration. What is the main reason for this?
options: Outward recoil of the lung and inward recoil of the chest wall
Inward recoil of the lung balanced by outward recoil of the chest wall
items.why: At FRC the lung recoils inward and the chest wall springs outward, so the pleural space is held at negative pressure. A pneumothorax abolishes this and the lung collapses.
notes: Reversed: the lung recoils inward, not outward, and the chest wall outward.
Surfactant lowers surface tension, reducing the lung's tendency to collapse.
The diaphragm is relaxed at end-expiration; negative pressure persists without muscle activity.

items.topic: Peripheral neuropathy and nerve palsies: diabetes, B12, carpal tunnel, common peroneal nerve
items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has night-time tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking the hand. Examination shows thenar wasting and a positive Phalen test. What is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?
items.why: Carpal tunnel syndrome is confirmed with nerve conduction studies, which show slowed median nerve conduction across the wrist. This is especially useful with thenar wasting, as it guides surgical release.
notes: MRI of the cervical spine is for suspected radiculopathy, which would not give this median nerve pattern.
B12 deficiency causes a symmetric sensory neuropathy, not a median nerve distribution.
X-ray does not assess nerve compression and rarely changes management.

items.topic: Biostatistics: sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, NNT, relative vs absolute risk
items.stem: A diagnostic test correctly identifies 90 of 100 people who have a disease. Which measure does this describe?
items.why: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive (TP/[TP+FN]). Here 90/100 = 90%.
notes: Specificity is the proportion of people without disease who test negative; this stem concerns diseased people.
PPV is the proportion of positive tests that are true positives; the denominator is test-positive people, not diseased people.
NPV is the proportion of negative tests that are truly disease-free; it is not calculated among diseased people.

items.topic: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: rupture presentation, surveillance and repair thresholds
items.stem: Which physical principle best explains why the risk of rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm rises sharply as its diameter increases?
options: Law of Laplace: wall tension rises with radius
Bernoulli principle: velocity falls with dilation
Poiseuille law: resistance rises with radius
Starling law: preload increases stroke volume
items.why: Laplace's law: wall tension is proportional to pressure × radius (divided by wall thickness), so a larger aneurysm has greater wall stress and rupture risk.
notes: Bernoulli relates pressure and velocity; it does not explain rupture risk with size.
Poiseuille resistance falls, not rises, with increasing radius, and concerns flow.
Starling law relates to cardiac function, not aortic wall stress.

items.topic: Facial weakness: Bell's palsy vs upper motor neurone lesion (forehead sparing), prednisolone
items.stem: A patient with a right middle cerebral artery stroke has left lower facial weakness but can wrinkle both sides of the forehead. What explains the forehead sparing?
options: The frontalis muscle is supplied by the trigeminal nerve
Upper facial motor neurones receive bilateral corticobulbar input
The chorda tympani supplies the forehead
Forehead muscles receive only ipsilateral cortical input
items.why: The facial nucleus part supplying the forehead gets corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, so a unilateral upper motor neurone lesion spares the forehead.
notes: Frontalis is supplied by the facial nerve, not the trigeminal nerve.
The chorda tympani carries taste and parasympathetic fibres, not forehead motor supply.
Forehead input is bilateral, which is why it is spared.

items.topic: Acute asthma and COPD exacerbation: severity assessment, nebulised and IV therapy, NIV
items.stem: A patient with severe acute asthma becomes drowsy and the PaCO2 is 5.5 kPa (normal). What does this indicate?
options: Respiratory muscle fatigue and impending respiratory failure
items.why: In severe asthma, hyperventilation lowers CO2; a normal or rising PaCO2 signals fatigue and impending failure and is an ominous sign.
notes: Improvement would show lower work of breathing and clinical improvement, not drowsiness.
Metabolic acidosis would not explain drowsiness with normal CO2 here.
Drowsiness shows deterioration, not a good response.

items.topic: Obstructive sleep apnoea: screening tools, CPAP, commercial and private driver fitness
items.stem: A 45-year-old commercial truck driver has an Epworth score of 16, BMI 38 and witnessed apnoeas. Sleep study shows severe OSA. He is starting CPAP. What is the most appropriate advice about driving?
options: Stop driving until treatment is effective and symptoms controlled, with specialist review
Continue driving as CPAP is not required for licence
items.why: Assessing Fitness to Drive says commercial drivers with severe OSA and sleepiness must not drive until treated effectively with symptoms controlled, then need periodic review.
notes: Untreated sleepy severe OSA is unfit for commercial driving.
Daylight restriction does not remove sleepiness-related crash risk.
Weight loss is advised but fitness depends on treatment and symptom control, not a set weight.

items.topic: Head injury: GCS, CT head rules, anticoagulated patients, extradural vs subdural haematoma
items.stem: A young man has a lucid interval after a blow to the temple, then deteriorates with a fixed dilated pupil. Which vessel is most likely torn, causing an extradural haematoma?
items.why: The middle meningeal artery runs under the pterion and is torn by a temporoparietal fracture, causing arterial bleeding into the extradural space. Bridging veins cause subdural haematoma.
notes: Bridging veins bleed into the subdural space, typically in older patients with atrophy, with a slower course.
Anterior communicating aneurysm rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage, not extradural haematoma.
Vein of Galen injury is rare and not the classic cause of extradural haematoma.

items.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health: MBS 715 health assessment, cultural safety, earlier screening ages
items.stem: A 31-year-old Aboriginal man, a non-smoker with no known conditions, attends his GP for an MBS 715 health assessment. His BP is 128/80 mmHg. What cardiovascular risk step is recommended at this visit?
options: Defer until age 45 as for the general population
Assess absolute CVD risk now, as it starts from age 30
Only assess if he has a first-degree relative with CVD
Only assess if his blood pressure is above 140/90 mmHg
items.why: Australian guidelines start absolute CVD risk assessment at 30 years for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, versus 45 for others. The 715 is the vehicle for this.
notes: Age 45 applies to non-Indigenous adults; the Indigenous threshold is 30.
Family history modifies risk but is not required to trigger assessment at 30.
Assessment is not conditional on raised BP; risk calculation includes BP, lipids and other factors.

items.topic: Interstitial lung disease: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, drug-induced (amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin)
items.stem: Which change in lung mechanics is characteristic of pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Reduced compliance with reduced lung volumes
Increased airway resistance with raised TLC
Normal compliance with reduced diffusion only
items.why: Fibrosis stiffens the lung: reduced compliance, restrictive pattern with low TLC and FVC, preserved or high FEV1/FVC, and low DLCO.
notes: That describes emphysema.
Raised TLC and resistance suggest obstructive disease.
Compliance is reduced, and volumes fall.

items.topic: Vascular emergencies: acute limb ischaemia (6 Ps), mesenteric ischaemia
items.stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation develops a sudden cold, pale, pulseless leg. Which tissues are most sensitive to ischaemia and drive the urgency of revascularisation?
items.why: Nerve and muscle tolerate only about 4–6 hours of acute ischaemia before irreversible damage, so sensory and motor loss signal a threatened limb.
notes: Skin tolerates ischaemia longer than muscle and nerve.
Bone is relatively ischaemia-tolerant.
Tendon and fascia have low metabolic demand and tolerate ischaemia.

items.topic: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: four-pillar therapy (ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor), acute decompensation
items.stem: A man with HFrEF on ramipril is switched to sacubitril/valsartan. What must be done before the first dose?
options: Stop ramipril for at least 36 hours
Continue both drugs for one week
Give a loading dose of digoxin
items.why: Combining an ACE inhibitor with sacubitril raises angioedema risk through bradykinin accumulation, so a 36-hour washout is required.
notes: Co-administration is contraindicated because of angioedema risk.
Digoxin is unnecessary and unrelated.
Beta-blockers are continued as a pillar of therapy.

items.topic: Strongyloides, scabies and skin sores in remote communities: ivermectin, impetigo and APSGN/ARF links
items.stem: A man from a Strongyloides-endemic region needs prolonged high-dose prednisolone for vasculitis. Serology is positive. Which is the most appropriate action before starting steroids?
options: Treat with ivermectin before or alongside steroids
Defer treatment until symptoms of diarrhoea develop
items.why: Positive serology needs treatment with ivermectin (two doses, 2 weeks apart) before immunosuppression to prevent fatal hyperinfection. Eosinophilia can be suppressed by steroids, so it is unreliable.
notes: Waiting for symptoms risks hyperinfection syndrome with sepsis.
Albendazole is less effective than ivermectin for Strongyloides.
Steroids suppress eosinophils, so monitoring is unreliable and dangerous.

items.topic: Type 2 diabetes: HbA1c diagnosis, stepwise therapy, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs for cardiorenal benefit, annual cycle of care
items.stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, previous myocardial infarction and eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m² has HbA1c 63 mmol/mol on maximally tolerated metformin. Which add-on is most appropriate for cardiorenal protection?
items.why: In type 2 diabetes with established cardiovascular disease or CKD, add an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA for proven cardiorenal benefit, independent of HbA1c.
notes: Sulfonylureas lower glucose but have no cardiorenal benefit and risk hypoglycaemia.
DPP-4 inhibitors are cardiovascularly neutral and do not protect the kidneys.
Pioglitazone can cause fluid retention and heart failure, so it is not preferred here.

items.topic: Abnormal uterine bleeding: PALM-COEIN, fibroids, endometrial sampling
items.stem: A 16-year-old has heavy irregular bleeding 2 years after menarche. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?
options: Anovulation with unopposed oestrogen and no progesterone
Corpus luteum persistence with prolonged progesterone
Excess prostaglandin from a copper device
items.why: Immature hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis causes anovulatory cycles. Unopposed oestrogen builds a thick, unstable endometrium that sheds irregularly and heavily (AUB-O).
notes: Persistent corpus luteum causes delayed, prolonged shedding, but anovulation is the usual cause here.
She has no device; this does not fit.
Hyperprolactinaemia causes amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea rather than heavy bleeding.

items.topic: Mandatory reporting: child abuse, notifiable conduct of practitioners (Ahpra), notifiable diseases
