items.stem: A GP in NSW sees a 6-year-old with bruising and a disclosure that a parent hit them with a belt. The GP believes the child is at risk of significant harm. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report to child protection (Child Wellbeing Unit or helpline) and document
Wait for parental consent before reporting
Refer to a paediatrician and review in four weeks
Report only if the injuries are fractures
items.why: Doctors are mandatory reporters in NSW where there are reasonable grounds to suspect risk of significant harm; consent is not required. Document the findings and report.
notes: Parental consent is not required; reporting overrides confidentiality.
Delay leaves the child at risk; reporting duty is immediate.
The threshold is risk of significant harm, not fractures.

items.topic: Kidney stones: renal colic, CT KUB, the obstructed infected kidney as an emergency
items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has left flank pain, fever 39.2°C, rigors and BP 90/55. CT KUB shows a 6 mm left proximal ureteric stone with hydronephrosis. After resuscitation and IV antibiotics, what is the next step?
options: Urgent decompression with ureteric stent or nephrostomy
Ureteroscopic stone removal at next elective list
items.why: An obstructed infected kidney is a urological emergency. Urgent decompression by stent or percutaneous nephrostomy is needed; definitive stone treatment is delayed until sepsis resolves.
notes: Medical expulsive therapy is inappropriate with sepsis and obstruction.
Lithotripsy in active infection risks worsening sepsis; decompress first.
Elective removal delays source control in sepsis.

items.topic: Burns: TBSA estimation, fluid resuscitation, ANZBA referral criteria, airway burns
items.stem: Using the rule of nines in an adult, what percentage of TBSA does the entire anterior trunk represent?
items.why: In adults the anterior trunk is 18% and posterior trunk 18%. Each arm is 9% and each leg is 18%, head 9%.
notes: 9% is one arm or the head.
27% is not a rule of nines region.
36% is the whole trunk, front and back.

items.topic: Acute coronary syndrome: STEMI vs NSTEACS on ECG, reperfusion timing, dual antiplatelet therapy
items.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with 30 minutes of chest pain at rest. ECG shows 1 mm ST depression in V4–V6. High-sensitivity troponin I is elevated and rising. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Ischaemic symptoms with ST depression and a rising troponin indicate NSTEMI, as myocardial necrosis is shown by the troponin. Unstable angina has no troponin rise.
notes: STEMI requires persistent ST elevation or a new LBBB-equivalent pattern.
Unstable angina has a normal troponin; here it is elevated.
Pericarditis causes diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, not regional ST depression.

items.topic: Status epilepticus: benzodiazepine first, second-line agent, timeline
items.stem: A 35-year-old man is still having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure 5 minutes after onset. Glucose is normal. Which is the best immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous midazolam 0.05 mg/kg or intramuscular midazolam 10 mg
items.why: A benzodiazepine is first-line once a seizure lasts 5 minutes. Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg is an effective option if there is no IV access; second-line agents follow if seizures persist.
notes: Levetiracetam is second-line, used if seizures continue after benzodiazepines.
Phenytoin is second-line and is not given before a benzodiazepine.
Anaesthetic induction is for refractory status after first and second-line agents have failed.

items.topic: Irritable bowel syndrome: Rome IV, excluding red flags, low-FODMAP diet
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had 8 months of recurrent abdominal pain, at least once weekly, relieved by defecation and with altered stool form. She has normal weight, Hb, CRP and a negative coeliac serology. Which feature would most need further investigation before diagnosing IBS?
items.why: Rectal bleeding is a red flag (as are weight loss, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, age over 50 onset, family history of bowel cancer or IBD) requiring investigation. The other features are typical of Rome IV IBS.
notes: Bloating is common in IBS and not a red flag.
Pain related to defecation is a core Rome IV criterion.
Stress exacerbation is typical of IBS.

items.topic: Consent, capacity and confidentiality: mature minors (Gillick), substitute decision-makers, exceptions
items.stem: An 80-year-old man with advanced dementia lacks capacity and needs non-urgent surgery. He has no appointed guardian or enduring power. Three adult children disagree. Who is the appropriate decision-maker under state law?
options: The person responsible, determined by statutory hierarchy
items.why: Where no appointed decision-maker exists, state legislation sets a hierarchy of the 'person responsible' (e.g. spouse, carer, then relatives). Disputes go to the guardianship tribunal.
notes: The doctor cannot consent for non-urgent treatment on the patient's behalf.
Birth order does not confer authority.
Executives are not statutory substitute decision-makers.

items.topic: Kawasaki disease: diagnostic criteria, IVIG and aspirin, coronary aneurysms
items.stem: Kawasaki disease is a systemic vasculitis. Which vessel size is primarily affected, accounting for coronary artery aneurysms?
options: Large elastic arteries such as the aorta
Small vessels with immune complex deposition
items.why: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis with a predilection for the coronary arteries, causing dilatation and aneurysm.
notes: Large-vessel vasculitis includes Takayasu and giant cell arteritis.
Small-vessel immune complex vasculitis includes Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis).
The disease affects medium arteries, not capillaries alone.

items.topic: Pleural effusion: Light's criteria, transudate vs exudate causes, empyema drainage
items.stem: A pleural fluid sample has fluid:serum protein ratio 0.3, fluid:serum LDH ratio 0.4, and fluid LDH below two-thirds of the upper limit of the serum normal. In a patient with ankle oedema, which is the likely cause?
items.why: Light's criteria are not met (protein ratio <0.5, LDH ratio <0.6, fluid LDH <2/3 upper serum limit), so this is a transudate. Cardiac failure is the commonest cause.
notes: Parapneumonic effusions are exudates and meet Light's criteria.
Malignant effusions are typically exudates.
PE usually causes an exudate, occasionally a transudate, and is a less likely cause here.

items.topic: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: weight-based IM adrenaline, ASCIA action plans, early allergen introduction
items.stem: A healthy 5-month-old with no eczema is to start solids. According to ASCIA guidance, what is the best advice about introducing peanut and egg?
options: Introduce them around 6 months, but not before 4 months, as part of the diet
Delay peanut until 12 months of age
Delay egg until 2 years of age
Introduce only after skin prick testing
items.why: ASCIA advises introducing allergenic foods (peanut butter paste, well-cooked egg) in the first year, when the infant is ready at about 6 months and not before 4 months. Delay does not prevent allergy.
notes: Delaying peanut increases allergy risk and is not recommended.
Delaying egg is not recommended and may increase risk of egg allergy.
Routine testing is not required in low-risk infants; it is only considered for high-risk infants.

items.topic: Orthopaedic emergencies: hip fracture and orthogeriatric care, compartment syndrome, open fractures, septic arthritis
items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has a hot swollen knee, fever 38.8°C and refuses to weight-bear. What is the most important next step?
options: Joint aspiration for microscopy and culture before antibiotics
Oral anti-inflammatories and review in 48 hours
items.why: Suspected septic arthritis needs urgent joint aspiration or washout for Gram stain and culture, then IV antibiotics. Do not delay for imaging.
notes: Delay risks cartilage destruction.
MRI delays definitive diagnosis and drainage.
Oral outpatient treatment is inappropriate before diagnosis and drainage.

items.topic: Methamphetamine and other stimulant use: acute agitation, psychosis, harm minimisation
items.stem: A 28-year-old man with methamphetamine intoxication is agitated, sweaty and paranoid, HR 128, temp 37.8°C. Verbal de-escalation in a quiet room has failed. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral or parenteral benzodiazepine, such as diazepam or midazolam
items.why: After failed de-escalation, benzodiazepines are first-line for stimulant agitation, treating agitation, tachycardia and hypertension. Antipsychotics are second-line.
notes: Naloxone reverses opioids, which are not implicated here.
Beta-blockers risk unopposed alpha stimulation and are avoided.
Thiamine and glucose are not indicated without alcohol-related or hypoglycaemic features.

items.topic: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline dose, refractory anaphylaxis, observation period
items.stem: Which mechanism of adrenaline is most important for reversing upper airway oedema and hypotension in anaphylaxis?
options: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction reducing mucosal oedema and raising vascular tone
Beta-2 mediated inhibition of IgE production
items.why: Alpha-1 agonism causes vasoconstriction, raising blood pressure and reducing mucosal oedema; beta-1 raises output and beta-2 causes bronchodilation and limits mediator release.
notes: Adrenaline does not reduce IgE production.
Adrenaline is not antimuscarinic.
It does not inhibit histamine synthesis; it opposes its effects physiologically.

items.topic: Fever in the returned traveller: malaria (thick and thin films), dengue, typhoid
items.stem: A 28-year-old returns from Bali with 5 days of fever, severe myalgia and retro-orbital pain. Platelets are 60 ×10⁹/L, haematocrit rising, and she has abdominal pain and persistent vomiting. Which is the best next step?
options: Admit for fluid monitoring as warning signs of severe dengue are present
Start empirical ceftriaxone for typhoid and discharge
items.why: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and rising haematocrit with falling platelets are dengue warning signs; admit for monitored fluids around defervescence. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin.
notes: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and are avoided in dengue.
Ceftriaxone does not address the likely dengue and she needs admission.
Prophylactic platelets are not recommended without significant bleeding.

items.topic: Cardiovascular drugs: ACEi/ARB hyperkalaemia and the triple whammy, beta-blockers, digoxin and amiodarone toxicity
items.stem: A 74-year-old man with heart failure takes perindopril and frusemide. He starts regular ibuprofen for knee pain and develops gastroenteritis. Creatinine rises from 100 to 220 micromol/L. Which prescribing combination is described by the 'triple whammy'?
items.why: An ACEi or ARB, a diuretic and an NSAID together, especially with volume depletion, markedly increase the risk of acute kidney injury. Withhold them during dehydrating illness.
notes: Beta-blockers are not part of the triple whammy.
Statins are not involved in the renal haemodynamic mechanism.
Digoxin is not part of the triple whammy, though it accumulates in AKI.

items.topic: Fatty liver (MASLD) and alcohol-related liver disease: fibrosis assessment, abstinence, alcoholic hepatitis
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains hepatic steatosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)?
options: Insulin resistance increasing adipose lipolysis and hepatic de novo lipogenesis
Increased hepatic beta-oxidation exceeding triglyceride supply
Impaired hepatic glucose uptake causing hypoglycaemia
items.why: Insulin resistance increases free fatty acid flux from adipose tissue and hepatic de novo lipogenesis, while export and oxidation are inadequate, so triglyceride accumulates.
notes: Beta-oxidation is typically impaired or overwhelmed, not excessive.
VLDL export is insufficient relative to input, not excessive.
Hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia are typical, not hypoglycaemia.

items.topic: Postoperative complications: fever by postoperative day, anastomotic leak, wound infection, AKI
items.stem: A man is oliguric 24 hours after a long operation with intraoperative hypotension. Urine sodium is high and urine osmolality is similar to plasma. Which process best explains this?
options: Renal tubular epithelial injury impairing concentration
items.why: Ischaemic acute tubular necrosis impairs sodium reabsorption and concentrating ability, giving high urinary sodium and isosmolar urine. Prerenal states give avid sodium retention.
notes: Activated RAAS in prerenal AKI gives low urine sodium and concentrated urine.
Obstruction is a postrenal cause and does not typically give this pattern; a bladder scan would show it.
Raised ADH produces concentrated urine, not isosmolar urine.

items.topic: Febrile convulsions and childhood epilepsy: simple vs complex, counselling parents
items.stem: Which is a feature of a complex febrile seizure?
options: Focal features or recurrence within 24 hours
items.why: Complex febrile seizures are focal, last longer than 15 minutes, or recur within 24 hours. Simple ones are generalised, brief and single.
notes: A 2-minute seizure is brief, which fits a simple seizure.
Generalised tonic-clonic activity is typical of simple febrile seizures.
Age 2 years is within the typical window of 6 months to 6 years.

items.topic: Anxiety disorders: GAD and panic disorder, CBT first, SSRIs, avoiding benzodiazepine dependence
items.stem: Benzodiazepines reduce anxiety by enhancing which neurotransmitter action?
options: GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency
items.why: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening and producing neuronal inhibition. Tolerance and dependence follow with prolonged use.
notes: That is the SSRI mechanism.
NMDA blockade is the mechanism of ketamine, not benzodiazepines.
Benzodiazepines do not increase noradrenaline release.

items.topic: Ovarian masses: torsion, cyst rupture, ovarian cancer (CA-125, risk of malignancy)
items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain and vomiting. Urine hCG is negative. Ultrasound shows a 7 cm ovarian cyst with an enlarged ovary; Doppler shows arterial flow is present. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Serum CA-125 and repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks
Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation
Analgesia, antiemetics and discharge with review in 1 week
items.why: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis; preserved Doppler flow does not exclude it. Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion conserves the ovary, even if it looks dusky.
notes: Delay risks ovarian loss, and CA-125 is not useful in a young woman with acute pain.
Discharge risks ovarian necrosis; suspected torsion needs prompt surgical assessment.
Oophorectomy is not first-line; detorsion usually salvages the ovary, and laparoscopy is preferred.

items.topic: Endometriosis and polycystic ovary syndrome: diagnosis, fertility, metabolic risk
items.stem: Which pathophysiological feature underlies the hyperandrogenism and anovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome?
options: Hyperinsulinaemia and raised LH driving ovarian theca androgen production
Low LH with high FSH causing follicular arrest
Excess cortisol suppressing the ovarian axis
items.why: Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia and raised LH pulsatility stimulates theca cells to make androgens, and reduces SHBG, increasing free androgen. This impairs follicle maturation.
notes: PCOS typically has a raised LH:FSH ratio, not low LH with high FSH.
Cortisol excess is Cushing syndrome, a differential rather than the PCOS mechanism.
Hyperprolactinaemia is a differential for oligomenorrhoea, not the mechanism of PCOS.

items.topic: Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending weakness, FVC monitoring, IVIG
items.stem: Which measure best predicts impending neuromuscular respiratory failure in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
items.why: Respiratory muscle weakness causes a falling vital capacity before hypoxia or hypercapnia. Hypercapnia and desaturation are late signs.
notes: Hypercapnia is a late sign, after the patient is already failing.
Saturation stays normal until late because of compensatory tachypnoea.
A chest X-ray does not measure respiratory muscle strength.

items.topic: Alcohol: NHMRC guideline (no more than 10 standard drinks a week and 4 on any day), brief intervention
items.stem: A 42-year-old man drinks 3 standard drinks most evenings, with 6 on Saturdays. He has a positive AUDIT-C, no withdrawal history and no dependence. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start naltrexone and review in one year
Brief intervention advising no more than 10 drinks a week and 4 on any day
Reassure, as his intake is within NHMRC limits
items.why: He drinks about 21 to 27 standard drinks a week, above the NHMRC limits of 10 a week and 4 on any day. A brief intervention with feedback and advice is first-line.
notes: No dependence or withdrawal history, so inpatient withdrawal is unnecessary.
Pharmacotherapy is for moderate to severe use disorder, not first-line here.
He exceeds both the weekly and single-day limits.

items.topic: Skin cancer: melanoma (features, excision margins), BCC and SCC, Australia's high incidence
items.stem: A 55-year-old man has a 1.5 mm Breslow thickness invasive melanoma on his back, diagnosed on excisional biopsy with narrow margins. What is the recommended wide excision margin?
items.why: Australian guidelines recommend 1–2 cm margins for melanoma 1.01–2 mm thick (1 cm for ≤1 mm... 5–10 mm for in situ). Margins above 2 cm give no benefit.
notes: Appropriate for in situ melanoma (5–10 mm), not an invasive 1.5 mm lesion.
1 cm alone is for thin melanomas up to 1 mm; 1.5 mm allows 1–2 cm.
3 cm is not recommended; 2 cm is the maximum even for thicker melanomas.

items.topic: Diabetic kidney disease: albuminuria, ACEi/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors
items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m², urine ACR 25 mg/mmol and BP 128/78 on perindopril at maximal dose. HbA1c is 7.4%. Which addition most reduces her risk of kidney disease progression?
items.why: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) added to an ACEi/ARB slow CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular events in diabetic kidney disease, even at modest glycaemic effect.
notes: Amlodipine lowers BP but gives no renoprotection beyond BP, and her BP is controlled.
Sulfonylureas do not slow CKD and risk hypoglycaemia at reduced eGFR.
Spironolactone adds hyperkalaemia risk; it is not the first add-on over an SGLT2 inhibitor.

items.topic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change in children, membranous in adults, thrombosis and infection risk
items.stem: A 55-year-old man has nephrotic syndrome from biopsy-proven membranous nephropathy. He has serum albumin 18 g/L, a sudden left flank pain and haematuria. Doppler shows no hydronephrosis. Which complication should be suspected first?
items.why: Membranous nephropathy with low albumin (<20-25 g/L) carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis and VTE due to urinary loss of antithrombin and a hypercoagulable state. Flank pain and haematuria are typical.
notes: Infection risk is raised, but fever and pyuria would be expected rather than an acute thrombotic picture.
A calculus is possible, but hydronephrosis is absent and the nephrotic hypercoagulable state is the stronger link.
Papillary necrosis occurs with diabetes, analgesics or sickle cell disease, not nephrotic syndrome.

items.topic: Acute appendicitis: clinical scores, imaging in children and in pregnancy
items.stem: A 26-year-old at 24 weeks' gestation has 2 days of right-sided abdominal pain and vomiting. Examination shows right flank tenderness. Ultrasound is non-diagnostic and she is stable. What is the most appropriate next imaging?
items.why: In pregnancy, ultrasound first, then non-contrast MRI if non-diagnostic, avoiding radiation. CT is reserved for when MRI is unavailable or the patient is unstable.
notes: CT delivers fetal radiation; use only if MRI is unavailable.
X-ray is low yield and gives radiation.
Delay risks perforation, which carries high fetal loss.

items.topic: Infectious diarrhoea and C. difficile: oral rehydration, traveller's diarrhoea, antibiotic-associated colitis
items.stem: A 70-year-old woman, 5 days into amoxicillin-clavulanate for cellulitis, has 8 watery stools daily with abdominal cramping. Stool PCR is positive for toxigenic C. difficile. Creatinine and white cell count are mildly raised and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, and stop the inciting antibiotic if possible
Oral loperamide and oral rehydration alone
items.why: Current Australian guidance favours oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin for C. difficile, and the inciting antibiotic should be stopped where possible. Antimotility agents are avoided.
notes: Loperamide is avoided and does not treat the infection.
IV metronidazole alone is not first line; metronidazole is now second-line.
Fluoroquinolones are a risk factor for C. difficile, not treatment.

items.topic: Suicide and self-harm: risk formulation, safety planning, when to detain
items.stem: Which of the following is the strongest single predictor of future suicide in a patient presenting after self-harm?
items.why: Previous self-harm is the strongest predictor of later suicide. Risk factors are used for formulation, but no tool predicts who will die.
notes: Women attempt more often, but men die by suicide more often.
Employment is generally protective.
Living with family is generally protective; living alone raises risk.

items.topic: Cushing's syndrome: exogenous steroids as the commonest cause, screening tests
items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has weight gain, bruising and proximal weakness. She takes no steroids. Which is an appropriate initial screening test for Cushing syndrome?
items.why: Screening uses late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol or a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Confirm abnormal results before localising.
notes: Random cortisol varies diurnally and cannot screen.
ACTH is used after biochemical confirmation to find the cause.
High-dose suppression helps localise cause, not screen.

items.topic: Antipsychotics: extrapyramidal effects, metabolic syndrome, QT prolongation, clozapine monitoring
items.stem: A 28-year-old man on clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia presents with fever and sore throat. His neutrophil count is 0.8 × 10^9/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue clozapine and repeat the count in one week
Reduce the clozapine dose by half and give paracetamol
Switch to olanzapine the same day without further tests
Cease clozapine and urgently refer for haematology review and management of neutropenia
items.why: Neutrophils below 1.0 × 10^9/L on clozapine, with fever, suggest severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis. Stop clozapine and manage urgently with haematology input.
notes: Continuing risks life-threatening infection.
Dose reduction does not treat agranulocytosis; cessation is required.
A febrile neutropenic patient needs urgent assessment first, and switching blindly is inappropriate.

items.topic: Microcytosis: thalassaemia trait vs iron deficiency, antenatal carrier screening
items.stem: Which finding best distinguishes beta-thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency in a patient with microcytosis?
options: Raised red cell count with normal or high ferritin
Low ferritin with raised red cell count
Raised red cell distribution width with low red cell count
Low transferrin saturation with high ferritin
items.why: Thalassaemia trait gives a high red cell count with marked microcytosis and normal iron stores; iron deficiency has low ferritin and a low red cell count.
notes: Low ferritin indicates iron deficiency, which typically has a low red cell count.
Raised RDW with low RCC fits iron deficiency.
Low saturation with high ferritin suggests inflammation, not thalassaemia trait.

items.topic: Abnormal uterine bleeding: PALM-COEIN, fibroids, endometrial sampling
items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with BMI 38 has had 8 months of irregular heavy bleeding. Pelvic ultrasound shows endometrial thickness 14 mm and no fibroids. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.why: Women over 45, or younger with risk factors such as obesity, with persistent AUB need endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia or cancer. A thickened endometrium raises concern.
notes: FSH is unreliable in perimenopause and does not exclude endometrial pathology.
Waiting delays diagnosis in a high-risk woman.
CA-125 is not a screening test for endometrial cancer and is non-specific.

items.topic: Orthopaedic emergencies: hip fracture and orthogeriatric care, compartment syndrome, open fractures, septic arthritis
items.stem: A displaced intracapsular neck of femur fracture carries a high risk of avascular necrosis. Disruption of which vessels is mainly responsible?
options: Nutrient artery of the femoral shaft
Retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery
items.why: The femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular vessels from the medial circumflex femoral artery, which run along the neck within the capsule and are torn in displaced intracapsular fractures.
notes: The nutrient artery supplies the shaft, not the femoral head blood supply after a neck fracture.
The ligamentum teres artery is minor in adults and does not sustain the head.
The superior gluteal artery supplies gluteal muscles and is not the key head supply.

items.topic: Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending weakness, FVC monitoring, IVIG
items.stem: A 35-year-old man has 3 days of ascending leg weakness and paraesthesia, areflexia, and a recent diarrhoeal illness. What CSF finding is typical?
options: Raised protein with normal cell count
items.why: Albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein, normal white cells) is typical of Guillain-Barré, though it may be normal in the first week.
notes: Neutrophils and low glucose indicate bacterial meningitis.
Oligoclonal bands suggest multiple sclerosis.
Pleocytosis (>50 cells) should prompt consideration of another diagnosis such as HIV or Lyme.

items.topic: Dementia: Alzheimer vs vascular vs Lewy body vs frontotemporal, reversible causes, capacity
items.stem: Which pathological protein deposit is the hallmark of dementia with Lewy bodies?
items.why: Lewy bodies are intraneuronal aggregates of alpha-synuclein (cortical and brainstem). Alzheimer disease shows amyloid plaques and tau tangles; FTD shows tau, TDP-43 or FUS.
notes: Tau tangles characterise Alzheimer disease (and some FTD), not Lewy body disease.
Amyloid plaques are the Alzheimer hallmark.
TDP-43 inclusions occur in some FTD and ALS, not Lewy body dementia.

items.topic: Hyponatraemia: volume assessment, SIADH, safe correction rate (osmotic demyelination)
items.stem: A patient has euvolaemia, plasma osmolality 255 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 450 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 60 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains the hyponatraemia in SIADH?
options: Excess ADH causing free water retention via aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting ducts
Aldosterone deficiency causing renal sodium wasting
Reduced GFR from low effective arterial volume
Primary excess water intake with maximally dilute urine
items.why: Inappropriate ADH inserts aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct, retaining free water and diluting plasma sodium. Urine is inappropriately concentrated (>100 mOsm/kg) with urinary Na >30 mmol/L.
notes: Aldosterone deficiency gives hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, with hyperkalaemia; volume status here is euvolaemic.
Low effective arterial volume drives ADH in heart failure or cirrhosis, but those are hypervolaemic states, not SIADH.
Primary polydipsia gives maximally dilute urine (<100 mOsm/kg), not 450.

items.topic: Childhood immunisation: National Immunisation Program schedule, catch-up, true contraindications
items.stem: A 12-month-old attends for scheduled vaccines. He has a runny nose and a temperature of 37.9°C, is feeding well and is otherwise well. His older sibling had anaphylaxis to egg years ago. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Defer all vaccines until he is afebrile for 2 weeks
Defer MMR until egg allergy testing is done
Give vaccines only in hospital under observation
items.why: Minor illness with low-grade fever is not a contraindication. Only anaphylaxis to a vaccine or component, or specific immunocompromise for live vaccines, are true contraindications.
notes: Minor illness without systemic upset is not a reason to delay immunisation.
Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR, and the sibling's history is irrelevant anyway.
Routine hospital observation is unnecessary without a past anaphylactic reaction to a vaccine.

items.topic: Drug dosing in renal impairment: metformin, DOACs, gentamicin, lithium
items.stem: Why does lithium accumulate to toxic levels when eGFR falls?
options: It is renally excreted unchanged and reabsorbed with sodium in the proximal tubule
It is metabolised by hepatic CYP3A4, which fails in CKD
It is highly protein bound and displaced by uraemic toxins
It is secreted by P-glycoprotein into bile
items.why: Lithium is almost entirely cleared by the kidney and reabsorbed like sodium, so reduced GFR or volume depletion raises levels. It has a narrow therapeutic index.
notes: Lithium is not hepatically metabolised.
Lithium is not protein bound.
Biliary secretion is not a route of lithium elimination.

items.topic: Suicide and self-harm: risk formulation, safety planning, when to detain
items.stem: A 35-year-old man presents after an overdose. He now has ongoing intent to die, a plan, refuses help and wants to leave. He has severe depression and no capacity to weigh the risk. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Discharge with a safety plan and GP follow-up in a week
Assess under mental health legislation for involuntary treatment
Discharge to his family with a no-suicide contract
Allow him to leave and offer a crisis line number
items.why: With persisting intent, a mental illness and impaired decision-making, he should be assessed for involuntary treatment under the state Mental Health Act. Safety plans and contracts do not suffice for imminent risk.
notes: Safety planning is for lower risk, not ongoing intent with refusal of care.
No-suicide contracts have no evidence and are not protective.
Letting him leave fails the duty of care when risk is high and capacity is impaired.

items.topic: Menopause: menopausal hormone therapy benefits and risks, premature ovarian insufficiency
items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with an intact uterus starts menopausal hormone therapy for hot flushes. Why must a progestogen be added to her oestrogen?
options: To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed oestrogen
To prevent breast cancer from oestrogen
To increase bone density beyond that from oestrogen
To reduce the risk of venous thromboembolism
items.why: Unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial proliferation, raising hyperplasia and cancer risk. A progestogen induces secretory change and shedding; it is not needed after hysterectomy.
notes: Progestogen does not protect the breast; combined therapy carries a small increase in breast cancer risk.
Bone benefit comes from oestrogen; progestogen adds little.
Oral oestrogen raises VTE risk; adding progestogen does not lower it.

items.topic: Kawasaki disease: diagnostic criteria, IVIG and aspirin, coronary aneurysms
items.stem: A 6-month-old has had fever for 6 days and irritability with a rash, but only 2 other classic features. CRP is high and echo is normal. What is the best next step?
options: Treat as incomplete Kawasaki disease with IVIG
Wait for more criteria before treating
items.why: Infants under 12 months with prolonged fever and raised inflammatory markers often have incomplete Kawasaki disease. Treat early with IVIG, since coronary risk is highest in infants and a normal early echo does not exclude it.
notes: This risks missed treatment and coronary aneurysm.
Waiting delays therapy; incomplete presentations are common in infants and need prompt treatment.
Antibiotics alone do not treat Kawasaki disease.

items.topic: Labour and fetal surveillance: progress of labour, CTG interpretation (RANZCOG), instrumental birth
items.stem: A CTG shows repetitive late decelerations. What is the underlying physiological mechanism?
options: Uteroplacental insufficiency causing chemoreceptor-mediated vagal response to hypoxaemia
items.why: Late decelerations reflect reduced uteroplacental oxygen transfer during contractions; fetal hypoxaemia triggers a chemoreceptor-mediated vagal response, lagging the contraction.
notes: Head compression produces early decelerations that mirror contractions.
Cord compression produces variable decelerations.
Maternal pain does not cause the characteristic lagging deceleration.

items.topic: Irritable bowel syndrome: Rome IV, excluding red flags, low-FODMAP diet
items.stem: A low-FODMAP diet is used to reduce symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome. Which mechanism best explains why poorly absorbed short-chain carbohydrates cause bloating and diarrhoea?
options: They are osmotically active and fermented by colonic bacteria to produce gas
They directly damage the small bowel villi and cause malabsorption
They stimulate gastrin release and increase gastric acid secretion
They inhibit pancreatic lipase and cause steatorrhoea
items.why: FODMAPs are poorly absorbed, draw water into the lumen osmotically and are fermented by colonic bacteria, producing gas and distension. This triggers symptoms in a visceral hypersensitive gut.
notes: Villous damage is the mechanism in coeliac disease, not with FODMAPs; the mucosa is normal.
FODMAPs do not act through gastrin or acid secretion.
Lipase inhibition causes fat malabsorption (e.g. orlistat), not FODMAP symptoms.

items.topic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar state: fluids, insulin, potassium, SGLT2-inhibitor euglycaemic DKA
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on dapagliflozin presents with vomiting and malaise after 2 days of poor intake. Glucose 11 mmol/L, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L, ketones 5.0 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observe and recommence dapagliflozin when eating
Give IV sodium bicarbonate and oral fluids
Give IV fluids only, as glucose is below 14 mmol/L
Stop dapagliflozin; treat as DKA with IV fluids, insulin with dextrose, and potassium
items.why: This is SGLT2-inhibitor euglycaemic DKA. Stop the drug and treat as DKA with fluids, fixed-rate insulin plus dextrose to clear ketones, and potassium replacement.
notes: Continuing the drug risks persisting ketosis; it must be ceased.
Bicarbonate is not routine at pH 7.15 and oral fluids are inadequate.
Insulin is needed to switch off ketogenesis despite near-normal glucose.

items.topic: Hypertension: confirming the diagnosis (home or ambulatory BP), first-line agents, secondary causes, hypertensive emergency
items.stem: A 50-year-old man has clinic BP readings of 152/94 mmHg on two visits, with no end-organ damage. What is the best next step to confirm the diagnosis?
items.why: Australian guidelines recommend confirming raised clinic BP with ambulatory (preferred) or home BP monitoring before diagnosing hypertension, to exclude white-coat hypertension.
notes: Treatment should follow confirmation, unless BP is severely raised or there is end-organ damage.
A 12-month delay is inappropriate for readings this high without confirmation.
Renal angiography is for suspected renovascular disease, not routine confirmation.

items.topic: Acute coronary syndrome: STEMI vs NSTEACS on ECG, reperfusion timing, dual antiplatelet therapy
items.stem: Ticagrelor is added to aspirin after an acute coronary syndrome. What is ticagrelor's mechanism of action?
options: Reversible antagonism of the platelet P2Y12 receptor
items.why: Ticagrelor reversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor and does not need metabolic activation. Clopidogrel and prasugrel block it irreversibly.
notes: This is aspirin's mechanism, which ticagrelor complements.
Tirofiban is the GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor, given IV.
Rivaroxaban and apixaban inhibit factor Xa; ticagrelor does not.

items.topic: Obesity: metabolic complications, GLP-1 RA pharmacotherapy, bariatric surgery
items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with obesity (BMI 38 kg/m²) on semaglutide has sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Cease semaglutide and check serum lipase
Continue semaglutide and start a proton pump inhibitor
Reduce the semaglutide dose by half
items.why: GLP-1 RAs are associated with pancreatitis and gallbladder disease. Suspected pancreatitis requires stopping the drug and checking lipase; do not restart if confirmed.
notes: Continuing the drug risks worsening possible pancreatitis.
Dose reduction is inadequate when pancreatitis is suspected.
Imaging may follow, but acute assessment and stopping the drug come first.

items.topic: Opioid use disorder: buprenorphine and methadone, long-acting injectable buprenorphine, take-home naloxone
items.stem: Which pharmacological property of buprenorphine explains its ceiling effect on respiratory depression and its risk of precipitated withdrawal?
options: Full mu-opioid agonism with short half-life
items.why: Buprenorphine binds mu receptors with high affinity but low intrinsic activity, so it displaces full agonists and can precipitate withdrawal while limiting respiratory depression.
notes: Full agonism describes methadone, which has no ceiling effect.
Kappa activity does not explain these features.
NMDA antagonism is a secondary property of methadone, not buprenorphine's ceiling.

items.topic: Absolute cardiovascular risk and lipids: 2023 Australian CVD risk calculator, statin thresholds, familial hypercholesterolaemia
items.stem: Which mechanism explains how statins lower plasma LDL cholesterol?
options: Inhibit intestinal cholesterol absorption via NPC1L1
Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors
Activate lipoprotein lipase to clear triglycerides
Bind bile acids in the gut, preventing reabsorption
items.why: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis, which upregulates LDL receptors and increases LDL clearance from plasma.
notes: That is ezetimibe's mechanism.
Fibrates act through PPAR-alpha to increase lipoprotein lipase activity.
That is the mechanism of bile acid sequestrants such as colestyramine.

items.topic: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline dose, refractory anaphylaxis, observation period
items.stem: A 30-year-old woman (65 kg) develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension after a wasp sting. She has had one IM adrenaline dose with no improvement after 5 minutes. What is the next step?
options: Give hydrocortisone 200 mg IV and observe
Give promethazine IM and reassess in 15 minutes
Start adrenaline IV infusion straight away without further IM doses
items.why: Adult dose is 0.5 mg (0.01 mg/kg) IM into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response. Start an infusion if there is refractory anaphylaxis after multiple IM doses, with fluids.
notes: Steroids and antihistamines are not first-line and do not treat shock.
Antihistamines are adjuncts only and delay adrenaline.
Infusion is for refractory cases after repeated IM doses, with expert/ICU input.

items.topic: Transfusion: indications, reactions (TRALI, TACO, haemolytic), Patient Blood Management
items.stem: An 82-year-old man with heart failure becomes dyspnoeic, hypertensive (190/100) with raised JVP and bilateral crackles 2 hours into his second unit of red cells. SpO2 is 88%. After stopping the transfusion, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Sit upright, give oxygen and intravenous frusemide
Restart transfusion at a slower rate
items.why: This is TACO: hypertension, raised JVP and pulmonary oedema. Stop the transfusion, sit upright, give oxygen and a diuretic such as frusemide.
notes: Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, which has hypotension, wheeze and urticaria rather than hypertension and raised JVP.
Transfusion should not be restarted until stable and reassessed; it worsens overload.
Fluid bolus would worsen pulmonary oedema.

items.topic: Infectious diarrhoea and C. difficile: oral rehydration, traveller's diarrhoea, antibiotic-associated colitis
items.stem: Oral rehydration solution is effective even in secretory diarrhoea such as cholera. Which mechanism underlies this?
options: Sodium–glucose cotransport in the enterocyte drives water absorption
Glucose inhibits chloride secretion by blocking CFTR
Glucose directly stimulates colonic aldosterone release
Sodium is absorbed by passive diffusion through tight junctions only
items.why: SGLT1 couples sodium and glucose uptake, which remains intact in secretory diarrhoea, and water follows osmotically. This is the basis of ORS.
notes: Glucose does not block CFTR; secretion continues but absorption is enhanced.
Aldosterone is not released by glucose in the colon in this way.
Coupled cotransport, not passive paracellular diffusion, is the mechanism.

items.topic: Inherited bleeding disorders: haemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, preoperative assessment
items.stem: A 30-year-old man with severe haemophilia A presents with a swollen painful knee after minor trauma. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Urgent factor VIII replacement before imaging, then haematology advice
Aspirate the joint first and then give factor VIII
Oral tranexamic acid and review in 48 hours
items.why: Suspected haemarthrosis in haemophilia needs prompt factor VIII (recombinant) replacement, ideally within hours, before investigations, with early haematology input. Early treatment preserves the joint.
notes: Aspiration is not routine and is done only after factor replacement if needed.
Tranexamic acid alone is inadequate for a significant joint bleed in severe haemophilia.
FFP contains low factor VIII concentration; specific factor concentrate is preferred.

items.topic: Bowel obstruction: small vs large bowel, adhesions, hernias, volvulus, conservative vs operative care
items.stem: A patient has a small bowel obstruction and profuse vomiting. Which acid-base and electrolyte disturbance is most likely from loss of gastric contents and third-space fluid?
items.why: Vomiting loses H+ and Cl-, causing hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; volume depletion drives aldosterone-mediated K+ loss. Late ischaemia may cause lactic acidosis.
notes: That pattern occurs with diarrhoea or saline excess, not vomiting.
Respiratory alkalosis is not the primary disturbance here.
Potassium is lost, not retained, with vomiting and aldosterone activation.

items.topic: Acute behavioural disturbance: de-escalation, safe sedation, medical causes
items.stem: Midazolam is used for sedation of acute behavioural disturbance. Through which mechanism does it act?
options: Enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency
Blocks histamine H1 and muscarinic receptors only
items.why: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A, increasing channel opening frequency and causing sedation. Antipsychotics such as droperidol act at D2.
notes: That is the mechanism of antipsychotics such as haloperidol or droperidol.
Antihistamine action is not the benzodiazepine mechanism.
NMDA antagonism is the mechanism of ketamine.

items.topic: Bipolar disorder: mania, lithium levels, toxicity and renal/thyroid monitoring, valproate in women of childbearing potential
items.stem: Lithium is almost entirely renally cleared. Which change most likely raises serum lithium concentration?
items.why: Thiazides reduce sodium and volume, increasing proximal lithium reabsorption and raising levels. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and dehydration act likewise.
notes: Sodium loading increases lithium excretion and lowers levels.
Acetazolamide increases lithium excretion and lowers levels.
Increased GFR in pregnancy lowers levels.

items.topic: Chronic kidney disease: staging by eGFR and urine ACR, Kidney Health Check for at-risk adults, slowing progression
items.stem: Which finding is the earliest and most sensitive marker of glomerular filtration barrier damage in diabetic kidney disease?
options: Red cell casts in the urine
items.why: Albuminuria reflects loss of charge and size selectivity of the glomerular barrier and appears before eGFR falls. The urine ACR is the key early marker and also predicts progression.
notes: Creatinine rises late, after substantial nephron loss.
Urine output is usually preserved in CKD until advanced stages.
Red cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis, not typical diabetic nephropathy.

items.topic: Contraception and early medical abortion: LARC, emergency contraception, drug interactions, mifepristone-misoprostol
items.stem: What is the main mechanism by which mifepristone contributes to early medical abortion?
options: Prostaglandin E1 agonism causing cervical softening
Progesterone receptor antagonism, withdrawing decidual support
Oxytocin receptor activation causing uterine contraction
Inhibition of hCG secretion by the trophoblast
items.why: Mifepristone blocks progesterone receptors, causing decidual breakdown, cervical softening and increased uterine sensitivity to prostaglandin. Misoprostol (a PGE1 analogue) then causes contractions and expulsion.
notes: That is misoprostol's action, given 24–48 hours after mifepristone.
Oxytocin receptor activation is not how either drug acts; oxytocin is not used in early medical abortion.
Mifepristone does not inhibit hCG secretion; hCG falls as a consequence of decidual and trophoblast detachment.

items.topic: Common GP presentations: fatigue, low back pain red flags, skin checks and sun protection, PSA shared decision-making
items.stem: A 45-year-old man has low back pain. Which finding is the most concerning red flag for spinal infection or malignancy?
options: Night pain with unexplained weight loss and fever
Pain beginning after lifting a box
Stiffness that eases within minutes of moving
items.why: Fever, weight loss, night or constant pain suggest infection or malignancy. Mechanical pain that varies with posture and movement is typically benign.
notes: Pain with sitting and varying with posture suggests a mechanical cause.
A clear mechanical trigger suggests musculoskeletal strain.
Brief morning stiffness is mechanical; inflammatory back pain stiffness lasts over 30 minutes.

items.topic: Coeliac disease: tTG-IgA on a gluten-containing diet, duodenal biopsy, associated conditions
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with iron deficiency anaemia and type 1 diabetes has bloating. She has avoided gluten for 3 months and her GP's tTG-IgA is negative (total IgA normal). What is the best next step?
options: Exclude coeliac disease, as the negative result is reliable
Start gluten challenge for at least 6 weeks, then repeat tTG-IgA
Order HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing to confirm the diagnosis
Proceed to duodenal biopsy while she remains gluten-free
items.why: Serology and biopsy are unreliable once gluten is withdrawn. Eat gluten daily (about 6 weeks) before repeat testing. HLA typing only helps exclude disease.
notes: Testing on a gluten-free diet gives false negatives.
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 has a high negative predictive value but cannot confirm diagnosis.
Biopsy can be falsely normal if gluten has been avoided.

items.topic: Meningococcal disease: purpuric rash, pre-hospital benzylpenicillin, contact prophylaxis
items.stem: A 19-year-old university student has fever, headache and a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. The GP is 40 minutes from hospital and she has no known allergy. What is the best action before transfer?
options: Give IV or IM benzylpenicillin immediately, then transfer
Perform a lumbar puncture in the surgery first
Wait for hospital blood cultures before any antibiotic
items.why: Suspected meningococcal disease needs immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin (or ceftriaxone) before transfer; do not delay for investigations. Lumbar puncture is not appropriate in a shocked patient.
notes: LP delays treatment and is risky in shock or rash with sepsis.
Delaying antibiotics increases mortality.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate for this emergency.

items.topic: Peripheral arterial disease: claudication, ankle-brachial index, risk-factor control, when to refer
items.stem: Why does intermittent claudication in peripheral arterial disease occur with exercise and settle with rest?
options: Fixed stenosis cannot increase flow to meet muscle demand
items.why: A fixed atherosclerotic stenosis allows adequate flow at rest but cannot increase it with exertion, so ischaemic pain occurs and eases once demand falls.
notes: Venous valve failure causes venous insufficiency, with heaviness and oedema.
Nerve compression describes neurogenic claudication, which eases with sitting or flexion rather than just stopping.
Calcium-related spasm does not explain exertional, rest-relieved pain.

items.topic: COPD: spirometry diagnosis, COPD-X stepwise inhalers, exacerbations, oxygen target 88-92%
items.stem: A 66-year-old ex-smoker with COPD, on a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, remains breathless with one exacerbation in the past year. According to COPD-X stepwise therapy, what is the usual next step?
items.why: For persistent symptoms or exacerbations on monotherapy, COPD-X advises dual long-acting bronchodilator therapy (LAMA plus LABA).
notes: Long-term oral corticosteroids cause harm and are not recommended.
Azithromycin is considered later for frequent exacerbations despite optimal inhaled therapy.
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and is not a routine next step.

items.topic: Pituitary disease: prolactinoma, acromegaly, hypopituitarism, bitemporal hemianopia
items.stem: A pituitary macroadenoma expands upward and compresses the optic chiasm. Which retinal fibres are damaged first, producing bitemporal hemianopia?
options: Nasal retinal fibres from each eye, which cross
Temporal retinal fibres from each eye, which cross
Nasal retinal fibres from each eye, which stay uncrossed
Temporal retinal fibres from the ipsilateral eye only
items.why: Nasal retinal fibres, carrying the temporal visual fields, decussate at the chiasm and are compressed centrally. Temporal fibres stay ipsilateral.
notes: Temporal retinal fibres do not cross; they pass laterally in the chiasm.
Nasal fibres cross; they do not stay uncrossed.
Unilateral temporal fibre loss would give a nasal field defect in one eye, not bitemporal loss.

items.topic: Meningococcal disease: purpuric rash, pre-hospital benzylpenicillin, contact prophylaxis
items.stem: What best explains the non-blanching purpuric rash of meningococcaemia?
options: Endotoxin-induced DIC and vascular injury causing bleeding into the skin
Type I hypersensitivity with mast cell degranulation
Direct bacterial invasion of the epidermis causing blistering
Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli
items.why: Neisseria meningitidis lipo-oligosaccharide triggers endothelial injury, microthrombi and DIC, causing petechiae and purpura that do not blanch.
notes: Mast cell degranulation causes blanching urticaria.
Epidermal blistering describes staphylococcal scalded skin or bullous impetigo.
Glomerular immune complexes do not cause the purpuric rash.

items.topic: Hypoglycaemia: sulfonylurea and insulin causes, treatment, driving rules
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman on gliclazide with eGFR 30 is brought in confused. BGL is 2.1 mmol/L. She cannot swallow safely and has no IV access yet. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
items.why: With no IV access and an unsafe swallow, IM glucagon 1 mg is appropriate (IV 10% glucose once access is gained). Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia recurs, so she needs admission and observation.
notes: Unsafe swallow with reduced consciousness makes oral gel an aspiration risk.
Octreotide is used for recurrent sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia after glucose, not as first-line rescue.
Oral route unsafe, and discharge is wrong given prolonged sulfonylurea effect in renal impairment.

items.topic: Gastroenteritis and dehydration: clinical dehydration assessment, oral rehydration, ondansetron
items.stem: A 2-year-old has had 1 day of vomiting and watery diarrhoea. He is alert, mildly reduced skin turgor, slightly dry mucous membranes, normal capillary refill and has vomited twice in ED. He refuses fluids. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give ondansetron then trial oral rehydration solution
Start intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride bolus 20 mL/kg
Give loperamide and discharge with oral fluids
Send stool culture and start oral azithromycin
items.why: Mild to moderate dehydration with vomiting: a single dose of ondansetron improves oral rehydration success and reduces need for IV fluids. Antimotility drugs and routine antibiotics are not recommended.
notes: A bolus is for shock or severe dehydration; he has normal perfusion and should first have oral or nasogastric rehydration.
Loperamide is not recommended in young children with gastroenteritis.
Most gastroenteritis is viral and self-limiting; antibiotics and routine culture are not indicated.

items.topic: Child and adolescent mental health: ADHD, autism, adolescent depression, HEADSS assessment
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains how methylphenidate improves symptoms of ADHD?
options: Blocks dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake in the prefrontal cortex
Blocks postsynaptic D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway
Enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening
items.why: Methylphenidate blocks dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, increasing synaptic catecholamines in frontostriatal circuits. Lisdexamfetamine also increases release.
notes: D2 blockade is the mechanism of antipsychotics, which do not treat core ADHD symptoms.
Enhancing GABA-A is the mechanism of benzodiazepines, which are not used for ADHD.
Irreversible MAO inhibition is the mechanism of older antidepressants, not stimulants.

items.topic: Fatty liver (MASLD) and alcohol-related liver disease: fibrosis assessment, abstinence, alcoholic hepatitis
items.stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and BMI 34 has steatosis on ultrasound and mildly raised ALT. Which is the best next step to assess for advanced fibrosis?
options: Calculate FIB-4 from age, AST, ALT and platelets
items.why: FIB-4 is the first-line non-invasive fibrosis screen in primary care; indeterminate or high scores prompt elastography (FibroScan).
notes: Ultrasound is insensitive for fibrosis.
Biopsy is reserved for unclear cases after non-invasive tests.
Ferritin does not stage fibrosis.

items.topic: Dementia: Alzheimer vs vascular vs Lewy body vs frontotemporal, reversible causes, capacity
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with moderate dementia refuses to move into residential care. She understands the information and can retain it, but says she is 'perfectly safe' and cannot weigh the risks. What is the best next step?
options: Find she lacks capacity for this decision, as she cannot use and weigh the information
Find she has capacity because she understands and retains the information
Proceed under her son's wishes without further assessment
Assume capacity is lost because she has a dementia diagnosis
items.why: Capacity is decision-specific and requires understanding, retaining, using/weighing information and communicating a choice. Inability to weigh risks means she lacks capacity for this decision; involve the substitute decision-maker.
notes: Understanding and retention alone are not enough; she must also use and weigh the information.
Family cannot decide without a formal capacity assessment and legal authority.
A diagnosis of dementia does not alone mean incapacity; capacity is assessed per decision.

items.topic: Phaeochromocytoma: paroxysmal symptoms, plasma metanephrines, alpha-blockade before surgery
items.stem: A 50-year-old man has biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma with a 4 cm adrenal mass and is awaiting adrenalectomy. Which preoperative regimen is most appropriate?
options: Alpha-blocker such as phenoxybenzamine, then add beta-blocker if tachycardic
No medication; proceed to surgery urgently
items.why: Alpha-blockade for 1–2 weeks (with salt and fluid loading) comes first; beta-blocker is added only afterwards for tachycardia.
notes: Beta-blockade alone leaves unopposed alpha stimulation, risking hypertensive crisis.
Diuretics and fluid restriction worsen volume contraction and postoperative hypotension.
Unprepared surgery risks intraoperative hypertensive crisis.

items.topic: Child protection: non-accidental injury patterns, mandatory reporting
items.stem: A GP examines a 4-year-old with multiple bruises and a patterned handprint on the thigh. The explanation is vague. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report to the state child protection authority and arrange paediatric assessment
Wait to gather proof before involving any agency
Seek the parents' consent before making any report
Document findings and review the child in 4 weeks
items.why: Where there is reasonable belief of significant harm, doctors must notify child protection services (mandatory in most states and territories) and arrange urgent assessment. Proof and parental consent are not required.
notes: Proof is not required; reasonable suspicion is enough.
Parental consent is not required for a report.
Delay leaves the child at risk.

items.topic: Faltering growth: growth charts, organic vs psychosocial causes
items.stem: A child with faltering growth has a normal length but a low weight. Which cause is most likely to produce this pattern?
items.why: Inadequate energy intake affects weight first, then head circumference and length last. Endocrine causes and genetic short stature affect length early.
notes: Growth hormone deficiency impairs linear growth, with relatively preserved weight.
Hypothyroidism causes short stature, with weight relatively preserved or increased.
Turner syndrome causes short stature from early on, not isolated low weight.

items.topic: Electrolyte emergencies: hyperkalaemia, severe hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia
items.stem: A 60-year-old on dialysis has weakness. K+ is 7.4 mmol/L and ECG shows broad QRS and peaked T waves. IV calcium has been given. What is the next best treatment to lower serum potassium?
items.why: Insulin with glucose (plus nebulised salbutamol) rapidly shifts potassium into cells after membrane stabilisation. Definitive removal needs dialysis in this patient.
notes: Binders act too slowly for an emergency with ECG changes.
Saline does not reliably lower potassium and risks overload in dialysis patients.
Bicarbonate is of limited benefit unless severe acidosis exists.

items.topic: Adverse drug reactions and interactions: CYP450 inducers and inhibitors, reporting to the TGA
items.stem: A GP suspects a patient's rash is an adverse reaction to a newly marketed medicine. How should the GP report this in Australia?
options: Report to the TGA (for example via the Adverse Event Reporting System online)
Report only to the medicine's pharmacy of dispensing
Wait for confirmation by dechallenge before reporting any event
Report only if the reaction is serious and fatal
items.why: Health professionals can report suspected adverse reactions to the TGA online, and reporting is encouraged for suspected reactions, especially to new medicines. Proof of causation is not required.
notes: The TGA is the national reporting body; pharmacy notification alone does not meet this.
Causation need not be proven before reporting a suspected reaction.
Non-serious reactions are also valuable to report, especially for new medicines.

items.topic: Melioidosis: Top End and north Queensland, wet season, diabetes, meropenem
items.stem: Burkholderia pseudomallei causes melioidosis. Which statement best explains its distribution and risk factors?
options: It lives in soil and surface water, and diabetes impairs host neutrophil defence
It is transmitted person to person by respiratory droplets
It lives only in livestock and spreads through milk
items.why: B. pseudomallei is an environmental Gram-negative bacillus in tropical soil and water. Infection follows inhalation or inoculation, mostly in the wet season, and diabetes is the major risk factor.
notes: Person-to-person spread is very rare.
Milk spread describes brucellosis.
It is a bacterium, not a virus.

items.topic: Infective endocarditis: modified Duke criteria, people who inject drugs, prosthetic valves, empirical therapy
items.stem: Which event is the usual initiating step in the pathogenesis of native valve infective endocarditis?
options: Bacteraemia infecting normal, undamaged endothelium directly
Endothelial injury with deposition of a sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus
Immune complex deposition on the valve leaflets
Papillary muscle rupture causing turbulent flow
items.why: Endothelial damage from turbulent flow or injury forms a sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis); transient bacteraemia then seeds it to form a vegetation.
notes: Wrong: most organisms cannot adhere to healthy endothelium (S. aureus is a partial exception); a damaged surface is usually needed first.
Wrong: immune complexes cause the secondary phenomena such as glomerulonephritis and Roth spots, not the initial vegetation.
Wrong: this is a complication of valve disease or infarction, not the initiating step.

items.topic: Myeloproliferative neoplasms: polycythaemia vera (JAK2), essential thrombocythaemia
items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with JAK2-positive polycythaemia vera has a haematocrit of 0.58 and no prior thrombosis. She is on no treatment. Which regimen is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Venesection to haematocrit below 0.45 plus low-dose aspirin
items.why: Initial PV management is venesection to keep haematocrit under 0.45 plus low-dose aspirin to reduce thrombosis. Cytoreduction (e.g. hydroxycarbamide) is added for high-risk disease (age over 60 or prior thrombosis).
notes: Aspirin is recommended unless contraindicated, as it reduces arterial and venous thrombotic events.
Anticoagulation is not first-line prophylaxis without a thrombotic event.
Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML, not PV.

items.topic: Headache: subarachnoid haemorrhage red flags, migraine treatment and prophylaxis, medication-overuse headache
items.stem: A 42-year-old woman has a sudden severe occipital headache that peaked within a minute while exercising, 3 hours ago, with neck stiffness. She is alert, neurologically normal. Non-contrast CT brain at 2 hours is reported normal. What is the next step?
options: Lumbar puncture, or CT angiography, to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
items.why: Thunderclap headache needs SAH excluded. CT within 6 hours of onset by an expert is highly sensitive, but here the CT was at 2 hours with high suspicion, so LP (xanthochromia) or CTA is still needed per local protocol.
notes: Discharge risks missing a sentinel bleed or aneurysm with high rebleed mortality.
Triptans are vasoconstrictors and inappropriate before SAH is excluded.
Outpatient delay is unsafe; the work-up should be completed urgently.

items.topic: Cardiac arrest: ANZCOR adult and paediatric ALS algorithms, shockable rhythms, reversible causes
items.stem: A 60-year-old man is in cardiac arrest with VF. He has had two shocks and CPR is ongoing with IV access and adrenaline already due. Per ANZCOR, which drug is given after the third shock?
items.why: ANZCOR ALS: in shock-refractory VF/pVT give adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, then adrenaline every second cycle.
notes: Calcium is only for specific causes such as hyperkalaemia, not routine VF.
Bicarbonate is not routine; it is for select causes such as TCA overdose or hyperkalaemia.
Atropine is no longer used in cardiac arrest algorithms.

items.topic: Family and domestic violence and elder abuse: asking safely, safety planning, reporting
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman discloses in a private consultation that her partner has choked her and threatened to kill her. She has two children, is not ready to leave and does not want police involved. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Make a safety plan and offer referral to 1800RESPECT or a local service
Notify police immediately against her wishes
Document nothing to avoid the record being accessed
items.why: Strangulation and death threats are high-risk indicators. Respect autonomy, assess immediate risk, make a safety plan, offer referrals (1800RESPECT) and document factually. Mandatory reporting applies to children at risk in some jurisdictions.
notes: Adult competent patients' confidentiality applies; police are contacted without consent only if there is a serious imminent threat to life.
Telling her to leave is directive; the period around leaving is high-risk and the decision is hers, supported by a plan.
Accurate, factual documentation is recommended; it can support later legal action.

items.topic: Vertigo: BPPV (Dix-Hallpike, Epley) vs vestibular neuritis vs posterior circulation stroke (HINTS)
items.stem: In benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, brief vertigo is triggered by head movement. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Endolymph excess distending the cochlear duct
Inflammation of the vestibular nerve after a viral illness
Displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal
items.why: Otoconia displaced from the utricle enter a semicircular canal (usually posterior) and cause abnormal endolymph movement with head position change, producing brief vertigo.
notes: Endolymphatic hydrops describes Ménière disease, with hearing loss and tinnitus.
This describes vestibular neuritis, which causes prolonged continuous vertigo.
Cerebellar ischaemia causes persistent vertigo with ataxia, not brief positional episodes.

items.topic: Snakebite: pressure immobilisation bandage, coagulopathy testing (20-minute whole blood clotting test), antivenom indications
items.stem: Why is a pressure immobilisation bandage applied after an Australian elapid snakebite?
options: It slows lymphatic flow, delaying venom reaching the circulation
It neutralises venom at the bite site
It prevents local tissue necrosis by increasing perfusion
It occludes arterial inflow to the limb
items.why: Elapid venom is large and moves mainly via lymphatics; pressure and immobilisation reduce lymph flow and muscle movement, delaying systemic envenomation. Arterial flow must not be occluded.
notes: Bandaging does not neutralise venom; only antivenom does.
Venom is not limited by perfusion; the aim is to reduce lymphatic spread, not boost perfusion.
The bandage should be firm like a sprain wrap, not a tourniquet; distal pulses should remain.

items.topic: Acute coronary syndrome: STEMI vs NSTEACS on ECG, reperfusion timing, dual antiplatelet therapy
items.stem: A 58-year-old man has 40 minutes of central chest pain. ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in V2–V5. He is at a hospital with no PCI capability; transfer to a PCI centre will take over 3 hours. No contraindications. What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?
options: Fibrinolysis, then transfer to a PCI centre
Wait for troponin result before deciding
Heparin and aspirin only, then transfer for angiography next day
Transfer for primary PCI without any fibrinolysis
items.why: When primary PCI cannot be achieved within about 120 minutes of first contact, fibrinolysis should be given promptly (ideally within 30 minutes), followed by transfer to a PCI centre.
notes: STEMI is diagnosed on ECG and reperfusion should not wait for troponin.
Antithrombotics alone do not reperfuse an occluded artery in STEMI.
Delay beyond 120 minutes makes PCI-only inferior when fibrinolysis is available and safe.

items.topic: Hypertension: confirming the diagnosis (home or ambulatory BP), first-line agents, secondary causes, hypertensive emergency
items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has hypertension, hypokalaemia and a suppressed renin. Excess of which hormone best explains her hypertension?
options: Aldosterone, causing sodium retention and potassium loss
Adrenaline, causing vasoconstriction through alpha receptors
Angiotensin II, causing efferent arteriolar constriction
items.why: Primary aldosteronism causes sodium and water retention and renal potassium loss, with renin suppressed by volume expansion. Screen with aldosterone-renin ratio.
notes: Cortisol excess (Cushing) can cause hypokalaemia, but suppressed renin with this picture points to aldosterone.
Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension without the typical hypokalaemia and suppressed renin.
Angiotensin II would be raised with high renin, as in renal artery stenosis, not suppressed.

items.topic: Developmental milestones and red flags: speech delay, autism, motor delay referral
items.stem: At what age does a typically developing child usually first walk independently?
items.why: Most children walk independently by about 12 to 15 months. Failure to walk by 18 months warrants assessment.
notes: 6 to 8 months is the age of sitting without support.
9 to 10 months is typically crawling and pulling to stand.
Walking has usually occurred well before this; this age is when running and kicking emerge.

items.topic: Antenatal care and screening: booking tests, combined first-trimester screening and NIPT, RhD immunoprophylaxis
items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 at 28 weeks is RhD negative with no anti-D antibodies on screening. She has had no bleeding. Which routine prophylaxis is recommended in Australia?
options: Anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 weeks only
Anti-D 250 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks
Anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks
Anti-D after birth only, if the baby is RhD positive
items.why: Australian guidelines recommend routine antenatal anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks for RhD-negative non-sensitised women. Postnatal anti-D is still given if the baby is RhD positive.
notes: A single dose at 28 weeks is not the schedule; a second dose is given at 34 weeks.
250 IU is the dose for sensitising events before 12 weeks, not routine antenatal prophylaxis.
Postnatal-only prophylaxis misses sensitisation during pregnancy; antenatal doses are also recommended.

items.topic: Airway emergencies: upper airway obstruction, rapid sequence intubation principles, tension pneumothorax
items.stem: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the left chest. He is gasping, SpO2 82%, HR 140, BP 70/40, trachea deviated right, absent left breath sounds. What is the immediate management?
options: Wait for a chest X-ray to confirm
Left chest decompression (finger thoracostomy or needle)
items.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; immediate decompression, preferably finger thoracostomy in the 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior to mid-axillary line, then an intercostal catheter. Positive pressure ventilation first can worsen it.
notes: Delay for imaging in an unstable patient is dangerous.
Positive pressure ventilation before decompression can cause arrest.
Fluid does not relieve the obstruction.

items.topic: Sexually transmitted infections: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, the syphilis outbreak and congenital syphilis, contact tracing
items.stem: A 24-year-old man has dysuria and urethral discharge. Urine NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. He has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate treatment per current Australian guidelines?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM with azithromycin 1 g orally
items.why: Because of resistance, uncomplicated gonorrhoea is treated with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g orally. Also test for other STIs, arrange contact tracing and test of cure.
notes: Azithromycin alone promotes resistance and is not adequate.
Quinolone resistance is widespread in Australia.
Penicillin treats syphilis, not gonorrhoea, given resistance.

items.topic: Hepatitis B and C: serology interpretation, DAA cure for hepatitis C, HCC surveillance, migrant and First Nations prevalence
items.stem: Hepatitis B serology shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive and anti-HBs positive. How is this interpreted?
options: Acute infection in the window period
items.why: Anti-HBc with anti-HBs and negative HBsAg means natural infection that has cleared. Vaccination gives anti-HBs alone. Reactivation can occur with immunosuppression.
notes: Chronic infection has persistent HBsAg.
Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, without anti-HBc.
Window period has HBsAg and anti-HBs both negative, with anti-HBc present but no anti-HBs.

items.topic: National Immunisation Program: childhood, adolescent HPV, adults over 65, pregnancy (influenza, pertussis, RSV)
items.stem: A healthy woman at 33 weeks' gestation, in autumn, has had no vaccines this pregnancy. What is the best advice?
options: Give dTpa, influenza and RSV (RSVpreF) vaccines now
Give influenza now; defer dTpa and RSV until after birth
Give dTpa and MMR vaccine now
Give RSV vaccine now; give dTpa after birth
items.why: dTpa, influenza and RSVpreF (28 to 36 weeks) are all recommended in pregnancy, and can be co-administered. dTpa is best at 20 to 32 weeks but can be given later.
notes: Delaying dTpa and RSV vaccine until after birth loses the passive antibody protection for the newborn.
MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
dTpa should be given in pregnancy, not after birth, so the newborn gets maternal antibody.

items.topic: Early pregnancy bleeding: ectopic pregnancy (beta-hCG, ultrasound, methotrexate), miscarriage
items.stem: Which hormone, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy and is measured in a urine or serum pregnancy test?
items.why: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast rescues the corpus luteum so progesterone continues until the placenta takes over at about 8–10 weeks. It is the basis of pregnancy tests.
notes: Human placental lactogen rises later and alters maternal glucose metabolism; it is not the pregnancy test marker.
Oestriol is a placental oestrogen; it does not maintain the corpus luteum.
Relaxin softens ligaments and is not the pregnancy test hormone.

items.topic: Fitness to drive and work: Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive', the doctor's duties, workers' compensation
items.stem: In Australian workers' compensation, what is the role of the treating GP when completing a medical certificate for an injured worker?
options: Certify capacity for work and suggest suitable duties, not just total incapacity
Decide whether the claim is accepted
Certify only complete time off work
items.why: The GP certifies diagnosis and work capacity, recommending suitable or modified duties, as early safe return to work aids recovery. The insurer decides liability, not the GP.
notes: Liability decisions are made by the insurer.
The GP doesn't control budgets; rehabilitation providers and insurers do.
Certificates should specify capacity, not default to total incapacity, since work is generally good for health.

items.topic: Smoking and vaping cessation: Ask-Advise-Help, NRT and varenicline, the 2024 vaping reforms
items.stem: Varenicline helps people quit smoking. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Blockade of dopamine reuptake in the nucleus accumbens
Partial agonism at α4β2 nicotinic receptors
Full agonism at α7 nicotinic receptors
items.why: Varenicline is a partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors. It eases withdrawal and craving while blunting the reward from smoking.
notes: Not an MAO inhibitor.
Dopamine reuptake blockade is closer to bupropion's proposed action, which is not varenicline's.
Its key action is at α4β2, as a partial rather than full agonist.

items.topic: Haemochromatosis: HFE C282Y, ferritin and transferrin saturation, venesection
items.stem: In HFE haemochromatosis, which change in hepcidin explains the increased iron absorption?
options: Inappropriately low hepcidin, so ferroportin stays active
Low hepcidin, which downregulates divalent metal transporter
Absent transferrin, which frees iron for absorption
items.why: HFE mutation reduces hepcidin production. Without hepcidin, ferroportin is not degraded, so enterocytes and macrophages release excess iron.
notes: High hepcidin degrades ferroportin and reduces absorption.
Low hepcidin does not downregulate iron uptake; absorption increases.
Transferrin is present, and saturation is high, not absent.

items.topic: Epidemiology and evidence: study designs, bias and confounding, screening principles, lead-time bias
items.stem: Which criterion for a population screening program is most essential to justify screening for a condition?
options: Accepted treatment that improves outcomes if started early
A highly sensitive test regardless of cost
A high lifetime prevalence in older adults
Availability of the test in private clinics
items.why: Wilson–Jungner principles require an important condition with a detectable latent phase and accepted, effective treatment that improves outcomes when started early.
notes: Test performance matters but cost-effectiveness and acceptability are also needed; sensitivity alone is not sufficient.
Prevalence is relevant but does not justify screening without effective early treatment.
Access via private clinics is irrelevant to program justification.

items.topic: Thrombocytopenia: ITP, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, TTP/HUS (schistocytes)
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has fever, confusion, haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 12 x10^9/L, raised LDH and schistocytes on the film. INR and fibrinogen are normal, and creatinine is mildly raised. What is the most appropriate urgent treatment?
items.why: This is TTP (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, normal coagulation). Urgent plasma exchange with corticosteroids is lifesaving; send ADAMTS13 first and avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding.
notes: Platelet transfusion may fuel microthrombi and is avoided in TTP unless life-threatening bleeding.
ITP lacks haemolysis and schistocytes; steroids alone are inadequate in TTP.
IVIG treats ITP but is not definitive for TTP.

items.topic: Dementia: Alzheimer vs vascular vs Lewy body vs frontotemporal, reversible causes, capacity
items.stem: Which drug used in Alzheimer disease acts by increasing synaptic acetylcholine?
items.why: Donepezil inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising synaptic acetylcholine. Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist.
notes: Memantine blocks NMDA receptors, reducing glutamate excitotoxicity.
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic with no cholinergic enhancing action.
Selegiline is an MAO-B inhibitor, not a cholinesterase inhibitor.

items.topic: Orthopaedic emergencies: hip fracture and orthogeriatric care, compartment syndrome, open fractures, septic arthritis
items.stem: Why does septic arthritis cause rapid joint destruction if untreated?
options: Bacterial toxins and neutrophil enzymes degrade articular cartilage
Synovial fluid hyperviscosity compresses the cartilage
Immune complexes deposit in subchondral bone
Urate crystals erode the cartilage matrix
items.why: Bacterial products and host neutrophil proteases and cytokines degrade cartilage proteoglycans within days, so urgent washout and antibiotics are needed.
notes: Fluid hyperviscosity is not the mechanism; purulent effusion raises pressure but enzymes are key.
Immune complex deposition characterises some inflammatory arthritides, not acute bacterial destruction.
Urate crystals cause gout, a non-infective mimic.
