items.topic: Mosquito-borne viruses: Ross River, Barmah Forest, Murray Valley encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, dengue in north Queensland
items.stem: Dengue haemorrhagic features and plasma leakage are most often seen at which time in a secondary dengue infection with a different serotype?
options: On the first day of fever
items.why: Antibody-dependent enhancement in heterotypic secondary infection increases immune activation, causing capillary leak at the critical phase near defervescence (days 3-7).
notes: Early febrile phase precedes leakage.
Leakage is not delayed weeks.
Incubation is before symptoms.

items.topic: Fever in the returned traveller: malaria (thick and thin films), dengue, typhoid
items.stem: A 26-year-old returns from India with 8 days of stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, constipation and abdominal pain. Blood cultures grow Salmonella Typhi. Which is the best empirical antibiotic choice given regional resistance?
items.why: Typhoid acquired in South Asia is frequently quinolone-resistant and increasingly multidrug or extensively drug-resistant, so ceftriaxone is the empirical choice until susceptibilities return.
notes: Fluoroquinolone resistance is very common from South Asia.
Amoxicillin has high resistance and is not empirical therapy.
Doxycycline is not effective treatment for typhoid.

items.topic: Facial weakness: Bell's palsy vs upper motor neurone lesion (forehead sparing), prednisolone
items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents 24 hours after sudden right facial droop involving the forehead, with an inability to close the right eye. There is no limb weakness and ear examination is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.why: This is Bell's palsy, with lower motor neurone signs. Prednisolone started within 72 hours improves recovery, and eye lubrication and taping at night prevent corneal damage.
notes: Antivirals alone are not beneficial; they are not recommended as sole therapy.
Forehead involvement with no other deficits indicates a lower motor neurone lesion, not stroke.
Eye care is essential, and steroids improve outcomes if started early.

items.topic: Consent, capacity and confidentiality: mature minors (Gillick), substitute decision-makers, exceptions
items.stem: Which of the following is a required element of valid consent to treatment?
items.why: Valid consent requires capacity, voluntariness and adequate information. Age and writing are not strict requirements; capacity is decision-specific.
notes: Mature minors can consent; age alone does not determine validity.
Family agreement is not required for a capable adult.
Verbal or implied consent can be valid; writing is for evidence or high-risk procedures.

items.topic: Hepatitis B in pregnancy and the newborn: HBsAg screening, birth-dose vaccine and HBIG
items.stem: Which maternal marker indicates the highest infectivity and risk of perinatal hepatitis B transmission?
options: HBeAg positivity with high HBV DNA
items.why: HBeAg positivity and high viral load reflect active replication and the greatest transmission risk. Maternal antiviral therapy is considered in the third trimester with high DNA.
notes: Anti-HBs indicates immunity.
Isolated anti-HBc reflects past exposure and is not a marker of high infectivity.
Anti-HBe suggests lower replication and lower infectivity.

items.topic: Cirrhosis complications: ascites and SBP, hepatic encephalopathy, varices, Child-Pugh
items.stem: In cirrhosis with portal hypertension, which mechanism is the main driver of sodium and water retention leading to ascites?
options: Splanchnic vasodilatation causing effective arterial underfilling and RAAS activation
Raised plasma oncotic pressure from increased hepatic albumin synthesis
Primary renal tubular defect causing sodium wasting
items.why: Portal hypertension causes splanchnic vasodilatation (nitric oxide), lowering effective arterial volume; RAAS and ADH activate, retaining sodium and water. Hypoalbuminaemia also contributes.
notes: Albumin synthesis falls in cirrhosis, lowering oncotic pressure rather than raising it.
The kidney retains sodium avidly, not wastes it.
Hepatic clearance of aldosterone is reduced, so levels rise, not fall.

items.topic: Hernias: inguinal vs femoral, incarceration and strangulation
items.stem: What landmark distinguishes an inguinal hernia from a femoral hernia?
options: Position relative to the pubic tubercle
Position relative to the inferior epigastric vessels only
Position relative to the anterior superior iliac spine
items.why: Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernias lie below and lateral to it, through the femoral canal.
notes: Epigastric vessels separate direct from indirect, not inguinal from femoral.
The ASIS marks the inguinal ligament origin but not the hernia distinction.
Umbilicus is relevant to umbilical hernias.

items.topic: Asthma: Australian Asthma Handbook stepwise care, as-needed budesonide-formoterol, acute severe asthma
items.stem: A 19-year-old with asthma presents with severe wheeze, speaking single words and SpO2 88% on air. She has had no response to initial care. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Oxygen, repeated salbutamol and ipratropium, and systemic corticosteroid
items.why: Life-threatening or severe asthma needs oxygen, frequent salbutamol with ipratropium, and early systemic corticosteroids, with escalation if there is no response.
notes: Montelukast has no role in acute severe asthma.
Infection is not the primary problem; antibiotics and physiotherapy do not treat bronchospasm.
Inhaled steroid alone is inadequate and discharge is unsafe at this severity.

items.topic: Interstitial lung disease: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, drug-induced (amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin)
items.stem: A 68-year-old man on long-term amiodarone for atrial fibrillation develops progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass change and a low DLCO. Infection is excluded. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: Suspected amiodarone pulmonary toxicity: stop the drug, switch rhythm control, and consider corticosteroids if symptomatic or severe. Seek cardiology input.
notes: This would worsen toxicity.
Nitrofurantoin itself causes pulmonary toxicity.
There is no evidence of heart failure; continuing the drug risks progression.

items.topic: Antidepressants: SSRI hyponatraemia in older adults, serotonin syndrome, tricyclic overdose
items.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents one hour after amitriptyline overdose. She is drowsy, with BP 85/50 mmHg and QRS 140 ms on ECG. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
items.why: A wide QRS or hypotension in tricyclic overdose reflects sodium channel blockade. Treat with intravenous sodium bicarbonate.
notes: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses as it may precipitate seizures.
Amiodarone can worsen conduction block and QT prolongation.
Physostigmine risks seizures and asystole in tricyclic overdose.

items.topic: Myeloproliferative neoplasms: polycythaemia vera (JAK2), essential thrombocythaemia
items.stem: Most patients with polycythaemia vera carry an acquired JAK2 V617F mutation. What is the main effect of this mutation on haemopoietic progenitor cells?
options: Constitutive cytokine-independent signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway
Loss of function of the erythropoietin gene
Fusion of BCR and ABL1 producing a tyrosine kinase
Impaired iron uptake by erythroid precursors
items.why: JAK2 V617F is a gain-of-function mutation causing constitutive JAK-STAT signalling, so progenitors proliferate without needing erythropoietin. Serum erythropoietin is therefore low in PV.
notes: The mutation does not affect the erythropoietin gene; erythropoietin is suppressed, not lost, because of autonomous red cell production.
BCR-ABL1 defines chronic myeloid leukaemia, not PV.
Iron uptake is not the defect; PV may cause iron deficiency from overproduction, but that is secondary.

items.topic: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: sepsis and obstetric causes, coagulation profile
items.stem: A 60-year-old man with septic shock from pneumonia is bleeding from line sites. Platelets 22 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, INR 2.1. Antibiotics and fluids are given. Which is the most appropriate additional management?
options: Platelets and fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate or concentrate) for active bleeding
items.why: Treat the cause first. In DIC with active bleeding, replace platelets (keep over 50), fibrinogen (keep over 1.5 g/L) and factors with plasma as required.
notes: Antifibrinolytics are generally avoided in DIC as they risk thrombosis in a prothrombotic state.
Therapeutic heparin would worsen bleeding with this profile.
Vitamin K alone will not correct consumptive coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia.

items.topic: Acute stroke: FAST, CT and CT perfusion, thrombolysis and endovascular clot retrieval eligibility
items.stem: A 68-year-old man has sudden right arm weakness and aphasia 90 minutes ago. BP is 170/95 mmHg, glucose 6.5 mmol/L. Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. He takes no anticoagulants. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Aspirin 300 mg and observe on a ward
Intravenous tenecteplase now, with CT angiography to assess for large vessel occlusion
Lower BP below 140/90 mmHg before any treatment
Wait for MRI before deciding on thrombolysis
items.why: Within 4.5 hours with haemorrhage excluded and no contraindications, give IV thrombolysis (tenecteplase) without delay, and image vessels for ECR candidacy. BP must be below 185/110 mmHg.
notes: Antiplatelet alone is inadequate in an eligible patient; aspirin is withheld until after thrombolysis and follow-up imaging.
BP of 170/95 is already below the 185/110 mmHg threshold; no lowering is needed.
Waiting for MRI delays treatment; time is brain, and non-contrast CT is sufficient.

items.topic: Kidney disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people: earlier screening, remote dialysis access
items.stem: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have higher rates of end-stage kidney disease. Which early marker is used to screen for kidney damage, starting earlier than in the general population?
items.why: Albuminuria (urine ACR) is the earliest marker of kidney damage, along with eGFR. Guidelines advise screening Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from age 30, or earlier if risk factors exist.
notes: Urea rises late and is affected by diet and hydration.
Specific gravity measures concentration and is not a screening marker for kidney damage.
Potassium rises only in advanced disease.

items.topic: Respiratory failure and ABG interpretation: type 1 vs type 2, when to start NIV
items.stem: A 72-year-old with COPD exacerbation has had 1 hour of optimal medical therapy. ABG on 28% oxygen: pH 7.28, PaCO2 70 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 32 mmol/L. He is drowsy but rousable. What is the next step?
options: Increase oxygen to a non-rebreather mask
items.why: Acute hypercapnic acidosis (pH below 7.35, PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) persisting after optimal therapy is the indication for NIV in COPD exacerbation. Intubate if NIV fails.
notes: High-flow oxygen can worsen hypercapnia; target saturation 88–92%.
Intubation is for NIV failure or contraindications, not first line here.
Bicarbonate is not indicated; ventilation corrects the acidosis.

items.topic: Osteoporosis: fracture risk, DXA, bisphosphonates and denosumab (rebound fractures after stopping)
items.stem: Denosumab reduces bone resorption by which mechanism?
options: Binds RANKL, preventing osteoclast formation and activation
Binds hydroxyapatite and is taken up by osteoclasts
Inhibits sclerostin to increase bone formation
items.why: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL, inhibiting osteoclast differentiation and function. Its effect is reversible, so stopping causes rapid bone turnover and rebound vertebral fractures.
notes: This describes bisphosphonates.
This describes teriparatide.
This describes romosozumab.

items.topic: Anticoagulants: warfarin INR and interactions, DOAC dosing in renal impairment, peri-procedural plans
items.stem: Warfarin prolongs the INR by reducing the activity of which group of coagulation factors?
items.why: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C and S). Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so INR rises first.
notes: Factors I, V, VIII and XIII are not vitamin K dependent; this is a mixed group.
These are contact pathway factors; they are not vitamin K dependent and do not affect INR with warfarin.
Factors III and IV are tissue factor and calcium, and V and VIII are not vitamin K dependent.

items.topic: Multiple myeloma: CRAB features, serum and urine paraproteins
items.stem: A 68-year-old man has back pain, fatigue, creatinine 220 µmol/L, corrected calcium 3.0 mmol/L, Hb 85 g/L and a high ESR. Urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which pair of tests is the best initial investigation for suspected myeloma?
options: Serum protein electrophoresis with serum free light chains
Serum PSA with lumbar spine MRI
items.why: Initial work-up of suspected myeloma is serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains (plus urine). Light chains are missed by dipstick, so a negative dipstick does not exclude Bence Jones proteinuria.
notes: Bone scans often miss lytic lesions as they are purely osteolytic; ferritin does not diagnose myeloma.
These would not identify a paraprotein.
PSA addresses prostate metastases, but the CRAB features and ESR point towards myeloma.

items.topic: Cancer screening programs: bowel (iFOBT 45-74), breast (mammography 50-74), cervical (HPV 25-74), lung (LDCT 50-70)
items.stem: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program uses an immunochemical faecal occult blood test, which needs no dietary restriction, unlike the older guaiac test. What property of the immunochemical test explains this?
options: It detects the peroxidase activity of haem in the stool
It detects tumour-specific DNA mutations shed into the stool
It uses antibodies specific for human globin
It measures faecal calprotectin from mucosal neutrophils
items.why: The iFOBT uses antibodies against human globin, so dietary animal blood and plant peroxidases do not react. Globin is also digested in the upper GI tract, so it favours lower bowel bleeding.
notes: This describes the guaiac test, which reacts with dietary peroxidases and red meat and so needs dietary restriction.
That describes a stool DNA test, which is not used in the national program.
Calprotectin is a marker of intestinal inflammation, not a bowel cancer screening test.

items.topic: Methamphetamine and other stimulant use: acute agitation, psychosis, harm minimisation
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman using methamphetamine daily asks to cut down but is not ready to stop. She injects occasionally. Which harm minimisation advice is most appropriate?
options: Offer sterile needles and syringes and blood-borne virus testing
Advise stopping all contact until she commits to abstinence
Prescribe dexamfetamine as the standard first-line treatment
Advise that smoking rather than injecting carries no risk
items.why: Harm minimisation includes sterile injecting equipment, BBV testing and vaccination, and psychosocial support such as CBT and contingency management. No medication is approved for methamphetamine use disorder.
notes: Requiring abstinence first is not harm minimisation and disengages patients.
Substitution with dexamfetamine is not standard and is not first-line.
Smoking still carries cardiac, psychosis and dependence risks.

items.topic: Methamphetamine and other stimulant use: acute agitation, psychosis, harm minimisation
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains the sympathomimetic toxidrome (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia) and euphoria caused by methamphetamine?
options: Reversal of monoamine transporters, releasing dopamine and noradrenaline
items.why: Methamphetamine enters terminals, disrupts vesicular storage and reverses DAT/NET, flooding synapses with dopamine and noradrenaline.
notes: Mu-opioid agonism gives sedation, miosis and respiratory depression.
GABA-A enhancement causes sedation, as with alcohol and benzodiazepines.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition gives a cholinergic toxidrome with bradycardia and secretions.

items.topic: Meningitis and encephalitis: LP, empirical ceftriaxone with or without benzylpenicillin and aciclovir, dexamethasone, contacts
items.stem: A 30-year-old man has fever, confusion and a new focal seizure over two days. Neck stiffness is absent. CT head is normal. After lumbar puncture, which empirical treatment is most appropriate?
items.why: Fever, altered mentation and seizures suggest HSV encephalitis, so give IV aciclovir promptly without waiting for results. Many add ceftriaxone until bacterial meningitis is excluded.
notes: Ceftriaxone alone leaves HSV untreated; aciclovir is needed.
Oral valaciclovir is inadequate for suspected encephalitis, which needs IV therapy.
Steroids alone do not treat the infection and are not indicated for suspected HSV encephalitis.

items.topic: Lithium and therapeutic drug monitoring: toxicity triggers (dehydration, NSAIDs, thiazides)
items.stem: Why does dehydration or sodium depletion raise serum lithium concentration?
options: Proximal tubules reabsorb lithium with sodium, so lithium retention increases
Lithium is metabolised by the liver and hepatic blood flow falls
Lithium binds albumin and is displaced
Lithium is secreted in the loop of Henle and secretion falls
items.why: Lithium is handled like sodium in the proximal tubule and is renally cleared. Sodium depletion increases proximal reabsorption of both, so levels rise.
notes: Lithium is not metabolised; it is excreted unchanged by the kidney.
Lithium is not protein bound.
Lithium is reabsorbed, not secreted, along the proximal nephron.

items.topic: Urinary tract infection: cystitis vs pyelonephritis, resistance, pregnancy
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has a routine midstream urine showing E. coli >10^8 CFU/L. She has no urinary symptoms and is afebrile. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat with targeted antibiotics according to susceptibilities
No treatment; repeat culture at 28 weeks
Treat only if she develops dysuria or fever
Single-dose fosfomycin only if nitrites are positive
items.why: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated, as it increases the risk of pyelonephritis, preterm birth and low birthweight. Choose an agent by susceptibility and safe in pregnancy, then confirm cure.
notes: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy, unlike in most non-pregnant adults.
Waiting for symptoms risks progression to pyelonephritis, which is why screening is done.
Treatment depends on culture and susceptibilities, not a dipstick nitrite result.

items.topic: Urological emergencies: testicular torsion, acute urinary retention, obstructed infected kidney
items.stem: A 38-year-old man has fever, loin pain and a 5 mm obstructing ureteric stone on CT, with hydronephrosis, BP 85/50 mmHg and HR 120. What is the most appropriate next step after IV fluids and antibiotics?
options: Urgent decompression with stent or nephrostomy
Oral tamsulosin and review in a week
items.why: An obstructed infected kidney is a urological emergency; urgent decompression (stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) is needed with antibiotics. Definitive stone treatment follows once sepsis resolves.
notes: Medical expulsive therapy is inappropriate in septic obstruction.
Delay risks septic shock; definitive treatment waits until infection is treated.
Lithotripsy in infected obstruction can worsen sepsis; decompress first.

items.topic: Hypercalcaemia: primary hyperparathyroidism vs malignancy, acute management
items.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is confused and dehydrated. Corrected calcium is 3.4 mmol/L. What is the first-line initial management?
items.why: Severe hypercalcaemia causes volume depletion, so rehydration with IV normal saline comes first, followed by an IV bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid.
notes: Cinacalcet is used in primary or parathyroid carcinoma hypercalcaemia, not as acute first-line in malignancy.
Furosemide is only used after rehydration if fluid overloaded; it risks worsening volume depletion.
Dietary calcium is irrelevant in acute malignant hypercalcaemia.

items.topic: Antidepressants: SSRI hyponatraemia in older adults, serotonin syndrome, tricyclic overdose
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman develops confusion two weeks after starting sertraline. Sodium is 122 mmol/L with concentrated urine. Which mechanism most likely explains this?
options: Inappropriate ADH secretion causing water retention
items.why: SSRIs can cause SIADH, producing euvolaemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine. Risk is highest in older women in the first weeks.
notes: Aldosterone deficiency causes hypovolaemic hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, not typical of SSRIs.
Nephrogenic DI causes dilute urine and hypernatraemia.
Polydipsia gives dilute urine, not concentrated.

items.topic: Delirium: causes, non-drug management, telling it from dementia
items.stem: An 84-year-old woman, day 2 after hip fracture repair, is agitated at night, pulling at her drip, and disoriented. Vitals are normal. She is aggressive only when staff approach. What is the best initial management?
options: Non-drug measures and a search for the cause
items.why: First-line delirium care is identifying and treating causes (pain, constipation, retention, infection, drugs) with non-drug measures: reorientation, glasses, sleep, mobilisation. Drugs are reserved for distress or danger.
notes: Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
Restraints increase agitation, injury and prolonged delirium.
Antipsychotics are a short-term last resort if non-drug measures fail and there is risk, not regular first-line.

items.topic: Liver function test patterns: hepatocellular vs cholestatic, isolated unconjugated bilirubin (Gilbert)
items.stem: A 45-year-old man has ALT 620 U/L, AST 540 U/L, ALP 110 U/L (normal) and bilirubin 35 µmol/L after a paracetamol overdose. Which pattern is this?
items.why: Markedly raised aminotransferases with near-normal ALP indicates hepatocellular injury. Cholestatic patterns show ALP and GGT disproportionately raised.
notes: Cholestasis has ALP/GGT predominance.
Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia has normal enzymes.
Infiltrative disease typically raises ALP with normal or mildly raised ALT.

items.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health: MBS 715 health assessment, cultural safety, earlier screening ages
items.stem: Chronic kidney disease occurs earlier in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Which developmental mechanism contributes, through low birthweight and prematurity?
items.why: Nephrogenesis finishes by about 36 weeks, so prematurity or growth restriction leaves fewer nephrons. Remaining nephrons hyperfilter and scar, raising lifetime CKD risk.
notes: Not a recognised mechanism; low nephron endowment, not excess basement membrane, links low birthweight to CKD.
Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension, not a feature of low birthweight programming.
Tubular capacity is not the primary issue; the problem is fewer glomeruli to share the filtration load.

items.topic: Transient ischaemic attack: urgent assessment, secondary prevention, carotid endarterectomy
items.stem: A 70-year-old man had a left hemispheric TIA 5 days ago. Carotid duplex and CT angiography show 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. He is fit for surgery. What is the best management?
options: Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks of the event
Medical therapy alone, as stenosis is under 90%
items.why: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70–99% benefits most from endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of symptoms, alongside best medical therapy.
notes: Benefit is established for 70–99% symptomatic stenosis; best medical therapy is also given but surgery is added.
Benefit decays with delay; waiting 3 months forfeits the early risk reduction.
Anticoagulation is not superior to antiplatelets for carotid atherosclerosis.

items.topic: Diabetes drugs: metformin and eGFR, SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA, sick-day rules), insulin errors
items.stem: By which mechanism do SGLT2 inhibitors predispose to euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: Glycosuria lowers glucose and insulin while raising glucagon, promoting ketogenesis
They block hepatic gluconeogenesis, causing lactate accumulation
They stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion, causing hypoglycaemia
They inhibit lipolysis, reducing ketone clearance
items.why: Urinary glucose loss lowers glucose and insulin and raises glucagon, driving lipolysis and ketogenesis despite normal glucose. Illness, fasting and surgery increase risk.
notes: Lactic acidosis relates to metformin, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
Insulin secretion is not stimulated; that is sulfonylurea action.
SGLT2 inhibitors promote, not inhibit, lipolysis and ketogenesis.

items.topic: Dialysis and kidney transplant: urgent dialysis indications, immunosuppressant side effects
items.stem: Tacrolimus is used after kidney transplantation. Through which mechanism does it suppress rejection?
options: Inhibiting calcineurin and reducing T-cell IL-2 production
Inhibiting inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase in lymphocytes
Blocking the IL-2 receptor on activated T cells
items.why: Tacrolimus binds FKBP12 and inhibits calcineurin, so NFAT is not activated and IL-2 transcription falls. Its toxicities include nephrotoxicity, tremor and diabetes.
notes: That describes mycophenolate.
That describes basiliximab.
That describes methotrexate.

items.topic: Bronchiolitis: supportive care (PREDICT guideline), when to give oxygen or high-flow, apnoea in young infants
items.stem: A 5-month-old has had 3 days of coryza and cough, with tachypnoea, subcostal recession and widespread crackles and wheeze. Oxygen saturation is 94% in room air and feeding is reduced but adequate. What is the best management?
options: Supportive care with minimal handling and no oxygen
Low-flow oxygen to keep saturation above 98%
items.why: PREDICT/Australasian guidance: bronchiolitis is managed supportively. Oxygen is not needed if saturations are 90% or above; avoid bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics.
notes: Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and are not recommended.
Corticosteroids are not effective in bronchiolitis.
Oxygen is indicated only if saturation is persistently below 90%; targeting above 98% is unnecessary.

items.topic: First seizure and epilepsy: investigation, antiseizure drug choice, Austroads driving rules, valproate in women
items.stem: Which mechanism of action best explains why carbamazepine can control focal seizures but may worsen generalised absence seizures?
options: Enhancement of GABA-A receptor chloride conductance
Blockade of T-type calcium channels in thalamus
Inhibition of synaptic vesicle protein SV2A
items.why: Carbamazepine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, limiting high-frequency firing in focal seizures. It can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures, which depend on thalamocortical T-type calcium currents.
notes: GABA-A enhancement is the benzodiazepine and barbiturate mechanism, and these do not worsen absence seizures.
T-type calcium blockade is how ethosuximide treats absence seizures; carbamazepine lacks this action.
SV2A binding is levetiracetam's mechanism; it is broad-spectrum and does not worsen absence seizures.

items.topic: Vascular emergencies: acute limb ischaemia (6 Ps), mesenteric ischaemia
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has had 3 hours of a painful, pale, cold left leg with absent pulses and reduced sensation and power. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Elevate the leg and apply warm packs
Wait for CT angiography before anticoagulating
Intravenous unfractionated heparin and urgent vascular review
items.why: Suspected embolic acute limb ischaemia with a threatened limb needs immediate heparin to prevent propagation, analgesia and urgent vascular surgical revascularisation.
notes: Outpatient assessment is unacceptable in a threatened limb.
Warming and elevation worsen ischaemia and delay treatment.
Heparin should not wait for imaging in a threatened limb.

items.topic: Gallstone disease: biliary colic, cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis (Charcot's triad), ERCP
items.stem: Which hormone, released from duodenal I cells in response to fat in the duodenum, causes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi?
items.why: Cholecystokinin is released in response to fat and protein; it contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. This explains biliary colic after fatty meals.
notes: Secretin stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion in response to duodenal acid.
Gastrin, from G cells, stimulates gastric acid secretion.
Motilin drives the migrating motor complex in fasting, not gallbladder emptying after meals.

items.topic: Diabetic emergencies: DKA, HHS, hypoglycaemia
items.stem: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and drowsiness. Glucose 28 mmol/L, pH 7.1, ketones 5.0 mmol/L, K+ 3.0 mmol/L. Fluids are running. What is the most appropriate next step regarding insulin?
options: Start IV insulin infusion now alongside potassium replacement
Give IV insulin bolus of 10 units and then infusion
Delay insulin until potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L
Delay insulin until potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L
items.why: With K+ below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin would drive potassium intracellularly and risk arrhythmia, so replace potassium first and start insulin once K+ is at least 3.3 mmol/L.
notes: Starting insulin with K+ 3.0 mmol/L risks dangerous hypokalaemia and arrhythmia.
Boluses are not recommended; and it does not address the low potassium.
Insulin is withheld only if K+ is below about 3.3 mmol/L, not until above 5.5 mmol/L.

items.topic: Opioid use disorder: buprenorphine and methadone, long-acting injectable buprenorphine, take-home naloxone
items.stem: A 40-year-old man on methadone for opioid use disorder is counselled on overdose prevention. Which is the most appropriate item to supply?
options: Take-home naloxone with instructions for family
items.why: Take-home naloxone (intranasal or injectable) should be offered to people at risk of opioid overdose and their contacts, available without prescription in Australia.
notes: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
Extra methadone increases overdose risk.
Activated charcoal is not a community overdose measure and risks aspiration.

items.topic: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: four-pillar therapy (ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor), acute decompensation
items.stem: A 74-year-old man with known HFrEF presents with acute pulmonary oedema, SpO2 88% on air, BP 150/90, and is warm and wet. What is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
items.why: Congested, normotensive acute decompensation needs IV loop diuretic and oxygen if hypoxic; consider nitrates and NIV if severe.
notes: IV beta-blockers can worsen acute decompensation.
Spironolactone is too slow to treat acute pulmonary oedema.
Verapamil is negatively inotropic and harmful in HFrEF.

items.topic: Polycystic kidney disease: inheritance, intracranial aneurysms, screening relatives
items.stem: A 40-year-old man has bilateral enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts. His mother and brother have the same condition. What is the most likely mode of inheritance?
items.why: ADPKD (PKD1 or PKD2 mutations) is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk. Autosomal recessive PKD presents in infancy.
notes: Autosomal recessive PKD presents in neonates or infants and parents are usually unaffected.
X-linked recessive disease would mainly affect males and not pass from mother to son in this pattern.
Mitochondrial inheritance passes through the mother to all children and is not the pattern of ADPKD.

items.topic: Cervical screening: HPV test every 5 years from 25 to 74 including self-collection, managing results
items.stem: A 35-year-old woman's cervical screening test shows oncogenic HPV (not 16/18) detected, with LBC showing negative or low-grade changes. What is the recommended management?
items.why: Oncogenic HPV (not 16/18) with negative/low-grade LBC is intermediate risk: repeat HPV testing in 12 months. Colposcopy is for HPV 16/18 or higher-grade cytology.
notes: Routine 5-yearly screening is for HPV not detected.
Colposcopy is indicated for HPV 16/18 or for high-grade cytology.
Not indicated.

items.topic: Pelvic inflammatory disease and STIs in women: empirical treatment, ectopic and infertility risk
items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia and mucopurulent discharge. She has cervical motion tenderness and temperature 37.8°C, is tolerating oral fluids, and hCG is negative. What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
options: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once, then doxycycline and metronidazole orally for 14 days
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days alone
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid orally for 5 days
items.why: Mild-to-moderate PID is treated empirically with ceftriaxone IM plus doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days, covering gonorrhoea, chlamydia and anaerobes. Treat early to protect fertility.
notes: Azithromycin alone does not cover anaerobes or reliably treat gonorrhoea, and one dose is too short for PID.
Doxycycline alone misses gonorrhoea and anaerobes and is too short a course.
This does not cover chlamydia or gonorrhoea adequately and is not a PID regimen.

items.topic: Sexually transmitted infections: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, the syphilis outbreak and congenital syphilis, contact tracing
items.stem: Treponema pallidum is transmitted across the placenta. Which feature of the organism and maternal disease best explains why congenital syphilis can occur in a mother with no symptoms?
options: Latent infection still permits spirochaetaemia that can seed the fetus
The organism is only released from genital ulcers
Maternal IgG blocks placental transfer of the organism
Fetal infection occurs only at delivery through the birth canal
items.why: Treponemes can circulate in the blood during early and sometimes latent infection, crossing the placenta from about the second trimester. Maternal screening is therefore essential even without symptoms.
notes: Ulcers are infectious by contact, but haematogenous spread occurs without lesions.
Maternal IgG does not prevent transplacental spread of treponemes.
Congenital syphilis is acquired transplacentally, not mainly at delivery.

items.topic: Lung cancer: presentations, paraneoplastic syndromes, National Lung Cancer Screening Program (LDCT for 50-70 with 30+ pack-years, from July 2025)
items.stem: A smoker has hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and low serum osmolality. Which lung cancer type most typically causes this paraneoplastic syndrome through ectopic ADH?
items.why: Small cell lung cancer arises from neuroendocrine cells and secretes ADH (SIADH) and ACTH. Squamous cell cancer typically causes PTHrP hypercalcaemia.
notes: Squamous cell cancer is classically linked with PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.
Adenocarcinoma is associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy and thromboembolism, not typical SIADH.
Large cell carcinoma can secrete hCG (gynaecomastia) but is not the classic SIADH cause.

items.topic: Asthma: Australian Asthma Handbook stepwise care, as-needed budesonide-formoterol, acute severe asthma
items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has asthma with symptoms twice weekly, using salbutamol only. She has had no recent exacerbations. According to the Australian Asthma Handbook, which is the preferred reliever approach?
options: Salbutamol as needed with no other change
items.why: The Handbook recommends as-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol as the preferred reliever for adults with mild asthma, reducing exacerbations compared with salbutamol alone.
notes: Montelukast is not preferred first-line and does not replace an inhaled corticosteroid-containing reliever.
LABA without an inhaled corticosteroid is unsafe in asthma.
SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended as it increases exacerbation risk.

items.topic: Inherited bleeding disorders: haemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, preoperative assessment
items.stem: A boy has recurrent haemarthroses. APTT is prolonged and PT is normal; the APTT corrects with normal plasma. Which role of factor VIII explains this?
options: Cofactor for factor IXa in activating factor X in the intrinsic pathway
Cofactor for factor VIIa in the extrinsic pathway
items.why: Factor VIII is a cofactor for factor IXa in the tenase complex activating factor X. Deficiency (X-linked haemophilia A) prolongs APTT with normal PT.
notes: The extrinsic pathway involves tissue factor and VIIa, measured by PT, which is normal.
Fibrin cross-linking is factor XIII.
Protein C is activated by thrombin-thrombomodulin and is anticoagulant.

items.topic: Mosquito-borne viruses: Ross River, Barmah Forest, Murray Valley encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, dengue in north Queensland
items.stem: A traveller plans 3 months working in rural Papua New Guinea and the Torres Strait islands during the wet season. Which prevention measure is most appropriate against Japanese encephalitis?
options: Japanese encephalitis vaccination and mosquito avoidance
items.why: Japanese encephalitis vaccine is recommended for those spending prolonged time in Torres Strait or PNG at risk, together with repellents and protective clothing.
notes: Doxycycline does not prevent viral infection.
Ribavirin is not used for prophylaxis.
Prolonged stay in risk areas warrants vaccination too.

items.topic: Australian zoonoses: Q fever, leptospirosis, brucellosis, psittacosis, occupational exposure
items.stem: Leptospira interrogans is shed in the urine of rodents and livestock. Through which route does it most commonly enter humans in Queensland cane and banana farms?
options: Abraded skin or mucous membranes exposed to contaminated water or soil
items.why: Leptospires enter through cuts, abraded skin or mucous membranes after contact with water or soil contaminated by animal urine. This explains flood and wet-season exposure.
notes: Inhalation of dust describes Q fever and psittacosis, not usual leptospirosis.
Leptospirosis is not mosquito-borne.
Unpasteurised milk is a brucellosis route.

items.topic: Alcohol use disorder and withdrawal: AUDIT, withdrawal scales, thiamine before glucose, acamprosate and naltrexone
items.stem: Abrupt cessation of chronic heavy alcohol intake causes tremor, tachycardia and seizures. Which change in neurotransmission best explains this?
options: Reduced GABA-A inhibition with increased NMDA glutamate activity
Increased GABA-A inhibition with reduced glutamate activity
Reduced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens only
Increased serotonin reuptake in the raphe nuclei
items.why: Chronic alcohol enhances GABA-A and inhibits NMDA; adaptation downregulates GABA and upregulates NMDA, so cessation leaves CNS hyperexcitability. This is why benzodiazepines (GABA-A agonists) treat withdrawal.
notes: This is the acute intoxicated state, not withdrawal; adaptation reverses it on cessation.
Dopamine changes relate to reward and craving, not the autonomic hyperactivity and seizures of withdrawal.
Serotonin reuptake changes do not explain withdrawal hyperexcitability.

items.topic: Pituitary disease: prolactinoma, acromegaly, hypopituitarism, bitemporal hemianopia
items.stem: A 52-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma presents with hypotension, vomiting and lethargy after pituitary surgery. Sodium is 124 mmol/L. Both cortisol and thyroxine are low. Which replacement should be given first?
items.why: Glucocorticoid must be replaced before thyroid hormone, because levothyroxine increases cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.
notes: Starting levothyroxine first can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Gonadal replacement is not urgent and comes later.
Desmopressin is for diabetes insipidus, not indicated by these findings.

items.topic: Spinal cord compression and cauda equina: red flags, urgent MRI, steroids in malignancy
items.stem: A 68-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer has 3 days of thoracic back pain, now with bilateral leg weakness and a sensory level at T8. He is still able to walk with help. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
items.why: Suspected malignant spinal cord compression is an emergency: give high-dose dexamethasone and arrange urgent whole-spine MRI, then oncology/neurosurgical and radiotherapy review to preserve function.
notes: Delay risks irreversible paralysis; imaging must be urgent, within hours.
Lumbar puncture risks neurological deterioration with a compressive lesion and doesn't define it.
Analgesia alone ignores a cord compression emergency.

items.topic: Antimicrobial stewardship: eTG choices, penicillin allergy assessment and delabelling, C. difficile risk
items.stem: Which hypersensitivity mechanism underlies immediate reactions such as urticaria and anaphylaxis occurring within an hour of a penicillin dose?
items.why: Type I hypersensitivity involves pre-formed specific IgE on mast cells, releasing histamine and tryptase on re-exposure. This is why immediate reactions are the main concern for delabelling.
notes: Immune complexes (type III) cause serum sickness days later.
T cell-mediated type IV reactions are delayed, like contact dermatitis or SCARs.
Type II cytotoxic reactions cause haemolytic anaemia, not urticaria.

items.topic: Pituitary disease: prolactinoma, acromegaly, hypopituitarism, bitemporal hemianopia
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 8 months of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Pregnancy test is negative, prolactin is 3800 mIU/L (repeated), and MRI shows a 7 mm pituitary microadenoma. Visual fields are normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
items.why: Dopamine agonists, usually cabergoline, are first-line for symptomatic prolactinoma, normalising prolactin and shrinking the tumour. Surgery is reserved for resistance or intolerance.
notes: Surgery is second-line for dopamine agonist resistance or intolerance.
Radiotherapy is rarely used and is slow with a risk of hypopituitarism.
The pill may restore bleeding but does not treat the tumour or galactorrhoea.

items.topic: Acute kidney injury: prerenal vs intrinsic vs post-renal, the 'triple whammy' (ACEi/ARB + diuretic + NSAID), contrast
items.stem: A 72-year-old man has 3 days of vomiting and diarrhoea. He takes perindopril, indapamide and regular ibuprofen. BP 95/60 mmHg, dry mucous membranes. Creatinine 220 µmol/L (baseline 90). Urine sodium is low, urine osmolality high. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Volume depletion plus ACEi, diuretic and NSAID reduces renal perfusion. Low urine sodium and concentrated urine show intact tubular function, typical of prerenal injury.
notes: ATN gives high urine sodium and isosmolar urine with muddy brown casts; it may follow prolonged prerenal injury.
Obstruction would not explain hypotension with concentrated, low-sodium urine.
AIN usually has rash, eosinophilia or white cells in urine, and tubular dysfunction with high urine sodium.

items.topic: Endometriosis and polycystic ovary syndrome: diagnosis, fertility, metabolic risk
items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has oligomenorrhoea and hirsutism. Ultrasound shows polycystic-appearing ovaries. TSH and prolactin are normal. According to the 2023 international guideline, which finding is needed to confirm PCOS?
options: Raised testosterone with a normal ultrasound
Raised LH:FSH ratio on day 3 bloods
Two of three: irregular cycles, hyperandrogenism, or ultrasound features
items.why: Rotterdam criteria need two of three features. Ultrasound or AMH can replace the ultrasound criterion in adults, and exclusion of other causes (thyroid, prolactin, congenital adrenal hyperplasia) is required.
notes: Testosterone alone is not diagnostic; two criteria are needed.
LH:FSH ratio is not a diagnostic criterion.
AMH can serve as an alternative to ultrasound, but a threshold alone does not confirm PCOS without another feature.

items.topic: Dyspepsia, GORD and peptic ulcer: H. pylori test and treat, NSAIDs, alarm features
items.stem: By which mechanism do NSAIDs predispose to peptic ulcer disease?
options: Increased gastric acid secretion by parietal cells
Reduced prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection via COX-1 inhibition
Impaired gastric emptying causing acid reflux
items.why: COX-1 inhibition reduces gastric prostaglandins, which normally promote mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow. Mucosal defence falls, even with normal acid.
notes: NSAIDs do not act mainly by raising gastrin.
Acid secretion is not primarily increased; the defence is weakened.
Delayed emptying is not the main mechanism.

items.topic: Pituitary disease: prolactinoma, acromegaly, hypopituitarism, bitemporal hemianopia
items.stem: Which hypothalamic signal normally regulates prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary, so that a pituitary stalk lesion raises prolactin?
items.why: Prolactin is under tonic inhibition by hypothalamic dopamine. Stalk compression or dopamine antagonists remove this and raise prolactin; dopamine agonists treat prolactinoma.
notes: TRH stimulates prolactin release modestly; it is not the tonic inhibitor.
Somatostatin inhibits GH and TSH, not the main prolactin brake.
GHRH stimulates somatotrophs (GH), not lactotrophs.

items.topic: HIV: testing, PrEP, PEP timing, opportunistic infections
items.stem: HIV causes immunodeficiency by infecting a specific cell population. Which cell and surface molecule is the main target that explains the rise in opportunistic infections?
options: CD4 T lymphocytes via CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4
items.why: HIV binds CD4 with a CCR5 or CXCR4 co-receptor, depleting CD4 T helper cells. Opportunistic infections rise as the count falls below about 200 cells/µL.
notes: CD8 cells are not the main target.
B cells are not the main target of HIV.
Neutrophils are not infected; their function is largely preserved.

items.topic: Spider and marine envenomation: funnel-web, redback, box jellyfish (vinegar), Irukandji syndrome
items.stem: What is the main mechanism by which funnel-web spider venom causes autonomic storm?
options: Prolongs opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
Blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
items.why: Delta-atracotoxin slows sodium channel inactivation, causing repetitive firing and massive autonomic neurotransmitter release.
notes: Postsynaptic nicotinic blockade describes curare-like toxins, not funnel-web venom.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is organophosphate toxicity.
Calcium channel blockade is not the funnel-web mechanism.

items.topic: Perioperative medicine: fasting, managing anticoagulants and diabetes drugs, VTE prophylaxis
items.stem: Which component of Virchow's triad is most increased by prolonged immobility during and after surgery?
items.why: Immobility and anaesthesia reduce venous flow in the calf, causing stasis. Surgery also adds hypercoagulability and endothelial injury.
notes: Endothelial injury is more related to direct vessel trauma.
Hypercoagulability arises from the surgical stress response rather than immobility.
Platelet dysfunction is not part of Virchow's triad.

items.topic: Dialysis and kidney transplant: urgent dialysis indications, immunosuppressant side effects
items.stem: A 55-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease missed dialysis. He is dyspnoeic with crackles, K+ 7.2 mmol/L with peaked T waves, and urea 48 mmol/L. After IV calcium gluconate, what is the definitive treatment?
items.why: Refractory hyperkalaemia with fluid overload in an anuric patient needs urgent dialysis. Calcium protects the myocardium temporarily, and insulin-dextrose shifts potassium, but neither removes it.
notes: Resin is slow and insufficient for life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
He is likely anuric or oliguric, so a diuretic will not work.
Bicarbonate has limited effect and adds sodium load.

items.topic: Croup: severity assessment, oral dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline
items.stem: A 2-year-old has a barking cough and stridor at rest, with suprasternal and subcostal recession. He is distressed but alert and saturation is 97%. What is the best initial treatment?
items.why: Moderate croup (stridor at rest with recession) is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (up to 0.6 mg/kg may be used); add nebulised adrenaline if severe.
notes: Prednisolone courses are not the standard for croup; single-dose dexamethasone is preferred.
Nebulised budesonide is an alternative but oral dexamethasone is first line in Australia.
Croup is viral; antibiotics are not indicated.

items.topic: Phaeochromocytoma: paroxysmal symptoms, plasma metanephrines, alpha-blockade before surgery
items.stem: Phaeochromocytomas arise from which cells, accounting for their catecholamine secretion?
items.why: Phaeochromocytomas arise from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla and secrete adrenaline, noradrenaline or dopamine.
notes: Zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone.
Zona fasciculata produces cortisol.
Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin.

items.topic: Absolute cardiovascular risk and the Heart Health Check: 2023 Australian CVD risk calculator
items.stem: Absolute CVD risk estimates the chance of events from atherosclerosis. Which is the earliest step in atherosclerotic plaque formation?
options: Retention and oxidation of LDL particles in the subendothelial intima
Smooth muscle migration forming a fibrous cap
items.why: Endothelial dysfunction allows LDL to be retained and oxidised in the intima, which then recruits monocytes that become foam cells. Fibrous cap formation, calcification and rupture come later.
notes: The fibrous cap forms later, after foam cells and a lipid core have developed.
Rupture and thrombosis are late complications that cause acute events.
Calcification is a late feature of established plaque.

items.topic: Febrile convulsions and childhood epilepsy: simple vs complex, counselling parents
items.stem: A 2-year-old had a 2-minute generalised seizure with a febrile viral illness and is now back to normal. You counsel the parents. What is the best advice about prevention of recurrence?
options: Give regular paracetamol to prevent recurrence
Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence of febrile seizures
items.why: Antipyretics do not reduce febrile seizure recurrence, and prophylactic anticonvulsants are not indicated for simple febrile seizures. Reassure and teach first aid.
notes: Paracetamol does not prevent recurrence, though it can be used for comfort.
Daily anticonvulsants are not indicated for simple febrile seizures.
Regular levetiracetam is not indicated for simple febrile seizures.

items.topic: Acid-base disorders: anion gap, Winter's formula, mixed disorders
items.stem: A 60-year-old man with vomiting and poor intake has pH 7.30, Na 140, Cl 90, HCO3 14 mmol/L, normal albumin. The anion gap is 36 and the delta ratio is about 2.4. What does this indicate?
options: Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Pure normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
High anion gap acidosis with concurrent metabolic alkalosis
items.why: A delta ratio above 2 means bicarbonate has fallen less than the gap has risen, indicating a concurrent metabolic alkalosis (here from vomiting).
notes: A pure HAGMA gives a delta ratio of about 1 to 2.
The anion gap is markedly raised, so this is not a normal gap acidosis.
Bicarbonate is low as the primary change, so this is not respiratory acidosis with compensation.

items.topic: Multiple myeloma: CRAB features, serum and urine paraproteins
items.stem: In multiple myeloma, which free light chain finding explains the cast nephropathy seen on renal biopsy?
options: Filtered Bence Jones protein precipitating with Tamm–Horsfall protein in distal tubules
Immune complex deposition in glomerular basement membranes
Renal artery stenosis from vascular infiltration
items.why: Excess monoclonal light chains are filtered and form casts with Tamm–Horsfall protein in distal tubules, causing obstruction and injury. Dipstick is often negative for protein as it detects albumin.
notes: Immune complex disease is not the mechanism of cast nephropathy.
Hypercalcaemia causes vasoconstriction and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not afferent dilatation.
Renal artery stenosis is not a feature of myeloma.

items.topic: Postoperative complications: fever by postoperative day, anastomotic leak, wound infection, AKI
items.stem: A 65-year-old man on postoperative day 6 after anterior resection has fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain and rising CRP. Which complication is most likely?
options: Surgical site infection of the wound
items.why: Anastomotic leak typically presents at days 5–7 with fever, tachycardia, pain and raised inflammatory markers; CT with contrast confirms it.
notes: Atelectasis causes fever in the first 48 hours.
Wound infection is usually day 5–7 with local erythema and discharge, but systemic abdominal pain after bowel anastomosis points to a leak.
UTI is possible but does not explain abdominal pain and tachycardia after bowel surgery.

items.topic: Diabetic emergencies: DKA, HHS, hypoglycaemia
items.stem: Which mechanism explains why ketones accumulate in diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: Insulin deficiency drives unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis
Excess insulin suppresses ketone clearance by the kidney
Hyperglycaemia directly converts glucose into acetoacetate
Cortisol deficiency blocks beta-oxidation of fatty acids
items.why: Absent insulin removes inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase, so free fatty acids flood the liver and are converted to ketones, causing anion gap acidosis.
notes: Insulin excess suppresses ketogenesis; it does not impair renal ketone clearance.
Ketones come from fatty acid oxidation, not direct glucose conversion.
Beta-oxidation is increased, not blocked, in DKA; counter-regulatory hormones are raised.

items.topic: Adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone stress dosing, hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia
items.stem: Why does primary adrenal insufficiency cause hyperkalaemia, but secondary adrenal insufficiency does not?
options: Cortisol deficiency directly impairs distal tubular potassium secretion
Raised ACTH inhibits renal potassium excretion
Aldosterone is lost only in primary disease, as the RAAS drives its release
Hyponatraemia shifts potassium out of cells
items.why: Aldosterone secretion depends mainly on angiotensin II and potassium, not ACTH. It is lost only when the adrenal cortex itself is destroyed, causing sodium loss and potassium retention.
notes: Cortisol deficiency causes hyponatraemia via ADH, but the hyperkalaemia is from aldosterone loss.
ACTH has no inhibitory effect on renal potassium excretion; it causes pigmentation in primary disease.
Hyponatraemia does not cause a transcellular potassium shift.

items.topic: Hyperkalaemia: ECG changes, calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, finding the cause
items.stem: A 66-year-old man with CKD has weakness. Potassium is 7.4 mmol/L and ECG shows broad QRS and peaked T waves. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
items.why: With ECG changes, give IV calcium gluconate first to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin-dextrose, salbutamol and potassium removal. Calcium does not lower potassium.
notes: Slow onset; it removes potassium but does not protect the heart immediately.
Shifts potassium but takes 15 to 30 minutes and does not protect the myocardium.
Shifts potassium, but is adjunctive and not first-line cardiac protection.

items.topic: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: four-pillar therapy (ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor), acute decompensation
items.stem: How do SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin benefit patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
options: They cause glycosuria and natriuresis, reducing preload and hospitalisation
They block the beta-1 receptor to slow the heart rate
They antagonise aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor
They inhibit neprilysin to raise natriuretic peptides
items.why: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalisation and cardiovascular death, irrespective of diabetes, partly through osmotic diuresis and natriuresis.
notes: That is the beta-blocker mechanism.
That is the mineralocorticoid antagonists' mechanism (spironolactone, eplerenone).
That is sacubitril, part of ARNI.

items.topic: Urinary tract infection: cystitis vs pyelonephritis, resistance, pregnancy
items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency. She is afebrile with no flank pain, is not pregnant, and has no vaginal discharge. Which is the most appropriate empirical oral treatment per eTG?
options: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
Cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 14 days
items.why: For uncomplicated cystitis, eTG first-line options include trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days, or alternatives such as cefalexin or nitrofurantoin. Fluoroquinolones are reserved because of resistance and adverse effects.
notes: Fluoroquinolones should be reserved for pyelonephritis or resistant organisms due to adverse effects and resistance.
Amoxicillin has high E. coli resistance and is not recommended empirically.
A 14-day course is far too long for uncomplicated cystitis.

items.topic: Urinary tract infection: cystitis vs pyelonephritis, resistance, pregnancy
items.stem: Which organism causes most community-acquired urinary tract infections, ascending from the periurethral flora via the urethra?
items.why: Uropathogenic E. coli, using P fimbriae and type 1 pili to adhere to urothelium, causes about 70–80% of community UTIs. Remember that females have a short urethra close to the anus.
notes: S. saprophyticus is the second most common cause in young sexually active women but is far less frequent than E. coli.
Proteus is associated with struvite stones and alkaline urine, and is a minority of UTIs.
Enterococcus is more often seen in healthcare-associated or catheter-related infection.

items.topic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn's vs ulcerative colitis, acute severe colitis, extraintestinal features
items.stem: A 28-year-old with known ulcerative colitis has 9 bloody stools daily, HR 110, temperature 38.2°C, CRP 80 mg/L. Intravenous hydrocortisone is started. What is the most appropriate additional step?
options: Daily abdominal X-ray and early surgical review
items.why: This is acute severe colitis (Truelove and Witts). Admit, give IV corticosteroids, thromboprophylaxis, monitor for toxic megacolon, involve surgeons early, and escalate to infliximab or ciclosporin if no response by day 3.
notes: Oral mesalazine is inadequate for acute severe colitis.
Antimotility agents risk precipitating toxic megacolon.
Azathioprine is slow-acting and not for acute rescue; this patient needs inpatient care.

items.topic: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar state: fluids, insulin, potassium, SGLT2-inhibitor euglycaemic DKA
items.stem: Why must potassium be monitored closely and replaced early once an insulin infusion starts in diabetic ketoacidosis, even if the initial serum level is normal or high?
options: Insulin drives potassium into cells, unmasking total body depletion
IV fluids cause potassium to bind to albumin
Ketones are cleared by the kidney together with potassium
items.why: Acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells and osmotic diuresis depletes total stores; insulin returns potassium into cells and serum levels fall rapidly.
notes: Insulin does not increase renal potassium reabsorption; its effect is cellular uptake.
Fluids dilute potassium but do not bind it to albumin.
Ketones are excreted as anions with sodium and potassium, but this is not why levels fall on insulin.

items.topic: Parkinson's disease: clinical diagnosis, levodopa, drug-induced parkinsonism
items.stem: Parkinson's disease results from loss of dopaminergic neurones in which structure?
items.why: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces striatal dopamine, producing bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor.
notes: The caudate receives the dopamine; it is not the site of primary neuronal loss.
The subthalamic nucleus is overactive downstream, not the site of loss.
Cerebellar disease causes ataxia and intention tremor, not parkinsonism.

items.topic: The Australian health system: Medicare, PBS, safety nets, authority scripts, mental health treatment plans
items.stem: A GP assesses a 28-year-old with moderate depression and plans a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan. After preparing it, when is the earliest recommended review of the plan?
options: Only when the patient requests it
After 6 sessions with a psychologist only
items.why: The GP should review the patient 4 weeks to 3 months after preparing the plan, then again after the course of services.
notes: Twelve months is too long for the initial review.
Review is scheduled by the GP, not left to patient request.
A further review follows the sessions, but the initial review is earlier.

items.topic: Australian zoonoses: Q fever, leptospirosis, brucellosis, psittacosis, occupational exposure
items.stem: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii. Which feature of the organism best explains why abattoir workers can be infected without direct animal contact?
options: It forms a hardy spore-like form that persists in dust and spreads by aerosol
It is transmitted by a tick vector that infests carcasses
It produces a heat-stable enterotoxin in raw meat
It penetrates intact skin from contaminated water
items.why: Coxiella burnetii forms resistant small-cell variants that survive in the environment and are inhaled as aerosols from birth products, hides and dust. Very few organisms are needed to infect.
notes: Ticks can carry it, but human infection is mainly by inhalation, not tick bite.
Q fever is not a toxin-mediated food poisoning.
Skin penetration from water describes leptospirosis, not Q fever.

items.topic: Opioids and analgesia: dose conversion, constipation, naloxone, Schedule 8 rules and real-time prescription monitoring
items.stem: A man on regular oral morphine develops hard stools and straining. Which mechanism best explains why opioid-induced constipation does not show tolerance over time?
options: Mu-receptor activation in the enteric nervous system reduces peristalsis and secretions
Opioids increase bile acid delivery to the colon, slowing transit
Opioids block cholinesterase in the gut wall
Opioids cause central vagal stimulation that raises sphincter tone only
items.why: Mu-opioid receptors in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses reduce propulsion and secretion and increase sphincter tone. Tolerance to this effect is minimal, so prophylactic laxatives are needed for as long as opioids continue.
notes: Opioids reduce, not increase, bile and pancreatic secretions; this is not the mechanism.
Opioids do not inhibit cholinesterase; they reduce acetylcholine release from enteric neurons.
The effect is mainly peripheral enteric, not central vagal, and involves more than sphincter tone.

items.topic: Postoperative complications: fever by postoperative day, anastomotic leak, wound infection, AKI
items.stem: A 50-year-old man on day 6 after open appendicectomy for perforation has fever and a red, tender, swollen wound with purulent discharge. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the best initial management?
options: Open the wound and drain the pus
items.why: Surgical site infection with pus needs source control: open the wound, drain and irrigate. Antibiotics are added for spreading cellulitis or systemic illness.
notes: Antibiotics alone are insufficient without drainage of pus.
Observation is inappropriate for a purulent infected wound.
Laparotomy is not needed when he is stable and the problem is superficial.

items.topic: Spinal cord compression and cauda equina: red flags, urgent MRI, steroids in malignancy
items.stem: In an adult, the spinal cord ends at approximately which vertebral level, so that a lesion below it causes lower motor neurone signs from compression of the cauda equina?
items.why: The adult conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2. Below this the canal contains lumbosacral nerve roots (cauda equina), so compression gives LMN signs, not UMN signs.
notes: The cord ends lower than T12; T12 is too high.
L4–L5 is where lumbar puncture is done, below the conus, but not where the cord ends.
S2 is the level of the end of the dural sac, not the spinal cord.

items.topic: Dyspepsia, GORD and peptic ulcer: H. pylori test and treat, NSAIDs, alarm features
items.stem: A 32-year-old man has 3 months of epigastric burning, relieved by food. He has no weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting or anaemia, takes no NSAIDs, and has not had treatment. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Test for H. pylori with stool antigen or urea breath test
Trial of lifelong high-dose proton pump inhibitor
items.why: Under 55 with no alarm features, test and treat H. pylori (urea breath test or stool antigen, off PPI for 2 weeks) is recommended for dyspepsia before endoscopy.
notes: No alarm features and young age; endoscopy is not first line.
Long-term PPI without testing misses a curable cause.
CT has no role in uncomplicated dyspepsia.

items.topic: Urological emergencies: testicular torsion, acute urinary retention, obstructed infected kidney
items.stem: Testicular torsion most often occurs in adolescents because of which anatomical variant?
options: Tunica vaginalis attached high on the cord (bell-clapper)
items.why: In the bell-clapper deformity, the tunica vaginalis covers the testis and epididymis completely, so the testis hangs free and can rotate. It is often bilateral.
notes: A long, not short, cord permits twisting.
A patent processus relates to hernia or hydrocele, not classic torsion.
Gubernaculum absence is not the typical cause.

items.topic: Otitis media: when to give antibiotics, chronic suppurative otitis media in First Nations children, hearing loss
items.stem: Why are young children more prone to acute otitis media than adults?
options: Their Eustachian tube is shorter, narrower and more horizontal
Their tympanic membrane is thicker and poorly vascularised
Their middle ear lacks a mucosal lining
Their Eustachian tube is longer and more vertical
items.why: In infants the Eustachian tube is short, narrow and horizontal, so it drains poorly and allows nasopharyngeal pathogens to reach the middle ear.
notes: The tympanic membrane is not thicker in children, and thickness does not explain the susceptibility.
The middle ear has a mucosal lining at all ages.
The tube is shorter and more horizontal in children; it lengthens and becomes more vertical with age.

items.topic: Sarcoidosis: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, hypercalcaemia, steroid indications
items.stem: Which mechanism explains hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis?
options: Increased renal reabsorption of calcium due to loss of calcitonin
Osteoclast activation by tumour-derived PTH-related peptide
Activated macrophages in granulomas converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol
items.why: Granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, unregulated by PTH, producing excess calcitriol and increased gut calcium absorption. PTH is suppressed.
notes: PTH is suppressed in sarcoid hypercalcaemia.
Calcitonin loss is not a mechanism of this.
PTHrP is a paraneoplastic mechanism, for example in squamous cell lung cancer.

items.topic: Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, myasthenic crisis, drugs that worsen it
items.stem: In myasthenia gravis, what is the main autoantibody target?
items.why: Antibodies to the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor reduce receptor numbers, so end-plate potentials fail, causing fatigable weakness.
notes: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
Sodium channel antibodies are not the cause of myasthenia gravis.
Axonal neurofilament is not the myasthenia target.

items.topic: Skin and soft tissue infection: cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, community-acquired MRSA
items.stem: A 35-year-old man who injects drugs has a 3 cm tender abscess on the forearm, no systemic features. Incision and drainage was done. Prior swab grew community-acquired MRSA. What is the most important management step?
options: Adequate incision and drainage alone is usually sufficient
Long-course IV vancomycin for all patients
Topical mupirocin to the wound only
items.why: For simple abscesses without systemic features, drainage is the key treatment; antibiotics are added only for systemic illness, extensive cellulitis, or immunosuppression.
notes: IV vancomycin is reserved for severe or systemic infection.
Flucloxacillin does not cover MRSA and is not required for a drained simple abscess.
Topical mupirocin is not treatment for an abscess.

items.topic: Absolute cardiovascular risk and lipids: 2023 Australian CVD risk calculator, statin thresholds, familial hypercholesterolaemia
items.stem: A 42-year-old man has LDL-C 6.2 mmol/L, tendon xanthomata, and his father had an MI at 48. He is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Lifestyle advice alone and recheck in 12 months
Calculate 5-year risk and treat only if over 10%
Start a high-intensity statin and arrange cascade screening of relatives
items.why: Clinically probable familial hypercholesterolaemia is treated regardless of the risk calculator: high-intensity statin, add ezetimibe if needed, and cascade-test first-degree relatives.
notes: Lifestyle alone is insufficient in FH.
The risk calculator does not apply to people with clinically diagnosed FH, who are treated regardless.
Fibrates are not first-line for raised LDL-C.

items.topic: Prescribing in pregnancy and breastfeeding: TGA pregnancy categories, teratogens (isotretinoin, ACEi, warfarin)
items.stem: A woman taking an ACE inhibitor for hypertension finds she is 10 weeks pregnant. Which fetal toxicity is the main reason ACE inhibitors are avoided, particularly in the second and third trimesters?
options: Premature closure of the ductus venosus
items.why: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II, which maintains fetal glomerular filtration. This causes renal failure, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia and skull hypoplasia.
notes: Neural tube defects are linked to valproate and carbamazepine (folate antagonism), not ACE inhibitors.
Fetal goitre is associated with antithyroid drugs or iodine excess, not ACE inhibitors.
Premature ductus arteriosus closure occurs with NSAIDs; the ductus venosus is not the target.

items.topic: Antimicrobial stewardship: eTG choices, penicillin allergy assessment and delabelling, C. difficile risk
items.stem: A 30-year-old reports a childhood benign rash with amoxicillin over 10 years ago, with no systemic features or anaphylaxis. She is well now. Which is the most appropriate step per Australian antibiotic allergy guidance?
options: Direct oral amoxicillin challenge to delabel
Skin prick testing for all penicillins first
Use of vancomycin for future infections
items.why: Low-risk histories (such as remote benign rash) can be delabelled by direct oral challenge, per ASCIA/eTG tools such as PEN-FAST. Delabelling reduces broad-spectrum use and C. difficile risk.
notes: Avoidance perpetuates an inaccurate label and leads to inferior, broader-spectrum therapy.
Skin testing is not needed for low-risk histories; direct challenge is safe.
Vancomycin is inferior for beta-lactam-susceptible infections and worsens stewardship.

items.topic: Prostate: BPH, PSA testing with shared decision-making, prostate cancer
items.stem: A 72-year-old man has bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms. Prostate is estimated at 70 mL on ultrasound, PSA 5.0 microgram/L, and he has no postural hypotension. Which drug combination best reduces his risk of progression and retention?
items.why: For a large prostate (more than about 30–40 mL) with bothersome symptoms, a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor plus an alpha-blocker reduces progression and retention risk. Dutasteride roughly halves PSA.
notes: An alpha-blocker gives quick symptom relief but does not shrink the gland or reduce retention risk long term.
Antimuscarinics treat overactive bladder symptoms and do not address gland size or progression.
Tadalafil improves symptoms but does not reduce prostate volume or progression.

items.topic: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease: Australian Jones criteria for high-risk groups, secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains how a group A streptococcal pharyngeal infection causes carditis in acute rheumatic fever?
options: Direct bacterial invasion of the heart valves
Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin
Streptolysin O toxin directly lysing myocytes
Bacterial superantigen causing Kawasaki-type coronary vasculitis
items.why: Immune response to group A streptococcal M protein cross-reacts with host cardiac proteins (e.g. myosin) in susceptible hosts: molecular mimicry. The heart is not infected.
notes: Wrong: the valves are not infected; cultures are sterile and the damage is autoimmune, which is why antibiotics do not treat the carditis.
Wrong: streptolysin O is the antigen behind the raised ASO titre, not the cause of the myocardial injury.
Wrong: this describes mechanisms proposed for Kawasaki disease or toxic shock, not the post-streptococcal autoimmune process of ARF.

items.topic: Syncope: cardiac red flags, ECG clues (long QT, Brugada, HCM), driving advice
items.stem: A 24-year-old man collapsed suddenly while swimming. His brother died suddenly aged 20. ECG shows QTc 510 ms. Which drug is the best long-term first-line therapy?
items.why: Syncope with swimming and a family history suggests long QT syndrome type 1. Non-selective beta-blockers such as nadolol are first-line, with an ICD for high-risk patients.
notes: Flecainide is not first-line for long QT syndrome and carries proarrhythmic risk.
Digoxin is proarrhythmic and does not reduce long QT risk.
Verapamil is not an established therapy for long QT syndrome.

items.topic: Childhood asthma: preventer criteria, spacers, acute management
items.stem: A 5-year-old has an acute asthma exacerbation. Which change in the airways is the main reason salbutamol rapidly relieves wheeze?
options: Bronchial smooth muscle relaxation via beta-2 receptors
Reduced airway mucosal oedema via glucocorticoid action
Blockade of leukotriene receptors on eosinophils
Thinning of mucus through increased ciliary clearance
items.why: Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist that raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, giving rapid bronchodilation. Corticosteroids act on inflammation over hours.
notes: Describes corticosteroid effect, which is slower and not how salbutamol works.
Describes montelukast, a preventer, not a reliever.
Mucociliary clearance is not the main mechanism of salbutamol's rapid effect.

items.topic: Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome: distinguishing features, management
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains the clonus, hyperreflexia and hyperthermia seen in serotonin syndrome?
options: Excess 5-HT2A stimulation in the brainstem and spinal cord
Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway
Excess GABA-A receptor activation in the cortex
Ryanodine receptor dysfunction in skeletal muscle
items.why: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic stimulation, especially 5-HT2A (and 5-HT1A), causing neuromuscular hyperactivity and hyperthermia. D2 blockade underlies neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
notes: D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway is the proposed mechanism of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with rigidity and bradyreflexia.
GABA-A activation causes sedation and hypotonia, not neuromuscular hyperactivity.
Ryanodine receptor dysfunction underlies malignant hyperthermia, a different condition triggered by anaesthetic agents.

items.topic: Hypertension in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia: aspirin for high-risk women, magnesium sulfate, timing of birth
items.stem: Which early placental abnormality is thought to underlie pre-eclampsia?
options: Inadequate remodelling of spiral arteries by extravillous trophoblast
Excessive trophoblast invasion into the myometrium with low-resistance flow
Primary maternal renal glomerular injury causing proteinuria
Placental overproduction of pro-angiogenic placental growth factor
items.why: Shallow trophoblast invasion leaves spiral arteries narrow, causing placental ischaemia and release of anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1), which cause maternal endothelial dysfunction.
notes: Excess invasion describes placenta accreta spectrum, not pre-eclampsia.
Renal involvement is a consequence of endothelial dysfunction, not the primary defect.
Pre-eclampsia features low placental growth factor and high sFlt-1, not overproduction.

items.topic: Australian zoonoses: Q fever, leptospirosis, brucellosis, psittacosis, occupational exposure
items.stem: A 40-year-old bird breeder has 1 week of fever, dry cough, headache and relative bradycardia. Chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation. Which organism is most likely?
items.why: Psittacosis follows exposure to infected birds (parrots, pigeons, poultry) and causes atypical pneumonia with headache and relative bradycardia. Treat with doxycycline.
notes: Pneumococcus is common, but bird exposure points elsewhere.
Legionella is linked to water systems and potting mix, with hyponatraemia.
Q fever follows livestock exposure, not birds.

items.topic: Dementia: Alzheimer vs vascular vs Lewy body vs frontotemporal, reversible causes, capacity
items.stem: A 74-year-old man has fluctuating alertness, well-formed visual hallucinations of children, mild parkinsonism and acting out his dreams. Memory is relatively preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism are core features of dementia with Lewy bodies. Avoid typical antipsychotics (severe sensitivity).
notes: Alzheimer disease presents with early prominent amnesia, without these core features.
Vascular dementia has stepwise decline and focal signs with vascular risk factors.
bvFTD presents with disinhibition, apathy and loss of empathy, with early personality change.

items.topic: Chronic kidney disease: staging by eGFR and urine ACR, Kidney Health Check for at-risk adults, slowing progression
items.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine ACR 8 mg/mmol on two samples over 4 months. Which CKD stage and category is this?
items.why: eGFR 45 to 59 is G3a. In men, ACR 2.5 to 25 mg/mmol (women 3.5 to 35) is A2, moderately increased. Persistence over 3 months confirms CKD.
notes: eGFR 52 is below 60, so this is stage 3, not 2.
G3b is eGFR 30 to 44, and A3 requires ACR above 25 mg/mmol in men.
A3 requires ACR above 25 mg/mmol in men (35 in women); 8 is A2.

items.topic: Iron deficiency anaemia: ferritin interpretation, oral vs IV iron, finding the cause
items.stem: Which protein, secreted by the liver, is raised in iron overload and inhibits iron absorption by degrading ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages?
