items.why: Hepcidin binds ferroportin, causing its internalisation and degradation, so less iron leaves enterocytes and macrophages. It is raised in inflammation, which explains anaemia of chronic disease.
notes: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; it is not an inhibitor of absorption and rises in iron deficiency.
Erythropoietin drives red cell production; it suppresses hepcidin rather than degrading ferroportin.
Ferritin stores iron intracellularly; it does not regulate ferroportin.

items.topic: Head injury: GCS, CT head rules, anticoagulated patients, extradural vs subdural haematoma
items.stem: An 82-year-old woman on apixaban falls at home and hits her head. She is GCS 15, has no vomiting or neurological deficit, and a 2 cm scalp haematoma. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: CT head only if symptoms develop
items.why: Anticoagulated patients with head injury need urgent CT head, even if GCS 15 and asymptomatic, because of the risk of occult or delayed intracranial bleeding.
notes: Unsafe: anticoagulant use is a risk factor mandating imaging.
Observation alone does not exclude intracranial haemorrhage in an anticoagulated patient.
Waiting for symptoms risks delayed diagnosis of a bleed.

items.topic: Diabetic kidney disease: albuminuria, ACEi/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors
items.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria starts an ACE inhibitor. Which mechanism most directly reduces intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria?
items.why: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole. Blocking it dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering glomerular capillary pressure and albuminuria. Expect a small, acceptable rise in creatinine.
notes: Afferent constriction is the effect of SGLT2 inhibitors via tubuloglomerular feedback, not ACE inhibitors.
Proximal sodium reabsorption is the target of SGLT2 inhibitors, not ACE inhibitors.
ACE inhibitors relax mesangial cells; contraction would reduce filtration surface area.

items.topic: Antimicrobial stewardship: eTG choices, penicillin allergy assessment and delabelling, C. difficile risk
items.stem: Why does broad-spectrum antibiotic use predispose to Clostridioides difficile infection?
options: It depletes protective colonic flora, allowing spore germination and toxin production
It directly stimulates toxin gene transcription
It raises gastric pH, allowing vegetative bacteria to survive
It suppresses neutrophil function in the gut
items.why: Disrupting the commensal microbiome removes colonisation resistance, so ingested spores germinate and produce toxins A and B. Narrow-spectrum, short courses reduce risk.
notes: Antibiotics do not directly upregulate toxin genes; the effect is through flora loss.
Raised gastric pH is a PPI-related risk factor and not the antibiotic mechanism.
Antibiotics do not primarily impair gut neutrophils.

items.topic: Obesity: metabolic complications, GLP-1 RA pharmacotherapy, bariatric surgery
items.stem: A 40-year-old man had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 18 months ago. He now has fatigue, a macrocytic anaemia and paraesthesia. Which long-term supplementation is essential after this operation?
items.why: Bypass reduces intrinsic factor and acid, so B12 deficiency is common and lifelong supplementation (with iron, calcium, vitamin D) is needed.
notes: Vitamin C deficiency is uncommon and does not cause macrocytosis with neuropathy.
Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not neuropathy or macrocytosis.
Folate is supplemented, not restricted.

items.topic: Antimicrobial stewardship: eTG choices, penicillin allergy assessment and delabelling, C. difficile risk
items.stem: A 72-year-old develops watery diarrhoea 6 days after starting clindamycin in hospital. Stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. Which is the first-line oral therapy per eTG for an initial episode?
items.why: Oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) is first-line for C. difficile infection, along with stopping the precipitating antibiotic where possible. Antimotility drugs should be avoided.
notes: IV metronidazole is no longer first-line and is reserved as an adjunct in severe cases.
Antimotility agents risk toxic megacolon.
Fluoroquinolones are a high-risk cause of C. difficile.

items.topic: Prostate: BPH, PSA testing with shared decision-making, prostate cancer
items.stem: A well 55-year-old man with no family history asks about PSA testing. Which approach is best, in line with Australian guidance?
options: Offer testing every 2 years from 50 with informed discussion of harms and benefits
Test only if he has symptoms
Refuse testing as it is not recommended
Do a digital rectal exam only, avoiding PSA
items.why: Australian guidelines recommend men aged 50–69 who choose to be tested have PSA every 2 years after shared decision-making about benefits and harms, including overdiagnosis.
notes: Asymptomatic men can choose testing after counselling; testing is not limited to symptoms.
Testing is not recommended routinely, but it is not refused if an informed man requests it.
DRE alone has poor sensitivity and is not recommended as a standalone screen.

items.topic: Prescribing in pregnancy and breastfeeding: TGA pregnancy categories, teratogens (isotretinoin, ACEi, warfarin)
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin (INR target 3.0) presents at 5 weeks' gestation, planning to continue the pregnancy. Warfarin embryopathy risk is greatest at 6–12 weeks. What is the best next step?
options: Continue warfarin unchanged to protect the valve
Stop all anticoagulation until the second trimester
Switch to aspirin alone during the first trimester
Specialist-led switch to therapeutic LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring
items.why: Warfarin is teratogenic at 6–12 weeks. In mechanical valves, urgent specialist planning is needed, usually switching to therapeutic LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring. DOACs are contraindicated.
notes: Continuing warfarin risks embryopathy in the sensitive window; if used, it needs specialist weighing of dose and risk.
Stopping all anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis and maternal death.
Aspirin alone gives inadequate protection against mechanical valve thrombosis.

items.topic: Thrombocytopenia: ITP, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, TTP/HUS (schistocytes)
items.stem: In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which mechanism explains the fall in platelets together with a paradoxical risk of thrombosis?
options: Antibodies to heparin-PF4 complexes activate platelets
Autoantibodies to GPIIb/IIIa cause splenic clearance
Marrow suppression from heparin reduces megakaryocytes
items.why: IgG against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes binds platelet FcγRIIa, causing activation, consumption and thrombin generation, so thrombosis occurs despite thrombocytopenia.
notes: This describes ITP, which causes bleeding rather than thrombosis.
This describes TTP, which does not follow heparin exposure.
Heparin does not suppress megakaryocytes; HIT is immune-mediated consumption.

items.topic: Sexually transmitted infections: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, the syphilis outbreak and congenital syphilis, contact tracing
items.stem: Chlamydia trachomatis is a common cause of urethritis and cervicitis. Which property of the organism explains why it is detected by NAAT rather than routine culture on agar?
options: It is an obligate intracellular bacterium
items.why: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium that cannot grow on cell-free media, so NAAT is the standard diagnostic test.
notes: It is not a Gram-positive spore-former.
Spirochaetes describe Treponema, not Chlamydia.
All bacteria contain nucleic acid; NAAT depends on this.

items.topic: Biostatistics: sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, NNT, relative vs absolute risk
items.stem: A screening test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%. It is applied to 1000 people in a population where disease prevalence is 1%. About what proportion of positive results are true positives?
items.why: 10 diseased: 9 true positives. 990 well: 99 false positives. PPV = 9/108, about 8–10%. PPV falls as prevalence falls.
notes: 90% is the sensitivity, not the PPV; PPV depends on prevalence.
50% would need a much higher prevalence, about 10%.
1% is just the prevalence; the test still enriches for disease above this.

items.topic: Antepartum haemorrhage: placenta praevia vs abruption, no vaginal examination until praevia is excluded
items.stem: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks presents with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding. She is stable and the uterus is soft and non-tender. What should be avoided until the placental site is known?
items.why: Painless bright bleeding suggests placenta praevia. A digital examination can provoke torrential haemorrhage, so avoid it until ultrasound has excluded praevia.
notes: CTG is needed to assess fetal wellbeing and is safe.
IV access and bloods are required in antepartum haemorrhage.
Ultrasound locates the placenta and is the investigation of choice.

items.topic: Anticoagulant reversal and major bleeding: vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran
items.stem: A 78-year-old man on warfarin presents with a large intracerebral haemorrhage and GCS 10. INR is 5.2. What is the most appropriate immediate reversal?
options: Prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K
items.why: Life-threatening warfarin bleeding needs rapid PCC to replace factors II, VII, IX, X, plus IV vitamin K 5–10 mg for sustained effect.
notes: Oral vitamin K is too slow for life-threatening bleeding.
FFP needs large volumes and is slower; PCC is preferred.
Tranexamic acid does not reverse warfarin's coagulopathy.

items.topic: Melioidosis: Top End and north Queensland, wet season, diabetes, meropenem
items.stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes in Darwin has fever, cough and hypotension in March, with bilateral nodular infiltrates and Gram-negative bacilli in blood cultures. Melioidosis is suspected. Which intravenous therapy is most appropriate?
items.why: Severe melioidosis needs intensive-phase IV meropenem (or ceftazidime) for at least 2 weeks, followed by eradication therapy with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for about 3 months or more.
notes: Ceftriaxone is not reliably active against B. pseudomallei.
Aminoglycosides are ineffective against it.
Flucloxacillin does not cover Gram-negative bacilli.

items.topic: Headache: subarachnoid haemorrhage red flags, migraine treatment and prophylaxis, medication-overuse headache
items.stem: Triptans relieve acute migraine mainly through agonism at which receptor?
items.why: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists: they cause cranial vasoconstriction and inhibit trigeminal release of CGRP. Hence they are contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease.
notes: 5-HT3 antagonism is the mechanism of ondansetron for nausea, not triptans.
D2 antagonism is how metoclopramide helps nausea and gastric stasis.
Beta-2 receptors are not the triptan target; propranolol, a beta blocker, is used for prophylaxis.

items.topic: Tuberculosis: latent vs active, migrants from high-incidence countries, notification and contact tracing
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman from a high-incidence country, now a new migrant, has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. She has no symptoms, a normal CXR and a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Positive IGRA with no symptoms and normal CXR indicates latent TB infection; offer treatment to reduce reactivation risk. IGRA cannot distinguish latent from active disease, so symptoms and imaging matter.
notes: No symptoms or radiological features of active disease.
IGRA is not affected by BCG, unlike the tuberculin skin test.
IGRA is specific to M. tuberculosis complex antigens; this is unlikely.

items.topic: Pulmonary embolism: Wells and PERC, CTPA vs V/Q (pregnancy, renal impairment), anticoagulation, thrombolysis for massive PE
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Her chest x-ray is normal and she has no leg symptoms. She has no asthma or lung disease. Which is the most appropriate imaging test?
items.why: With a normal chest x-ray in pregnancy, V/Q scanning is preferred: lower maternal breast radiation than CTPA and good diagnostic yield. CTPA is acceptable if the x-ray is abnormal or V/Q is unavailable.
notes: CTPA delivers higher breast radiation dose; it is second-line when the chest x-ray is normal.
Invasive pulmonary angiography is rarely used and has higher risk.
MRI chest is not a validated first-line test for PE in pregnancy.

items.topic: Acute kidney injury: prerenal vs intrinsic vs post-renal, the 'triple whammy' (ACEi/ARB + diuretic + NSAID), contrast
items.stem: A patient takes an ACE inhibitor, a thiazide diuretic and an NSAID, and becomes volume depleted. Which mechanism best explains the fall in glomerular filtration rate?
options: Afferent arteriole constriction with efferent arteriole dilatation
Afferent arteriole dilatation with efferent arteriole constriction
Direct tubular toxicity from the NSAID
Increased tubular reabsorption of sodium from the diuretic
items.why: NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation and ACE inhibitors remove angiotensin II efferent constriction, so intraglomerular pressure and GFR fall when volume depleted.
notes: This is the normal compensatory pattern in hypovolaemia; the drugs abolish it by doing the reverse.
NSAIDs can cause interstitial nephritis, but the triple whammy is haemodynamic, not direct tubular injury.
Diuretics reduce sodium reabsorption, causing volume loss, not increased reabsorption.

items.topic: Epidemiology and evidence: study designs, bias and confounding, screening principles, lead-time bias
items.stem: A cohort study finds coffee drinkers have more lung cancer. Smokers drink more coffee and smoking causes lung cancer. What is smoking in this association?
items.why: A confounder is associated with both exposure and outcome, is a cause of the outcome, and is not on the causal pathway. It can create a spurious association.
notes: Effect modification means the effect differs across strata; it is not the problem described.
A mediator lies on the causal pathway from exposure to outcome; smoking does not.
Recall bias is differential reporting of exposure in case-control studies, not this.

items.topic: Orthopaedic emergencies: hip fracture and orthogeriatric care, compartment syndrome, open fractures, septic arthritis
items.stem: An 84-year-old woman on apixaban has a displaced intracapsular hip fracture after a fall at home. She is haemodynamically stable with good analgesia. What is the best timing target for surgery?
options: After apixaban has been off for 7 days
items.why: Australian hip fracture standards recommend surgery within 48 hours at most, ideally within 24 to 36 hours. Anticoagulation alone should not cause prolonged delay.
notes: A 7-day delay greatly increases mortality and complications; DOAC delay is usually short.
72 hours exceeds the standard of surgery within 48 hours.
Delirium is a reason for orthogeriatric care, not for delaying surgery.

items.topic: The surgical abdomen in children: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting)
items.stem: A 10-day-old term neonate has sudden bilious vomiting and a soft abdomen. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent upper GI contrast study and surgical review
Trial of feed thickener and review in 1 week
Abdominal ultrasound for pyloric thickness in the morning
items.why: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Urgent upper GI contrast study (with resuscitation and surgical review) is needed, as bowel ischaemia is time-critical; unstable infants go straight to theatre.
notes: Bilious vomiting is never reflux; delay risks bowel necrosis.
Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious vomiting, and this delay is unsafe.
Air enema treats intussusception, which is not the likely diagnosis here.

items.topic: Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants: adrenal suppression, TB and hepatitis B screening before biologics
items.stem: A 54-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is to start adalimumab. She was born in Vietnam. Her chest X-ray is normal. Which pre-treatment screening is most appropriate?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay and hepatitis B serology
Sputum culture only, as the chest X-ray is normal
Hepatitis A serology and Mantoux only if symptomatic
items.why: Before TNF inhibitors screen for latent TB (IGRA or Mantoux) and hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs); reactivation can be severe. Risk is higher with birth in a high-prevalence country.
notes: Latent TB is asymptomatic with a normal X-ray and sputum is negative; test with IGRA or Mantoux.
Screening is not symptom-dependent, and hepatitis B (not A) is the reactivation risk.
Hepatitis C is worth checking but does not replace TB and hepatitis B screening.

items.topic: Acute leukaemia: blasts, pancytopenia, tumour lysis syndrome
items.stem: A 24-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia has WBC 150 x10^9/L and is about to start chemotherapy. Which intervention is the most important to prevent tumour lysis syndrome?
options: Vigorous intravenous hydration with allopurinol or rasburicase
Urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate infusion
items.why: Prevent TLS with aggressive IV hydration plus a urate-lowering agent (allopurinol, or rasburicase in high risk). Monitor U&E, urate, calcium and phosphate frequently.
notes: Calcium is given only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or arrhythmia, as it can precipitate calcium phosphate.
Alkalinisation is no longer recommended; it risks calcium phosphate precipitation and does not improve outcomes.
TLS causes hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia, so supplements would be harmful.

items.topic: Febrile neutropenia: piperacillin-tazobactam within an hour, risk assessment
items.stem: A 54-year-old woman, 8 days after chemotherapy, has temperature 38.6°C, HR 118, BP 84/50 and a neutrophil count of 0.1 x10^9/L. She has no penicillin allergy. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate after blood cultures result
Await G-CSF response before starting antibiotics
items.why: Febrile neutropenia is an emergency. Give empirical IV piperacillin-tazobactam within 60 minutes after cultures, without waiting for results; this patient is haemodynamically unstable and high risk.
notes: Oral therapy is only for carefully selected low-risk patients, not a hypotensive patient, and not after waiting for cultures.
Observation delays treatment; mortality rises with each hour of delay.
G-CSF is not a substitute for antibiotics and does not replace empirical therapy.

items.topic: Perioperative medicine: fasting, managing anticoagulants and diabetes drugs, VTE prophylaxis
items.stem: Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is held for longer before surgery in a patient with an eGFR of 35 mL/min/1.73 m². What is the main reason?
options: It is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4
It is mostly renally cleared, so its half-life lengthens
It is highly protein bound and displaced by renal failure
items.why: About 80% of dabigatran is renally excreted, so reduced renal function prolongs its half-life and the pre-operative withhold period.
notes: Rivaroxaban and apixaban have more CYP3A4 involvement; dabigatran does not.
Dabigatran has low protein binding, which is why it can be dialysed.
It acts on thrombin, not platelets; irreversible platelet binding describes aspirin or clopidogrel.

items.topic: Hyperthyroidism: Graves vs toxic nodule vs thyroiditis, thyroid storm, carbimazole agranulocytosis
items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with Graves disease started carbimazole 2 weeks ago. She now has fever and a sore throat. What is the most important immediate action?
options: Stop carbimazole and check a full blood count urgently
items.why: Fever or sore throat on carbimazole suggests agranulocytosis, usually in the first 3 months. Stop the drug and urgently check the neutrophil count; give broad-spectrum antibiotics if neutropenic.
notes: Continuing the drug risks fatal sepsis if agranulocytosis is present.
Raising the dose would worsen any marrow toxicity.
Radioiodine does not address the urgent possible neutropenic sepsis.

items.topic: Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change in children, membranous in adults, thrombosis and infection risk
items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has periorbital oedema, heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia after a viral illness. Which glomerular change best explains the proteinuria in minimal change disease?
options: Loss of podocyte foot processes with reduced charge selectivity
Subepithelial immune complex deposits with basement membrane spikes
Splitting of the glomerular basement membrane (type IV collagen defect)
items.why: Minimal change disease shows normal light microscopy but effaced podocyte foot processes on EM, losing the charge barrier and causing selective albuminuria. It is usually steroid-responsive.
notes: Subepithelial deposits with spikes describe membranous nephropathy, the common adult cause.
Mesangial IgA deposition is IgA nephropathy, which presents with haematuria.
Basement membrane splitting describes Alport syndrome, with haematuria and deafness.

items.topic: Tuberculosis screening: latent TB before biologics, active TB in migrants
items.stem: Why does anti-TNF therapy increase the risk of reactivation of latent tuberculosis?
options: It depletes B cells and so reduces antibody production
It blocks complement activation, preventing opsonisation
TNF is needed to maintain granulomas that wall off Mycobacterium tuberculosis
items.why: TNF-alpha, with macrophage and T-cell activation, sustains granuloma integrity. Blocking it lets dormant bacilli escape and reactivate.
notes: B-cell depletion is the mechanism of rituximab, not anti-TNF agents.
Neutrophil chemotaxis is not the main defect; TB containment relies on granulomas.
Complement is not the key defence against intracellular mycobacteria.

items.topic: Kidney stones: renal colic, CT KUB, the obstructed infected kidney as an emergency
items.stem: Where do ureteric stones most commonly become lodged?
options: Only at the pelvic brim, where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels
At the pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim and vesicoureteric junction
items.why: The ureter has three narrowings: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim crossing the iliac vessels, and the vesicoureteric junction (narrowest). Stones lodge at these sites.
notes: The pelvic brim is one site, but not the only one.
The urethra is not a ureteric site.
Papillae are sites of Randall's plaque formation, not ureteric obstruction.

items.topic: Hypercalcaemia: primary hyperparathyroidism vs malignancy, acute management
items.stem: Which biochemical pattern is most typical of hypercalcaemia of malignancy mediated by PTH-related peptide?
options: High calcium, suppressed PTH, low phosphate
High calcium, high PTH, low phosphate
High calcium, suppressed PTH, high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
High calcium, high PTH, high phosphate
items.why: PTHrP mimics PTH at the receptor, raising calcium and lowering phosphate, while negative feedback suppresses true PTH. High 1,25-vitamin D suggests lymphoma or granulomatous disease.
notes: High PTH with low phosphate is primary hyperparathyroidism.
Raised 1,25-vitamin D with suppressed PTH suggests granulomatous disease or lymphoma.
High PTH with high phosphate fits renal impairment or tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

items.topic: Cardiovascular drugs: ACEi/ARB hyperkalaemia and the triple whammy, beta-blockers, digoxin and amiodarone toxicity
items.stem: A 80-year-old woman with AF takes digoxin and has declining renal function. She presents with nausea, visual yellow haloes and a ventricular bigeminy rhythm. Which amiodarone-related fact is most relevant to her digoxin therapy?
options: Adding amiodarone raises digoxin levels, so digoxin dose should be roughly halved
Amiodarone lowers digoxin levels through P-glycoprotein induction
Amiodarone has no effect on digoxin
Amiodarone requires digoxin dose to be doubled
items.why: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein and renal clearance, raising digoxin levels by about 50 to 100%. Reduce the digoxin dose and monitor levels.
notes: Amiodarone inhibits, not induces, P-glycoprotein.
This is a significant, well-known interaction.
Doubling would worsen toxicity.

items.topic: Asthma: Australian Asthma Handbook stepwise care, as-needed budesonide-formoterol, acute severe asthma
items.stem: Which drug action explains why formoterol can be used as a reliever in asthma, unlike salmeterol in most guidelines?
options: Rapid onset of bronchodilation within minutes
items.why: Formoterol is a long-acting beta2 agonist with a fast onset (about 1–3 minutes), so it works as a reliever; combined with budesonide it also treats inflammation.
notes: Muscarinic antagonism is the mechanism of ipratropium or tiotropium, not formoterol.
Leukotriene synthesis inhibition is not a feature of formoterol; montelukast blocks the receptor.
Mast cell stabilisation is the proposed action of cromones, not formoterol.

items.topic: Opioid use disorder: buprenorphine and methadone, long-acting injectable buprenorphine, take-home naloxone
items.stem: A 31-year-old man with opioid use disorder on sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone is stable and adherent but has diversion concerns. He asks about an alternative. What is the best option?
options: Stopping buprenorphine and starting oral naltrexone
items.why: Long-acting injectable buprenorphine (weekly or monthly subcutaneous) suits stable patients, reducing diversion, daily dosing burden and missed doses.
notes: Naltrexone has poor retention and overdose risk on relapse after loss of tolerance.
Codeine is not opioid agonist treatment.
Oral morphine is not standard opioid agonist treatment for OUD.

items.topic: Burns: TBSA estimation, fluid resuscitation, ANZBA referral criteria, airway burns
items.stem: A 70 kg adult has 30% TBSA partial-thickness burns 1 hour ago. Using the Parkland formula, what volume of crystalloid is given in the first 8 hours from time of burn?
items.why: Parkland: 4 mL x kg x %TBSA = 8400 mL over 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from the time of burn (4200 mL), as Hartmann's.
notes: 2100 mL uses 2 mL/kg/%TBSA and halves again.
8400 mL is the 24-hour total.
6300 mL does not match any halving of the formula.

items.topic: Primary aldosteronism: aldosterone-renin ratio, hypertension with hypokalaemia
items.stem: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the distal nephron. Which combination of effects best describes its action?
options: Increased Na+ reabsorption and increased K+ secretion
Increased Na+ reabsorption and decreased K+ secretion
Decreased Na+ reabsorption and increased K+ secretion
Decreased Na+ reabsorption and decreased K+ secretion
items.why: Aldosterone upregulates ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase in principal cells, retaining Na+ and water and driving K+ (and H+ via intercalated cells) loss. Excess causes hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
notes: Aldosterone does not reduce K+ secretion; that is the effect of spironolactone or amiloride.
Aldosterone increases, not decreases, Na+ reabsorption.
This describes the opposite of aldosterone action.

items.topic: Phaeochromocytoma: paroxysmal symptoms, plasma metanephrines, alpha-blockade before surgery
items.stem: Why are plasma metanephrines more reliable than plasma catecholamines for detecting phaeochromocytoma?
options: Metabolised continuously within tumour cells, so levels are raised even between episodes
They have a longer half-life than catecholamines in plasma
They are produced only by the adrenal cortex
They are unaffected by any medication
items.why: Tumour cells metabolise catecholamines to metanephrines by COMT continuously, independent of episodic release, so levels stay raised.
notes: Half-life is not the main reason; the point is continuous intratumoral production.
They arise from the medulla or paraganglia, not the cortex.
Drugs such as tricyclics and SNRIs can cause false positives.

items.topic: Bronchiectasis: chronic wet cough in First Nations children, exacerbation management
items.stem: A 3-year-old Aboriginal boy in a remote community has had a daily wet cough for 8 weeks despite one course of amoxicillin. He is afebrile with a normal chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Protracted bacterial bronchitis or early bronchiectasis
items.why: A chronic wet cough over 4 weeks in a First Nations child suggests protracted bacterial bronchitis, which can progress to bronchiectasis. Treat with 2 weeks of amoxicillin-clavulanate and review.
notes: Asthma typically gives a dry, episodic cough with wheeze, not a daily wet cough.
Pertussis causes paroxysmal cough with whoop or vomiting, usually with a defined course, not a persistent wet cough.
Foreign body usually has sudden onset choking and focal signs; not a gradual chronic wet cough.

items.topic: Major depression: diagnosis, antidepressant choice, psychological therapy
items.stem: Which mechanism of action best describes sertraline, a first-line antidepressant for major depressive disorder?
options: Selective inhibition of serotonin reuptake at the presynaptic transporter
Irreversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase A and B
Blockade of presynaptic alpha2-adrenoceptors and 5-HT2 receptors
Selective inhibition of noradrenaline reuptake only
items.why: Sertraline is an SSRI: it blocks the serotonin transporter (SERT), raising synaptic serotonin. Benefit takes 2 to 4 weeks, though adverse effects start early.
notes: Describes older irreversible MAOIs such as phenelzine and tranylcypromine.
Describes mirtazapine, which is not an SSRI.
Describes selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors such as reboxetine, not SSRIs.

items.topic: Contraception and early medical abortion: LARC, emergency contraception, drug interactions, mifepristone-misoprostol
items.stem: A 24-year-old woman had unprotected sex 4 days ago. She is on day 12 of her cycle, BMI 24, and takes no medicines. She wants the most effective emergency contraception. What is the most effective option?
items.why: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception and works up to 5 days after unprotected sex (or up to 5 days after the earliest ovulation). It also gives ongoing contraception.
notes: Levonorgestrel is less effective than ulipristal or a copper IUD, and loses efficacy with higher BMI.
Ulipristal is effective to 120 hours and better than levonorgestrel, but is still less effective than a copper IUD.
The Yuzpe regimen is less effective and causes more nausea; it is not preferred.

items.topic: COPD: spirometry diagnosis, COPD-X stepwise inhalers, exacerbations, oxygen target 88-92%
items.stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD presents with an exacerbation, drowsy, with a respiratory rate of 28 and SpO2 99% on high-flow oxygen. What oxygen saturation target should be set?
items.why: In COPD with hypercapnic risk, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92% to avoid worsening hypercapnia; check blood gases.
notes: 94–98% is the usual target but risks CO2 retention in COPD.
Above 98% is excessive and dangerous here.
80–85% is dangerously low and risks hypoxia.

items.topic: Acute leukaemia: blasts, pancytopenia, tumour lysis syndrome
items.stem: A patient with acute leukaemia is found to have pancytopenia on the full blood count. What is the main mechanism of the pancytopenia?
options: Replacement of normal marrow by leukaemic blasts
Autoimmune destruction of circulating blood cells
Splenic sequestration of mature blood cells
Nutritional deficiency of B12 and folate
items.why: Clonal blasts proliferate and crowd out normal haematopoietic precursors, causing anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Blast count of 20% or more in marrow (or defining genetic lesion) supports acute leukaemia.
notes: Autoimmune destruction causes isolated cytopenias (e.g. ITP, AIHA), not marrow failure with blasts.
Hypersplenism may contribute in some conditions but is not the main mechanism in acute leukaemia.
Megaloblastic anaemia can cause pancytopenia but not circulating blasts.

items.topic: Pleural effusion: Light's criteria, transudate vs exudate causes, empyema drainage
items.stem: A 55-year-old man with pneumonia has a persisting effusion. Pleural fluid is turbid with pH 6.9, glucose 1.5 mmol/L and positive Gram stain. What is the most appropriate next step, with antibiotics?
options: Observation with repeat chest x-ray in 1 week
items.why: Pus, pH <7.2, low glucose or positive Gram stain indicates empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion needing prompt chest tube drainage plus antibiotics. Refer for fibrinolytics or surgery if drainage fails.
notes: Repeated needle aspiration is inadequate for established empyema.
Diuretics treat transudates; this is an infected exudate.
Observation risks a loculated, organised empyema and sepsis.

items.topic: Osteoporosis: fracture risk, DXA, bisphosphonates and denosumab (rebound fractures after stopping)
items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has had denosumab 60 mg six-monthly for 5 years for osteoporosis. She wishes to stop it. What is the most appropriate approach to reduce the risk of rebound vertebral fractures?
options: Give a bisphosphonate after the last dose, not simply stop
Stop and recheck DXA in 2 years
Stop and start calcium and vitamin D only
Extend the interval to yearly dosing
items.why: Stopping denosumab causes rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures; transition to an antiresorptive such as zoledronic acid is recommended, timed about 6 months after the last dose.
notes: Delayed DXA misses the rapid bone loss in the first months.
Calcium and vitamin D alone do not prevent rebound.
Lengthening the interval allows offset and rebound; it is not protective.

items.topic: Acute appendicitis: clinical scores, imaging in children and in pregnancy
items.stem: A 7-year-old boy has 24 hours of right iliac fossa pain, fever and vomiting. He has focal tenderness and guarding. Bloods show raised WCC and CRP. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate first-line imaging?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
items.why: Ultrasound is first-line in children to avoid radiation. CT is reserved for equivocal or non-diagnostic ultrasound where diagnosis remains uncertain.
notes: CT involves ionising radiation; reserve for inconclusive ultrasound in children.
Plain X-ray has poor sensitivity and specificity for appendicitis.
MRI is an option in selected cases but not first-line or readily available.

items.topic: Mandatory reporting: child abuse, notifiable conduct of practitioners (Ahpra), notifiable diseases
items.stem: Which public health principle best explains why laboratories and doctors must notify certain infectious diseases (e.g. measles) to state health authorities?
options: Enabling surveillance, contact tracing and outbreak control
Allowing Medicare to fund treatment of the patient
Permitting employers to exclude infected workers
Providing data for individual patient prognosis
items.why: Notification lets health authorities detect outbreaks, trace contacts and intervene (e.g. vaccination, isolation) to protect the population.
notes: Medicare funding does not depend on notification.
Workplace exclusion is not the purpose and would breach privacy.
Notification is for population surveillance, not individual prognosis.

items.topic: Infective endocarditis: modified Duke criteria, people who inject drugs, prosthetic valves, empirical therapy
items.stem: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs has fever 38.6 °C. Three of three blood culture sets grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echo shows no vegetation, with no emboli or murmur. By modified Duke criteria, what is the classification?
options: Definite endocarditis once Roth spots are excluded
items.why: Persistent S. aureus bacteraemia is one major criterion; injection drug use (predisposition) and fever are two minor. One major plus one or more minor is possible IE; definite needs two major or one major plus three minor.
notes: Wrong: definite needs two major criteria (e.g. positive cultures plus echo evidence) or one major plus three minor; he has one major and two minor.
Wrong: rejection requires an alternative diagnosis or resolution within 4 days of antibiotics; he fulfils criteria for possible IE.
Wrong: Roth spots would add a minor criterion, but the classification is not defined by excluding them; the statement is not how Duke works.

items.topic: Neonatal jaundice: physiological vs pathological, jaundice in the first 24 hours, phototherapy
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains physiological jaundice in a healthy term newborn at day 3?
options: High red cell turnover with immature hepatic glucuronyl transferase
Biliary atresia causing obstruction of conjugated bilirubin excretion
Increased gut sterility abolishing enterohepatic recirculation
Absent fetal haemoglobin breakdown after birth
items.why: Newborns have a high red cell mass and shorter red cell life plus immature UDP-glucuronyl transferase, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. Enterohepatic recirculation also adds to it.
notes: Biliary atresia causes prolonged conjugated jaundice, not physiological jaundice.
Gut sterility reduces bilirubin breakdown by bacteria, so enterohepatic recirculation increases, not abolishes.
Fetal haemoglobin breakdown is a main contributor to the bilirubin load.

items.topic: Valve disease: aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation murmurs, severity markers, TAVI vs surgical referral
items.stem: An 84-year-old frail woman with COPD has exertional dyspnoea and an ejection systolic murmur. Echo shows severe aortic stenosis (mean gradient 48 mmHg, valve area 0.8 cm²), with anatomy suitable for transfemoral access. What is the best next step?
options: Refer for surgical aortic valve replacement
Heart team referral for transcatheter aortic valve implantation
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive treatment
items.why: Symptomatic severe AS needs valve replacement. In patients aged over ~75–80 or with high surgical risk or frailty, and suitable anatomy, TAVI is preferred after heart team assessment.
notes: Wrong: open surgery carries higher risk in an elderly, frail patient with lung disease; TAVI is favoured for her.
Wrong: no drug therapy alters the course of symptomatic severe AS; delay carries a high mortality.
Wrong: valvuloplasty gives only short-lived benefit and is a bridge or palliative option, not definitive therapy.

items.topic: Atrial fibrillation: CHA2DS2-VA stroke risk (Australian 2018 guideline), DOAC choice, rate vs rhythm control
items.stem: Which mechanism describes how apixaban produces anticoagulation?
options: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase
items.why: Apixaban directly and selectively inhibits free and clot-bound factor Xa, reducing thrombin generation.
notes: Dabigatran is the direct thrombin inhibitor.
Warfarin works through vitamin K epoxide reductase.
Heparins act via antithrombin.

items.topic: Tuberculosis: latent vs active, migrants from high-incidence countries, notification and contact tracing
items.stem: Which immune mechanism contains Mycobacterium tuberculosis in latent infection?
options: Th1 cells releasing interferon-gamma activating macrophages in granulomas
items.why: Th1 CD4 cells release interferon-gamma, activating macrophages and forming granulomas that wall off bacilli. TNF-alpha blockade or HIV can reactivate disease.
notes: Neutrophils and complement are not the main control of intracellular mycobacteria.
Antibody-mediated mucosal defence does not contain intracellular TB.
Eosinophils are involved in helminth and allergic responses.

items.topic: Croup: severity assessment, oral dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline
items.stem: Which part of the airway is the narrowest in a young child and is the site of obstruction in croup?
items.why: The cricoid ring makes the subglottis the narrowest part in children; viral oedema here causes barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor.
notes: Epiglottic swelling is epiglottitis, a different, now rare, condition.
Bronchial involvement causes wheeze, not stridor.
Bronchiolar disease is bronchiolitis, with crackles and wheeze.

items.topic: Chest pain pathway: ECG, high-sensitivity troponin, EDACS-ADP and HEART risk tools
items.stem: Why is troponin a more specific marker of myocardial injury than CK-MB?
options: Cardiac troponin isoforms (I and T) are encoded by genes unique to myocardium
Troponin is released only during complete coronary occlusion
Troponin is produced only by ischaemic myocytes
Troponin is cleared within an hour so rises are transient
items.why: Cardiac troponin I and T are structurally distinct from skeletal isoforms, giving high myocardial specificity. Troponin signals injury of any cause, not just infarction, and stays elevated for days.
notes: Troponin rises in any myocardial injury, not only complete occlusion.
It is released from damaged myocytes, not produced by ischaemic ones.
Troponin remains raised for days, not an hour.

items.topic: Mental health law and capacity: state and territory Mental Health Acts, involuntary treatment criteria, consent
items.stem: Under the common law approach used in Australia, which of the following is a core element of decision-making capacity?
options: Ability to understand, retain and weigh relevant information
items.why: Capacity is decision-specific and requires the person to understand, retain, use or weigh information and communicate a choice. A psychiatric diagnosis or disagreement does not remove capacity.
notes: Disagreeing with advice does not indicate incapacity; capable adults may make unwise decisions.
A mental illness does not automatically remove capacity; it is assessed for each decision.
Age alone does not define capacity; mature minors may have capacity and some adults lack it.

items.topic: Medication safety and the law: Poisons Standard schedules (S2, S3, S4, S8), PBS authority, medication errors
items.stem: Under the Poisons Standard, which schedule applies to medicines such as morphine and oxycodone, which carry strict prescribing and storage requirements?
items.why: Schedule 8 drugs are Controlled Drugs with the strictest requirements: secure storage, records and often state prescribing permits. Schedule 4 needs a prescription only.
notes: S2 medicines are available over the counter from a pharmacy.
S3 medicines are supplied by a pharmacist without a prescription.
S4 is prescription only but without the stricter controls of S8.

items.topic: Fever in the returned traveller: malaria (thick and thin films), dengue, typhoid
items.stem: Plasmodium falciparum causes more severe disease than P. vivax. Which pathophysiological feature best explains this?
options: Infected red cells adhere to endothelium causing microvascular sequestration
It causes tertian fever with a 48-hour cycle only
items.why: Falciparum infects red cells of all ages, giving high parasitaemia, and sequestration of adherent cells in small vessels causes cerebral and organ dysfunction.
notes: Reticulocyte preference is typical of P. vivax, which causes milder disease.
Hypnozoites cause relapse in vivax and ovale, not falciparum.
Fever periodicity does not explain severity.

items.topic: Chest pain pathway: ECG, high-sensitivity troponin, EDACS-ADP and HEART risk tools
items.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with 2 hours of chest pain. ECG is normal. Using EDACS-ADP, he scores under 16, has no new ischaemic ECG changes, and 0 and 2-hour hs-troponin are below the cut-offs. How is he classified?
options: Low risk, suitable for early discharge
Intermediate risk, needs stress testing before discharge
High risk, needs admission for angiography
items.why: EDACS-ADP below 16 with no new ischaemic ECG changes and negative serial troponins identifies low risk for 30-day MACE, allowing early discharge with outpatient follow-up.
notes: Stress testing is not required for those meeting low-risk criteria.
High risk requires a positive troponin delta or high score.
A 12-hour troponin is not needed once the accelerated pathway is negative.

items.topic: Faltering growth: growth charts, organic vs psychosocial causes
items.stem: A 9-month-old girl has weight crossing from the 50th to below the 3rd centile. She is alert and examination is normal. A feeding history shows diluted formula and infrequent feeds. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Inadequate intake is the commonest cause of faltering growth, and a feeding history showing diluted formula and infrequent feeds explains it. Organic disease is less likely with a normal examination.
notes: Coeliac disease needs gluten exposure and usually brings GI symptoms.
Cystic fibrosis usually has respiratory or GI features and is not suggested here.
Congenital heart disease would show murmur, tachypnoea or feeding difficulty on examination.

items.topic: Multiple sclerosis: optic neuritis, MRI, relapse treatment
items.stem: In optic neuritis due to demyelination, a relative afferent pupillary defect occurs in the affected eye. What is the mechanism?
options: Slowed conduction in the optic nerve reduces afferent input
Paralysis of the iris sphincter muscle
Loss of sympathetic supply to the dilator pupillae
items.why: Demyelination slows and blocks conduction in the optic nerve, so the afferent signal is reduced. The affected pupil constricts less to direct light than to light from the normal eye.
notes: The efferent limb (CN III) is intact; a RAPD is an afferent defect.
Iris sphincter paralysis gives a dilated pupil with no reaction to either eye, not a RAPD.
Sympathetic loss causes Horner syndrome with miosis, not RAPD.

items.topic: Iron deficiency anaemia in adults: gastroscopy plus colonoscopy, coeliac screen
items.stem: Which site of the gastrointestinal tract is the principal site of dietary iron absorption, explaining why coeliac disease can present with iron deficiency?
items.why: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, where villous atrophy in coeliac disease impairs uptake. The terminal ileum absorbs B12 and bile salts.
notes: Terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts, not iron.
The stomach acidifies iron but does not absorb it significantly.
The colon does not absorb meaningful iron.

items.topic: Childhood immunisation: National Immunisation Program schedule, catch-up, true contraindications
items.stem: Why are live attenuated vaccines such as MMR not given to a child with severe primary immunodeficiency?
options: The attenuated organism can replicate and cause disease
Inactivated antigens fail to be presented on MHC
The adjuvant causes uncontrolled complement activation
Maternal antibodies will neutralise the vaccine virus
items.why: Live vaccines replicate in the host to produce immunity. Without effective immunity, replication is unchecked and can cause vaccine-strain disease.
notes: Live vaccines are not inactivated, and antigen presentation is not the reason for avoidance.
Live vaccines generally do not contain aluminium adjuvant, and complement activation is not the concern.
Maternal antibody can blunt response in infants, but it is not the reason for contraindication in immunodeficiency.

items.topic: Polycystic kidney disease: inheritance, intracranial aneurysms, screening relatives
items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has ADPKD. Her mother died of a subarachnoid haemorrhage at 45. She has no neurological symptoms. What is the most appropriate test to screen her for intracranial aneurysm?
options: CT or MR angiography of the brain
items.why: Screening for intracranial aneurysm is advised in ADPKD with a family history of aneurysm or SAH, using MR or CT angiography. Non-contrast CT cannot reliably show unruptured aneurysms.
notes: Non-contrast CT detects acute bleeding but is insensitive for unruptured aneurysms.
Lumbar puncture is for suspected SAH with a negative CT, not for screening.
Transcranial Doppler assesses flow velocity (e.g. vasospasm) and does not reliably detect aneurysms.

items.topic: Trauma primary survey: EMST/ATLS ABCDE, haemorrhagic shock, massive transfusion
items.stem: A 40-year-old has penetrating abdominal trauma, HR 130, BP 80/50, after 2 units of red cells. Massive transfusion is activated. Which transfusion strategy is most appropriate?
options: Red cells only until haemoglobin is above 100 g/L
Balanced red cells, plasma and platelets, with tranexamic acid
items.why: Massive transfusion uses balanced ratios of red cells, plasma and platelets (with fibrinogen), plus early tranexamic acid and damage control surgery. Avoid excess crystalloid.
notes: Red cells alone worsen dilutional coagulopathy.
Large crystalloid volumes worsen coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia.
Albumin does not replace clotting factors or platelets.

items.topic: Antepartum haemorrhage: placenta praevia vs abruption, no vaginal examination until praevia is excluded
items.stem: A 30-year-old at 36 weeks has sudden severe constant abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding after cocaine use. The uterus is hard and tender, and the CTG shows late decelerations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Painful bleeding with a hard, tender (woody) uterus and fetal compromise, with cocaine as a risk factor, indicates placental abruption. Praevia is typically painless.
notes: Praevia usually presents with painless bright bleeding and a soft uterus.
Vasa praevia bleeding occurs with membrane rupture and rapid fetal bradycardia, without a tender uterus.
Rupture usually occurs in labour or with a previous scar, with loss of the presenting part; abruption fits better here.

items.topic: Acid-base disorders: anion gap, Winter's formula, mixed disorders
items.stem: Using Winter's formula, what is the expected PaCO2 for a patient with metabolic acidosis and a bicarbonate of 12 mmol/L?
items.why: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 (±2) = 26 mmHg. A measured value above this suggests a concurrent respiratory acidosis.
notes: 24 is below the expected range of 24–28 only at its edge; the formula gives 26, the best answer.
36 would indicate inadequate compensation (a coexisting respiratory acidosis).
40 is normal PaCO2, meaning no respiratory compensation.

items.topic: Pericarditis and cardiac tamponade: ECG changes, echo, Beck's triad, colchicine
items.stem: A patient develops a rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion. Which mechanism best explains the fall in cardiac output in tamponade?
options: Impaired diastolic filling from raised intrapericardial pressure
Obstruction of the aortic outflow tract
Reduced venous return from systemic vasodilation
items.why: The pericardium is stiff, so a rapid effusion raises intrapericardial pressure, compresses the chambers and limits diastolic filling, reducing stroke volume. Contractility is initially preserved.
notes: Contractility is typically preserved in tamponade; the problem is filling, not pump failure.
Outflow obstruction describes conditions such as aortic stenosis or HOCM, not tamponade.
Systemic vasodilation is not the mechanism; systemic veins are distended with high venous pressure.

items.topic: Skin cancer: melanoma (features, excision margins), BCC and SCC, Australia's high incidence
items.stem: Which mechanism best explains why ultraviolet B radiation causes skin cancer?
options: Formation of pyrimidine dimers in DNA
Depletion of vitamin D in keratinocytes
Increased collagen cross-linking in the dermis
items.why: UVB causes cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers; unrepaired, they produce mutations such as in TP53 in keratinocytes. Australia's high incidence reflects high UV exposure and fair skin.
notes: UV does not suppress melanocyte division; mutation drives neoplasia.
UV promotes vitamin D synthesis rather than depleting it.
Dermal changes contribute to photoageing, not carcinogenesis.

items.topic: Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending weakness, FVC monitoring, IVIG
items.stem: A 40-year-old with Guillain-Barré syndrome for 4 days has worsening weakness, a weak cough and a falling forced vital capacity (now 1.5 L, from 3.0 L). What is the best next step?
options: Arrange urgent ICU review for ventilatory support and give IVIG
Start oral prednisolone and review in the morning
Continue ward observation with daily peak flow
items.why: A falling FVC (below about 20 mL/kg or rapidly declining) signals impending respiratory failure; escalate to ICU and give IVIG or plasma exchange. Corticosteroids do not help.
notes: Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Peak flow is unreliable; FVC with a falling trend needs urgent escalation.
Pyridostigmine is for myasthenia gravis and does not treat GBS.

items.topic: Australian zoonoses: Q fever, leptospirosis, brucellosis, psittacosis, occupational exposure
items.stem: A 52-year-old sheep farmer has undulant fever, night sweats and sacroiliitis. Brucella serology is positive after he drank raw goat milk overseas. No endocarditis is found. Which regimen is most appropriate?
items.why: Brucellosis needs prolonged combination therapy, typically doxycycline with rifampicin (or an aminoglycoside) for at least 6 weeks, to prevent relapse. Specialist advice is needed.
notes: Monotherapy and short courses lead to relapse.
Short azithromycin monotherapy is inadequate.
Short fluoroquinolone monotherapy is inadequate.

items.topic: Perinatal mental health: postnatal depression (EPDS), puerperal psychosis, drugs in breastfeeding
items.stem: Which factor mainly determines the infant's exposure to a maternal drug taken during breastfeeding?
options: Low molecular weight, high lipid solubility and low protein binding
High molecular weight and high protein binding
High ionisation at plasma pH of 7.4
items.why: Small, lipophilic, poorly protein-bound, un-ionised drugs pass readily into milk, which is slightly acidic and traps weak bases. Long half-life drugs and infant immaturity also increase risk.
notes: Large, highly protein-bound molecules transfer poorly into milk.
Ionised drugs cross membranes poorly, so less enters milk.
Half-life matters, but transfer depends on physicochemical properties, not half-life alone.

items.topic: Adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone stress dosing, hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia
items.stem: A 55-year-old man with known Addison disease presents with vomiting, BP 75/40 mmHg and drowsiness. Na 121, K 6.3 mmol/L. After starting IV 0.9% sodium chloride, what is the most appropriate immediate drug treatment?
items.why: Adrenal crisis needs immediate hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (or IM) plus rapid saline; do not delay for tests. Hydrocortisone at this dose gives sufficient mineralocorticoid effect.
notes: Fludrocortisone is oral, slow and not the life-saving drug in crisis.
Oral dexamethasone is inappropriate in a vomiting, shocked patient.
The usual oral replacement dose is inadequate and unreliable with vomiting.

items.topic: Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis: eTG antibiotics, pregnancy, catheters, asymptomatic bacteriuria
items.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a routine midstream urine culture growing E. coli >10^8 CFU/L. She is asymptomatic, with no fever. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat with a short antibiotic course guided by sensitivities
No treatment and repeat culture at 28 weeks
Single-dose fosfomycin only if culture repeats positive after delivery
items.why: Asymptomatic bacteriuria should be treated in pregnancy because it increases the risk of pyelonephritis, preterm birth and low birthweight. Choose an agent guided by susceptibilities, such as cefalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate.
notes: Not treating is appropriate in most non-pregnant adults, but not in pregnancy.
Waiting for symptoms risks pyelonephritis, which is more frequent in pregnancy.
Delaying until after delivery misses the window to prevent maternal and fetal complications.

items.topic: Bronchiolitis: supportive care (PREDICT guideline), when to give oxygen or high-flow, apnoea in young infants
items.stem: Why are infants under 3 months particularly prone to respiratory failure and apnoea in bronchiolitis?
options: Small airway radius, compliant chest wall and immature respiratory control
Large tonsils and adenoids obstructing the nasopharynx
Absent surfactant production after the neonatal period
Fixed bronchospasm from smooth muscle hypertrophy
items.why: Infants have narrow airways (resistance rises with 1/r^4), a compliant chest wall, fatigable diaphragm and immature central respiratory control, so oedema and mucus cause failure and apnoea.
notes: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is not the mechanism; it peaks later in childhood.
Surfactant is produced after term birth; its absence is not the cause.
Bronchiolitis obstruction is from oedema, mucus and debris, not fixed bronchospasm; bronchodilators are not effective.

items.topic: Inherited bleeding disorders: haemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, preoperative assessment
items.stem: A 40-year-old man has a prolonged APTT with normal PT, found before elective hernia repair. He has no bleeding history. Which result is the best next step?
options: Mixing study, then factor VIII, IX, XI, XII and vWF levels
Proceed to surgery since APTT alone is unimportant
items.why: An isolated prolonged APTT needs a mixing study and factor assays (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and vWF. Factor XII or lupus anticoagulant cause prolonged APTT without bleeding, while VIII, IX, XI deficiency may require cover.
notes: An unexplained prolonged APTT should be investigated before surgery to exclude a bleeding disorder.
FFP is not indicated without a defined deficiency or bleeding.
The PT is already normal and will not explain a prolonged APTT.

items.topic: Schizophrenia and first-episode psychosis: antipsychotic choice, metabolic monitoring, clozapine (neutropenia, myocarditis)
items.stem: A 28-year-old man on clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, 2 weeks after starting, has fever, chest pain, tachycardia and raised troponin and CRP. His neutrophil count is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reduce the dose by half and repeat troponin
Stop clozapine and arrange urgent cardiac assessment
items.why: Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically occurs in the first 4–6 weeks. Stop clozapine and arrange urgent cardiac assessment including echocardiography.
notes: Continuing risks fulminant myocarditis and death.
Dose reduction is inadequate when myocarditis is suspected; clozapine should be stopped.
Benzodiazepines do not treat myocarditis and add respiratory risk with clozapine.

items.topic: Major depression: diagnosis, antidepressant choice, psychological therapy
items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had 4 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and poor concentration. She is functioning, has no suicidal ideation and no past episodes. PHQ-9 is 12. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Psychological therapy such as CBT, with active monitoring
Start a benzodiazepine for sleep and review in 3 months
items.why: For mild to moderate depression, first-line treatment is psychological therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) plus lifestyle measures. Antidepressants are reserved for more severe or persistent illness or patient preference.
notes: Lithium augmentation is for treatment-resistant depression, not a first episode.
ECT is for severe, psychotic or life-threatening depression or after failed treatments.
Benzodiazepines do not treat depression and risk dependence; review should be sooner.

items.topic: Other poisonings: tricyclics (sodium bicarbonate), opioids, benzodiazepines, toxic alcohols, Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26
items.stem: Why does sodium bicarbonate treat QRS widening in tricyclic antidepressant overdose?
options: It increases extracellular sodium and pH, overcoming cardiac sodium channel blockade
It blocks muscarinic receptors in the heart
It binds tricyclics in the gut lumen
It enhances renal excretion of tricyclics by urinary alkalinisation
items.why: Tricyclics block fast cardiac sodium channels. Bicarbonate gives a sodium load and alkalinisation, which reduces drug binding to the channel and narrows the QRS.
notes: Tricyclics themselves are antimuscarinic; bicarbonate does not act at this receptor.
Binding in the gut is the role of activated charcoal, not bicarbonate.
Tricyclics are highly protein-bound and hepatically metabolised, so urinary alkalinisation is ineffective.

items.topic: Consent, capacity and confidentiality: mature minors (Gillick), substitute decision-makers, exceptions
items.stem: Which situation is a recognised exception permitting disclosure of confidential information without the patient's consent?
options: Serious and imminent threat to another person's life
A relative asking about the diagnosis
Curiosity of another treating team not involved in care
items.why: Confidentiality may be breached when required by law or to prevent serious, imminent harm to others. Disclosure should be limited to what is necessary.
notes: Relatives have no automatic right to information without consent.
Employers need patient consent for medical information.
Access should be limited to those involved in care.

items.topic: Acute coronary syndrome: STEMI vs NSTEACS on ECG, reperfusion timing, dual antiplatelet therapy
items.stem: A coronary artery is acutely occluded by a thrombus on a ruptured plaque, causing transmural myocardial ischaemia. Which ECG change most directly reflects this transmural injury?
options: ST-segment elevation in the leads facing the affected territory
Widespread PR-segment depression with saddle-shaped ST elevation
Prolongation of the QRS complex with a delta wave
Peaked T waves with a shortened QT interval only
items.why: Transmural injury produces an injury current seen as ST elevation in contiguous leads facing the affected myocardium. This is the STEMI pattern and prompts urgent reperfusion.
notes: Describes acute pericarditis, which is diffuse and not confined to a coronary territory.
Describes a delta wave of pre-excitation (WPW), not ischaemia.
Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia; this is not the hallmark of transmural infarction.

items.topic: Iron deficiency anaemia in adults: gastroscopy plus colonoscopy, coeliac screen
items.stem: A 58-year-old man has asymptomatic iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 105 g/L, ferritin 6 microgram/L). He has no overt bleeding and takes no NSAIDs. What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
options: Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies and colonoscopy
Repeat full blood count after iron replacement
items.why: In men and postmenopausal women, iron deficiency anaemia needs bidirectional endoscopy (gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies for coeliac disease, plus colonoscopy) to exclude GI malignancy. Coeliac serology is also done.
notes: FOBT is a screening test and is not appropriate for investigating established IDA.
CT does not adequately assess mucosal lesions or coeliac disease.
Treating without finding the cause risks missing malignancy.

items.topic: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: rupture presentation, surveillance and repair thresholds
items.stem: A 70-year-old man has an asymptomatic 5.5 cm infrarenal AAA found on ultrasound. He is fit for surgery. What is the most appropriate management?
items.why: Elective repair is generally recommended for asymptomatic AAA of 5.5 cm or more in men (or if symptomatic or rapidly growing), when fit for surgery.
notes: Annual surveillance suits roughly 3.0–4.4 cm aneurysms; 5.5 cm exceeds the threshold.
Risk factor management is adjunctive and does not prevent rupture at this size.
Frequent CT is unnecessary; this size warrants repair rather than surveillance.

items.topic: National Immunisation Program: childhood, adolescent HPV, adults over 65, pregnancy (influenza, pertussis, RSV)
items.stem: Pertussis vaccination in the third trimester protects newborns before their own vaccines. Which mechanism provides this protection?
options: Transfer of maternal T cells across the placenta
Active transplacental transport of maternal IgG
Absorption of maternal IgA from colostrum alone
items.why: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta via the neonatal Fc receptor, mainly in the third trimester. This gives passive immunity to the newborn.
notes: Maternal T cells do not provide passive protection to the neonate.
Breast milk IgA acts on mucosal surfaces and is not the main source of systemic protection against pertussis.
IgM is a large pentamer and does not cross the placenta.

items.topic: Acute asthma and COPD exacerbation: severity assessment, nebulised and IV therapy, NIV
items.stem: A 65-year-old with COPD has an exacerbation, RR 30, using accessory muscles. Despite nebulised bronchodilators and steroids, ABG on 28% oxygen shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 70 mmHg. What is the next best step?
options: Increase oxygen to high flow via non-rebreather
items.why: Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO2 >45 mmHg) persisting after initial therapy is the indication for NIV, which reduces intubation and mortality.
notes: Aminophylline is not recommended; it has a narrow therapeutic index and little benefit.
High-flow oxygen risks worsening hypercapnia; target SpO2 88–92%.
Intubation is reserved for NIV failure or contraindication.

items.topic: Spider and marine envenomation: funnel-web, redback, box jellyfish (vinegar), Irukandji syndrome
items.stem: A 25-year-old swimmer in tropical Queensland has severe back pain, sweating, vomiting, anxiety and hypertension 30 minutes after a barely visible sting. Local sting site is minimal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Irukandji syndrome typically appears 20–40 minutes after a minor sting, with severe pain, catecholamine excess and hypertension. Treat with analgesia (opioids) and watch for pulmonary oedema.
notes: Box jellyfish causes immediate severe pain with whip-like wounds and risk of arrest, not delayed systemic pain.
Redback bites give local pain and sweating, not a marine setting with delayed catecholamine excess.
Blue-ringed octopus causes paralysis, not hypertensive pain syndrome.

items.topic: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease: Australian Jones criteria for high-risk groups, secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin
items.stem: A 9-year-old Aboriginal child from remote Northern Territory has fever 38.5 °C, a hot swollen knee, CRP 80 mg/L and a raised ASO titre. ECG and echocardiogram are normal. Using the Australian criteria for high-risk groups, what is the diagnosis?
options: Not ARF as there is no carditis
items.why: In high-risk groups monoarthritis is a major criterion; fever ≥38 °C and CRP ≥30 mg/L are minor. One major plus two minor with evidence of recent GAS infection is definite ARF.
notes: Wrong: carditis is not required; one major plus two minor criteria and GAS evidence is sufficient.
Wrong: 'possible' ARF is reserved for presentations that do not quite meet criteria, such as suspected chorea or insufficient evidence; here criteria are met.
Wrong: 'probable' is not applied to a presentation that fully meets one major plus two minor criteria plus GAS evidence.

items.topic: Biostatistics: sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, NNT, relative vs absolute risk
items.stem: A statin reduces 5-year cardiovascular events from 2% to 1% in low-risk patients. A pharmaceutical flyer reports a 50% reduction. Which statement best interprets this for a patient?
items.why: ARR = 1%, so NNT = 100 over 5 years. The 50% is the relative risk reduction, which overstates benefit when baseline risk is low.
notes: 50 is the RRR figure mistaken as NNT.
ARR is 1 percentage point; 50% is the relative reduction.
The relative risk is 0.5 (1/2), not 2.0.

items.topic: Sepsis and septic shock: fluids, vasopressors, lactate
items.stem: In septic shock, widespread vasodilation and capillary leak cause hypotension. Which mechanism best explains why noradrenaline restores mean arterial pressure?
options: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction increasing systemic vascular resistance
Beta-2 mediated bronchodilation improving oxygen delivery
Dopamine-receptor renal vasodilation increasing urine output
Direct inhibition of nitric oxide synthase in the endothelium
items.why: Noradrenaline is mainly an alpha-1 agonist (with some beta-1), raising systemic vascular resistance and MAP in vasodilatory shock. It is the first-line vasopressor.
notes: Beta-2 effects are minimal with noradrenaline and are not how it restores MAP.
Dopamine-receptor effects are not the mechanism; renal-dose dopamine is not beneficial.
Noradrenaline does not inhibit nitric oxide synthase.

items.topic: Paracetamol and NSAIDs: maximum doses, NSAID renal, GI and cardiovascular risks
items.stem: In paracetamol overdose, which toxic metabolite accumulates once glucuronidation and sulfation pathways are saturated, and how is it normally detoxified?
items.why: CYP2E1 converts excess paracetamol to NAPQI, which is detoxified by glutathione. When glutathione is depleted NAPQI binds hepatocytes, causing necrosis; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.
notes: Salicylate relates to aspirin, not paracetamol.
NAPQI is correct but glucuronidation is the saturated pathway; NAPQI is cleared by glutathione.
Acetaldehyde is an ethanol metabolite.

items.topic: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: four-pillar therapy (ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor), acute decompensation
items.stem: A 66-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 30%) is on perindopril and carvedilol, euvolaemic, K+ 4.3 mmol/L, eGFR 60. He remains NYHA II. Which addition is most appropriate?
items.why: Four-pillar therapy adds an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor, each reducing mortality and hospitalisation in HFrEF. Monitor potassium and renal function.
notes: Amlodipine is neutral in HFrEF and is not a pillar of therapy.
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are harmful in HFrEF.
Digoxin lacks mortality benefit and is not preferred over disease-modifying pillars.

items.topic: Personality disorders: borderline personality disorder, DBT, crisis management
items.stem: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) for borderline personality disorder aims to build which core skill set?
options: Distress tolerance and emotion regulation, balanced with acceptance and change
Free association to uncover repressed conflicts
Challenging cognitive distortions in depression only
items.why: DBT combines acceptance and change strategies, teaching mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness. It reduces self-harm in borderline personality disorder.
notes: Free association is a psychoanalytic technique, not DBT.
Graded exposure is used for phobias and anxiety disorders.
DBT is not limited to depression, and it emphasises validation as well as cognitive change.

items.topic: Myeloproliferative neoplasms: polycythaemia vera (JAK2), essential thrombocythaemia
items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a persistent platelet count of 900 x10^9/L, normal haemoglobin, and a CALR mutation. Why can she have both thrombosis and mucosal bleeding?
options: Acquired loss of large von Willebrand factor multimers by adsorption to excess platelets
Deficiency of factor VIII from consumption
items.why: In essential thrombocythaemia, extreme thrombocytosis (usually over 1000) causes acquired von Willebrand syndrome as large vWF multimers bind platelets and are cleaved, giving bleeding despite thrombotic risk.
notes: Factor VIII is not consumed in ET; the coagulation cascade is not primarily affected.
Anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies cause immune thrombocytopenia, not thrombocytosis.
Antithrombin excess is not a feature of ET.

items.topic: Bowel obstruction: small vs large bowel, adhesions, hernias, volvulus, conservative vs operative care
items.stem: A 68-year-old with prior laparotomy has colicky pain, vomiting and distension for 2 days. She is afebrile with a soft abdomen, no peritonism, normal lactate. CT shows adhesional SBO with transition point and no ischaemia. What is the next step?
options: Nasogastric tube, IV fluids and serial review
items.why: Uncomplicated adhesional SBO is managed conservatively: 'drip and suck' with serial examination. Operate for peritonism, ischaemia, strangulation or failure to resolve over about 48-72 hours.
notes: No peritonism or ischaemia, so surgery is not yet indicated.
Colonoscopic decompression is for colonic pseudo-obstruction or sigmoid volvulus.
Laxatives are inappropriate in complete obstruction and discharge is unsafe.

items.topic: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn's vs ulcerative colitis, acute severe colitis, extraintestinal features
items.stem: Which histological or distribution feature best distinguishes Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis?
options: Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum
items.why: Crohn's disease is transmural and patchy (skip lesions) anywhere from mouth to anus, with granulomas and fistulae. Ulcerative colitis is mucosal and continuous from the rectum.
notes: Continuous rectum-up disease is typical of ulcerative colitis.
Mucosal crypt abscesses are characteristic of ulcerative colitis.
Pseudopolyps and backwash ileitis are features of ulcerative colitis.

items.topic: Antiseizure drugs: valproate teratogenicity, enzyme induction, phenytoin levels
items.stem: A woman taking carbamazepine starts the combined oral contraceptive pill and becomes pregnant despite taking it correctly. Which mechanism best explains the contraception failure?
options: Induction of hepatic CYP3A4 increasing hormone metabolism
Inhibition of CYP2D6 reducing activation of ethinylestradiol
Displacement of hormones from albumin binding sites
Reduced gastric absorption of oral hormones
items.why: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and primidone induce CYP3A4, speeding clearance of oestrogen and progestogen. Contraceptive failure results, so use an LNG-IUD or medroxyprogesterone.
notes: CYP2D6 is not the main pathway for ethinylestradiol, and carbamazepine induces rather than inhibits enzymes.
Displacement is relevant to phenytoin and valproate interactions, not to this contraceptive failure.
Absorption is not meaningfully altered by carbamazepine.

items.topic: Antiseizure drugs: valproate teratogenicity, enzyme induction, phenytoin levels
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with generalised epilepsy, well controlled on valproate, asks about planning a pregnancy. What is the best advice about her antiseizure medication?
options: Continue valproate and add high-dose folate
Seek specialist review to change to a safer drug such as lamotrigine before conception
Continue valproate but reduce to the lowest dose only in the third trimester
items.why: Valproate carries the highest risk of major malformations (neural tube defects) and neurodevelopmental harm. Switch before conception under specialist guidance; lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred.
notes: Folate does not remove valproate's teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk.
Carbamazepine is also teratogenic and may worsen some generalised seizure types.
Organogenesis occurs in the first trimester, so late dose reduction misses the critical window.

items.topic: Hypoglycaemia: sulfonylurea and insulin causes, treatment, driving rules
items.stem: Which mechanism explains how sulfonylureas such as gliclazide lower blood glucose and can cause hypoglycaemia?
options: Block pancreatic beta-cell K-ATP channels, causing insulin release independent of glucose
Inhibit hepatic gluconeogenesis through AMPK activation
Inhibit DPP-4, prolonging incretin action in a glucose-dependent way
Block renal SGLT2, increasing urinary glucose loss
items.why: Sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels on beta cells, depolarising them and triggering insulin release regardless of glucose level, so hypoglycaemia can be prolonged.
notes: Describes metformin, which rarely causes hypoglycaemia alone.
Describes DPP-4 inhibitors, whose effect is glucose-dependent so hypoglycaemia is uncommon.
Describes SGLT2 inhibitors, which do not cause hypoglycaemia alone.

items.topic: Status epilepticus: benzodiazepine first, second-line agent, timeline
items.stem: Which mechanism explains why intravenous midazolam terminates status epilepticus?
options: Increased frequency of GABA-A chloride channel opening
items.why: Benzodiazepines bind the GABA-A receptor and increase the frequency of chloride channel opening, enhancing inhibition. This is why they are first-line in status epilepticus.
notes: Sodium channel blockade is the action of phenytoin and carbamazepine, not benzodiazepines.
NMDA antagonism is the action of ketamine, which is used only in refractory cases.
GABA transaminase inhibition is the action of vigabatrin.

items.topic: Rhabdomyolysis: CK, myoglobinuria, fluids, hyperkalaemia
items.stem: Which mechanism is the main cause of acute kidney injury in rhabdomyolysis?
options: Tubular obstruction and toxicity from myoglobin with renal vasoconstriction
Obstruction of the ureters by uric acid stones
Renal artery thrombosis from raised CK
items.why: Myoglobin precipitates with Tamm-Horsfall protein in acidic urine, causing tubular obstruction. Haem-mediated oxidative injury and volume depletion with vasoconstriction add to it.
notes: Glomerular immune complex disease is not the mechanism; the injury is tubular.
Uric acid release contributes, but ureteric stones are not the main mechanism.
CK is a marker of muscle injury and does not cause arterial thrombosis.

items.topic: Neonatal jaundice: physiological vs pathological, jaundice in the first 24 hours, phototherapy
items.stem: A term baby is visibly jaundiced at 14 hours of age. Mother is blood group O Rh positive. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Measure serum bilirubin urgently and assess for haemolysis
Reassure as physiological jaundice and review at day 3
Advise sunlight exposure and frequent feeds only
Wait for a transcutaneous reading at 48 hours
items.why: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise, commonly haemolysis such as ABO or Rh incompatibility. Measure serum bilirubin urgently with blood group, Coombs test and FBC.
notes: Physiological jaundice does not appear within 24 hours.
Sunlight is not recommended and delays assessment.
Delaying assessment risks missing rapidly rising bilirubin.

items.topic: Mosquito-borne viruses: Ross River, Barmah Forest, Murray Valley encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, dengue in north Queensland
items.stem: A 28-year-old returns to Cairns after an outbreak area visit with fever 4 days, retro-orbital pain, rash and platelets 60 x10^9/L. Which test is best on day 4 of illness?
items.why: In the first 5-7 days of illness, dengue NS1 antigen or PCR is best. IgG alone does not indicate acute infection.
notes: IgG alone cannot show acute infection.
Malaria should be excluded but a film alone does not diagnose dengue.
Weil-Felix is obsolete.

items.topic: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: sepsis and obstetric causes, coagulation profile
items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has a massive postpartum haemorrhage after placental abruption. She oozes from cannula sites. Which coagulation profile best fits DIC?
options: Low platelets, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT and APTT, very high D-dimer
Low platelets, normal fibrinogen, normal PT and APTT, normal D-dimer
Normal platelets, isolated prolonged APTT, normal fibrinogen
Normal platelets, prolonged PT only, normal D-dimer
items.why: DIC shows thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenaemia, prolonged PT/APTT and markedly raised D-dimer. Fibrinogen falls early and critically in obstetric haemorrhage.
