notes: Normal coagulation and D-dimer suggest ITP or gestational thrombocytopenia.
Isolated prolonged APTT suggests haemophilia, vWD or heparin effect.
Isolated prolonged PT suggests early warfarin effect or vitamin K deficiency.

items.topic: Occupational lung disease: silicosis from engineered stone (banned in Australia from July 2024), asbestosis and mesothelioma
items.stem: A 68-year-old retired laggard (insulation worker) has 3 months of right chest pain, weight loss and dyspnoea. CXR shows a large right pleural effusion with nodular pleural thickening. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.why: Asbestos exposure with latency of decades, chest pain, weight loss and nodular pleural thickening suggests mesothelioma. Confirm with pleural tissue biopsy.
notes: Asbestosis is basal interstitial fibrosis, not nodular pleural thickening with effusion.
Benign effusion is self-limiting, earlier after exposure, and lacks nodular thickening and weight loss.
Silicosis causes upper-zone nodules, not pleural malignancy.

items.topic: Lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, staging
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has painless cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats and 8 kg weight loss. CT shows nodes above and below the diaphragm. Biopsy shows Reed–Sternberg cells. What is the Ann Arbor stage?
items.why: Nodal disease on both sides of the diaphragm is stage III. Night sweats and weight loss over 10% are B symptoms, so suffix B.
notes: Stage II is nodal disease on one side of the diaphragm only.
Suffix A means no B symptoms, but she has night sweats and weight loss.
Stage IV needs diffuse or disseminated extranodal involvement (e.g. marrow, liver).

items.topic: Alcohol use disorder and withdrawal: AUDIT, withdrawal scales, thiamine before glucose, acamprosate and naltrexone
items.stem: A 52-year-old man with heavy daily drinking and poor nutrition presents confused, ataxic, with nystagmus. Blood glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. Intravenous glucose is available. What is the most appropriate order of treatment?
options: Glucose first, then thiamine once alert
Oral thiamine only, with glucose withheld
Diazepam first, then thiamine after 24 hours
items.why: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy needs parenteral thiamine before or with glucose, as glucose can precipitate or worsen it in thiamine deficiency. Do not delay treating hypoglycaemia.
notes: Giving glucose before thiamine risks precipitating or worsening Wernicke encephalopathy.
Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol use disorder, and hypoglycaemia still needs treatment.
Delaying thiamine 24 hours risks irreversible brain injury.

items.topic: Postpartum haemorrhage: the 4 Ts, uterotonics, escalation
items.stem: A woman has 800 mL blood loss after vaginal delivery from uterine atony. Bleeding continues despite fundal massage and oxytocin, and help has been called. Which additional drug reduces bleeding and should be given early?
items.why: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV, given within 3 hours of birth, reduces death from bleeding in PPH. Give it alongside uterotonics and escalation.
notes: Mefenamic acid is an NSAID that impairs platelet function and does not treat PPH.
Frusemide does not control bleeding.
Vitamin K treats deficiency coagulopathy, not atony.

items.topic: Transient ischaemic attack: urgent assessment, secondary prevention, carotid endarterectomy
items.stem: A 66-year-old man had 20 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech this morning, now fully resolved. ABCD2 score is 5. BP 150/85 mmHg, in sinus rhythm. CT brain is normal. What is the most appropriate management now?
options: Aspirin 100 mg and GP review in 2 weeks
Urgent same-day specialist assessment, with antiplatelet therapy and carotid imaging
Elective outpatient carotid duplex next month
items.why: TIA is a medical emergency with high early stroke risk. Start antiplatelet therapy, statin and BP management, and arrange urgent specialist assessment with brain and carotid imaging.
notes: A 2-week delay leaves him exposed to the highest early stroke risk, which is within days.
Delay to next month is inappropriate; symptomatic carotid stenosis needs imaging within days.
Anticoagulation is for AF or cardioembolic source, not shown here in sinus rhythm.

items.topic: Family and domestic violence and elder abuse: asking safely, safety planning, reporting
items.stem: A GP suspects a patient is experiencing intimate partner violence. Which approach to raising the topic best reflects the principles of safe enquiry?
options: Ask directly in private, without the partner present, using non-judgemental questions
Ask with the partner in the room so both sides can be heard
Wait until the patient volunteers the information themselves
Ask through the partner's family member acting as interpreter
items.why: Enquiry about violence should be direct, non-judgemental and in private, with a professional interpreter if needed. Never ask in front of a partner or family member.
notes: The partner may be the perpetrator; asking in their presence risks the patient's safety and prevents honest disclosure.
Many patients will not disclose unprompted; clinicians should ask when indicators are present.
Family members should not interpret; use a professional interpreter and ask in private.

items.topic: Spinal and limb trauma: C-spine clearance (NEXUS, Canadian C-spine), Ottawa ankle and knee rules
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman inverted her ankle playing netball. She can take four steps. There is no bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, but she has tenderness over the navicular. What is the best next step?
options: Discharge with RICE; no imaging needed
items.why: Ottawa foot rules: imaging is needed for pain in the midfoot zone with tenderness at the navicular, base of 5th metatarsal, or inability to walk four steps. Her ankle series criteria are negative, so a foot X-ray is indicated.
notes: Navicular tenderness meets the Ottawa foot rule, so imaging is required.
Malleolar tenderness is absent, so ankle films are not indicated.
MRI is not a first-line test after injury.

items.topic: Pneumothorax: primary vs secondary, tension physiology, observe vs aspirate vs drain
items.stem: A 30-year-old man has blunt chest trauma. He is hypotensive (70/40), HR 140, SpO2 85%, with absent right breath sounds, tracheal deviation to the left and distended neck veins. What is the immediate management?
options: Right needle decompression then intercostal catheter
items.why: This is a clinical diagnosis of tension pneumothorax: decompress immediately without imaging, then insert an intercostal catheter. Positive pressure ventilation would worsen it.
notes: Delaying for imaging is dangerous in obstructive shock.
Positive pressure ventilation before decompression can worsen the tension.
Fluids do not relieve the obstruction to venous return.

items.topic: Macrocytic anaemia: B12 vs folate deficiency, pernicious anaemia, alcohol
items.stem: In pernicious anaemia, B12 deficiency results from loss of which substance, normally produced by gastric parietal cells?
items.why: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells (and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies) removes intrinsic factor, which is needed for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
notes: Acid helps release food-bound B12, but its loss alone does not abolish absorption; intrinsic factor is essential.
Pepsinogen is from chief cells and is not required for B12 absorption.
Transcobalamin II is a plasma carrier made elsewhere, not by parietal cells.

items.topic: Early pregnancy bleeding: ectopic pregnancy (beta-hCG, ultrasound, methotrexate), miscarriage
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 6 weeks' amenorrhoea has mild left iliac fossa pain and light bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable. Serum beta-hCG is 2500 IU/L, and transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a 2 cm left adnexal mass with no fetal heartbeat. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Intramuscular methotrexate if suitable, with follow-up of hCG
items.why: A stable woman with a small unruptured ectopic, no fetal heartbeat and a low hCG is suitable for methotrexate, with hCG monitoring. Surgery is for instability or rupture.
notes: Waiting 2 weeks is unsafe with a visible adnexal mass; rupture is possible.
Curettage treats intrauterine failed pregnancy; it will not treat a tubal ectopic.
Laparotomy is for haemodynamic instability or rupture, which she does not have.

items.topic: Lung cancer: presentations, paraneoplastic syndromes, National Lung Cancer Screening Program (LDCT for 50-70 with 30+ pack-years, from July 2025)
items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker has right-sided ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and shoulder pain radiating down the inner arm. Where is the most likely lesion?
options: Apical (Pancoast) tumour of the right lung
items.why: A Pancoast tumour invades the sympathetic chain (Horner syndrome) and the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1 pain). Contrast with SVC syndrome, which gives facial swelling and venous distension.
notes: Hilar nodes do not typically involve the sympathetic chain or lower brachial plexus.
A central bronchial tumour causes cough, haemoptysis or collapse, not Horner syndrome.
SVC obstruction gives facial plethora and distended neck veins, not Horner syndrome.

items.topic: Antenatal care and screening: booking tests, combined first-trimester screening and NIPT, RhD immunoprophylaxis
items.stem: Non-invasive prenatal testing analyses cell-free fetal DNA in maternal plasma from about 10 weeks. Which tissue is the main source of this DNA?
items.why: Cell-free 'fetal' DNA comes mainly from apoptotic placental trophoblast cells, so it reflects the placenta. This explains confined placental mosaicism causing false positives.
notes: Fetal nucleated red cells are rare in maternal blood and are not the main source of cell-free DNA.
Fetal lung epithelium is not a significant source of DNA in maternal plasma.
Amniotic fluid cells are obtained by amniocentesis, not shed into maternal plasma.

items.topic: First seizure and epilepsy: investigation, antiseizure drug choice, Austroads driving rules, valproate in women
items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has newly diagnosed genetic generalised epilepsy with myoclonic jerks. She has no contraception and may plan pregnancy. Which antiseizure medicine is the most appropriate first choice?
items.why: Lamotrigine is the preferred broad-spectrum option for women of childbearing potential. Valproate carries a high risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental harm, and should be avoided unless other options fail.
notes: Valproate is highly teratogenic and is a last-line choice in women who may become pregnant.
Carbamazepine can worsen myoclonic seizures in generalised epilepsy and is also teratogenic.
Phenytoin is a narrow-spectrum drug with teratogenic risk and is not suitable for generalised epilepsy.

items.topic: Eating disorders: anorexia nervosa medical admission criteria, refeeding syndrome
items.stem: A severely malnourished patient with anorexia nervosa is started on aggressive nutrition. Which mechanism best explains the hypophosphataemia that develops in refeeding syndrome?
options: Insulin surge drives phosphate into cells for glycolysis and ATP synthesis
Increased renal phosphate excretion from glucagon excess
Reduced gut absorption from raised gastric pH
Phosphate binding to newly formed bone mineral
items.why: Carbohydrate refeeding raises insulin, which drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and increases phosphorylated intermediates. Total body stores were already depleted, so serum levels fall sharply.
notes: Glucagon falls with feeding and insulin rises; the main problem is intracellular shift, not renal loss.
Gut absorption is not the main issue; the fall happens within days of feeding because of cellular uptake.
Bone remodelling is not rapid enough to explain the acute fall in serum phosphate.

items.topic: Prescribing in older adults: polypharmacy, deprescribing, anticholinergic burden, drugs that cause falls
items.stem: An 84-year-old woman in residential care has had two falls this month. She takes oxybutynin, temazepam, oxycodone and paracetamol. She has mild confusion and constipation. Which change best reduces her anticholinergic burden and fall risk first?
options: Increase the temazepam dose to improve sleep
Add a laxative and continue all current medicines
Add donepezil to treat the confusion
Stop oxybutynin and plan gradual benzodiazepine deprescribing
items.why: Oxybutynin is strongly anticholinergic and contributes to confusion, constipation and falls. Benzodiazepines and opioids also raise fall risk; taper benzodiazepines gradually.
notes: Increasing a benzodiazepine will worsen sedation and falls.
Treating the adverse effects with more drugs perpetuates a prescribing cascade.
Adding donepezil for drug-induced confusion is a prescribing cascade, and cholinesterase inhibitors oppose anticholinergics.

items.topic: Headache: subarachnoid haemorrhage red flags, migraine treatment and prophylaxis, medication-overuse headache
items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with migraine takes paracetamol-codeine on 18 days a month for headache, which is now daily and worse. Neurological examination is normal. What is the best management?
options: Increase codeine dose for headache control
Withdraw the overused analgesic and start migraine prophylaxis
Order MRI brain to exclude a tumour
items.why: This is medication-overuse headache (opioid-containing analgesics on 10 or more days a month). Withdraw the agent with education and start prophylaxis such as amitriptyline, propranolol or candesartan.
notes: More opioid perpetuates medication-overuse headache.
Regular simple NSAIDs risk further overuse headache and GI harm.
Normal examination and typical history do not need imaging first-line.
